In the Gaussian-integral representation the latter power follows by integrating a third Gaussian derivative in heat time. `lerayKernelBound_holds` proves this first-order estimate componentwise, not all the estimates for $l\ge0$.

adapted.N2-04.2.Breakdown.FarField.lerayKernelBound_hold: The undifferentiated tensor has an order-three bound, which alone would not give spatial integrability in dimension three. A single derivative gives order four and the radial tail $\int_R^\infty r^{-2}dr$. `lerayKernelBound_holds` concerns this first derivative at positive lag, not the estimate for all orders in (3.9).

ns-s3-oseen-scaling.Breakdown.FarField.kernelScaling_holds: Differentiating the tensor scaling gives $\partial_k(O_{\mu\tau})_{ij}(\sqrt\mu x)=\mu^{-2}\partial_k(O_\tau)_{ij}(x)$. In the Gaussian-integral construction the third derivative gains $\mu^{-3}$ and the heat-time integration gains $\mu$, giving the same $\mu^{-2}$ as the first Gaussian derivative. The linked theorem proves these derivative and Gaussian scaling laws, not the scaling of the undifferentiated Oseen tensor.

ns-s3-oseen-lp-scaling.Breakdown.FarField.kernelScaling_holds: Taking $x=\sqrt\tau y$ gives $\nabla O_\tau(x)=\tau^{-2}\nabla O_1(y)$ and $dx=\tau^{3/2}dy$. The $p$th root gives the factor $\tau^{-2+3/(2p)}$ for finite $p$, with $\tau^{-2}$ for $p=\infty$. The linked theorem supplies the pointwise scaling of the derivative components; the norm calculation uses their $L^p$ finiteness (boundedness when $p=\infty$) at positive time.
ns-s3-oseen-lp-scaling.Breakdown.FarField.kernelL1Bound_holds: At $p=1$ the radial integral bounding each derivative component is proportional to $\int_0^\infty r^2(r+\sqrt\tau)^{-4}dr=\tau^{-1/2}\int_0^\infty s^2(1+s)^{-4}ds$. Its finiteness gives the $L^1$ convolution bound and its time singularity is integrable at zero. The linked theorem proves this componentwise bound, rather than the exact scaling equality for all $p$.

ns-s3-derivative-convolution-definition.Breakdown.FarField.kernelConv: For $u,v\in X$, the tensor $F=u\otimes v$ belongs to $L^3$ by (3.1). At a fixed $\tau>0$, (3.9) gives $\nabla O_\tau\in L^{3/2}$, so the integral defining `kernelConv` is absolutely convergent at each $x$, with bound $C\|\nabla O_\tau\|_{3/2}\|F\|_3$. In particular the second formula of (3.10) does not require $F\in W^{1,1}$ as in the first.

ns-s3-tensor-product.Breakdown.FarField.tensorField: The divergence is taken in the second index: $\operatorname{div}(v\otimes u)_j=\sum_m\partial_m(v_j u_m)=(u\cdot\nabla)v_j+v_j\operatorname{div}u$. Thus the order of the factors is reversed relative to the advection notation. Symmetrization in (3.10) includes both orders.

ns-s3-convolution-mixed-inputs.Breakdown.FarField.BilinKernel: The formal identity `BilinKernel` is stated on the diagonal: $K(\tau)(u,u)=-\nabla O_\tau*(u\otimes u)$ almost everywhere. Subtract the identities for $u$ and $v$ from the one for $u+v$. On the left this leaves $2K(\tau)(u,v)$, by symmetry, and on the right it leaves $-\nabla O_\tau*(u\otimes v+v\otimes u)$.
ns-s3-convolution-mixed-inputs.Breakdown.FarField.bilinKernel_of_test_d: The paper's $L^{6/5}$ kernel estimate gives convergence in $L^6$. For the formal proof one may use $L^{3/2}$ instead: Hölder bounds the supremum of the difference of convolutions by the $L^3$ norm of the difference of the tensors times the kernel norm. The velocities converge in $L^6$, hence along a subsequence almost everywhere. This identifies the limits at fixed positive lag. The identity and decay on test fields are hypotheses of the extension theorem.

ns-s3-compact-monodromy.Breakdown.MonodromyStatement: In the period map the initial datum is varied, while the reference $u^*(t')$ in the mixed integral is fixed at each $t'$. Lemma 3.2 gives norm-null integrands for weakly null linearized trajectories, and (3.7) gives an integrable majorant. For the formal short-step proof, fix a test factor $f$ and truncate the last $\epsilon$ units, at cost $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$. At the remaining lags use $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)=G(\tau-\epsilon)K(\epsilon)(f,\cdot)$: the heat images of the compact closure at lag $\epsilon$ have compact closure over the bounded time interval. Approximation of the continuous coefficient curve by finite sums of such factors gives compactness of the mixed endpoint integral. The full return is obtained by composing short steps.

ns-s3-compactness-lemma.Breakdown.Freq.bilinCompact_holds: The conclusion concerns the global $X$ norm, even though the proof uses compactness on a ball. The linked `BilinCompact` requires the first factor to belong to `testSpan`, a dense subspace; this already suffices for `HasCompactKernel` in the period-map construction. The all-$X$ version follows by the operator-norm approximation in the next paragraph.

ns-s3-compactness-advection-formula.Breakdown.Freq.bilinTestFormula_holds: For $q=2\pi|\xi|$, the norm of the multiplier from $F_v$ to the gradient of $K(\tau)(\varphi,v)$ is bounded by $q^2 e^{-\tau q^2}/2\le1/(2\tau)$. Also $\|F_v\|_2\le2\|\varphi\|_\infty\|v\|_{L^2(B)}$. Thus $\|K(\tau)(\varphi,v)\|_X\le\tau^{-1}\|\varphi\|_\infty\|v\|_{L^2(B)}$. Writing the advection as a divergence has removed the need for strong convergence of $\nabla v$. The formal Fourier identity uses the advection $\operatorname{div}F_v$ itself.

adapted.N2-05.1.Breakdown.Freq.bilinCompact_holds: On $B$ the $L^2$ norm of $v$ is controlled by $|B|^{1/3}\|v\|_6$, so weak convergence in $X$ gives weak convergence in $H^1(B)$ and Rellich gives strong convergence in $L^2(B)$. This is sufficient for the displayed estimate. Lean uses a Fourier proof instead: the supported advections are uniformly bounded in $L^2$, their Fourier transforms are equicontinuous on bounded frequency sets, and positive-lag smoothing controls the tails. `BilinCompact` has the dense-test first-factor hypothesis; operator-norm closure gives the printed extension.

adapted.N2-06.1.Breakdown.HeatBilinear: For $\tau>1$ the heat-shift law gives $K(\tau)=G(\tau-1)K(1)$, hence $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K$. Thus even though the formal power bound is assumed only for $0<\tau\le1$, the time integral remains finite on every bounded interval. The actual paper estimate decays also for $\tau>1$.

pdf-item-equation-3-11.Breakdown.HeatBilinear: The continuity is strong, i.e. for each fixed datum $\chi$; a norm estimate on $e^{t\Delta}-I$ at $t=0$ is unnecessary. For a continuous free trajectory on $[a,b]$ its supremum norm is exactly $\|\chi\|_{\mathcal X}$, since the contraction bound is attained at $a$.

pdf-item-equation-3-12.Breakdown.HeatBilinear: The first identity concerns the output of $K(\tau)$ with its two arguments held fixed. It will allow the part of a time integral before a new initial time to be included in the new datum. For the second identity Lean only assumes the bound for $0<\tau\le1$; writing $K(\tau)=G(\tau-1)K(1)$ for $\tau>1$ gives the bound $C_K$ there. The integrable majorant needed below is therefore available on every finite interval.

ns-3late-abstract-mild.Breakdown.HeatBilinear.IsMildOn: On $[a,b)$, each integral in (2.4) only involves the compact interval $[a,t]$, $t<b$, on which the two inputs are bounded in $\mathcal X$. Thus the integral is well defined even when $\|u(t)\|_{\mathcal X}$ is unbounded as $t\uparrow b$. There is no initial assumption of a classical velocity or pressure.
ns-3late-abstract-mild.Breakdown.HeatBilinear.IsMildOnIcc: On $[a,b]$ the same identity holds at $b$ with a value $u(b)$ in $\mathcal X$. A solution on $[a,b)$ that extends continuously in $\mathcal X$ to $b$ satisfies the closed-interval identity by Lemma 3.3. Boundedness without such a limit is not what the definition requires.

ns-3late-lemma-3-3.Breakdown.VarConstIntegralStatement: If $M,N$ bound the input curves, the part of the integral where $0<t-t'<h\le1$ has $\mathcal X$ norm at most $4C_KMN h^{1/4}$. The bound is uniform in the output time. Thus the singular upper endpoint can be omitted and then restored in the norm of $\mathcal X$; one need not first find a pointwise spatial integral.
ns-3late-lemma-3-3.Breakdown.varConstIntegral: Put $T=b-a$ and change variables to $\tau=t-t\prime$. Extend the inputs by their endpoint values and integrate $K(\tau)(u(t-\tau),v(t-\tau))$ over $(0,T)$ with the indicator of $\tau<t-a$. For a fixed positive $\tau\ne t-a$ the integrand is continuous in $t$. Its norm has a common integrable majorant, $C_KMN\tau^{-3/4}$ up to lag one and $C_KMN$ thereafter in Lean. Dominated convergence proves continuity also at $a,b$.

ns-3late-lemma-3-4-equation.Breakdown.PieceOperatorStatement: The mixed term in the expansion at $f$ of $K(\tau)(f+h,f+h)$ is $2K(\tau)(f,h)$. Its time integral is linear in $h$ and its size need not be small. The source $g$ may be any continuous curve: setting $t=a$ gives $h(a)=g(a)$. `PieceOperatorStatement` supplies the bounded time-integral map and the free-heat map on a short interval.
ns-3late-lemma-3-4-equation.Breakdown.pieceOperator: On an interval of length $T\le1$ the operator $Ah=2\int_a^t K(t-t')(f(t'),h(t'))dt'$ has norm at most $8C_KT^{1/4}\|f\|_C$. Thus any bounded $f$ can be treated on sufficiently short intervals. This is the local bound used in Lean to invert $I-A$; Appendix A.1 instead changes the norm on the entire interval.
ns-3late-lemma-3-4-equation.Breakdown.Periodic.InverseAlgebra.Intern: The paper makes $A:h\mapsto2\int_a^t K(t-t')(f(t'),h(t'))dt'$ small without changing the length of the interval. The exponential weight in Appendix A.1 gives $\|A\|_\beta\le2C_K\|f\|_C\int_0^\infty e^{-\beta\tau}\tau^{-3/4}d\tau=2C_K\|f\|_C\Gamma(1/4)\beta^{-1/4}$. For sufficiently large $\beta$, $h=(I-A)^{-1}g$. The linked identity is the algebraic verification of this solution once $I-A$ has been proved invertible.

ns-3late-lemma-3-4-bound.Breakdown.Periodic.InverseAlgebra.Intern: For the weighted norm choose $q<1$ bounding the norm of the linear integral operator. The geometric series gives $\|(I-A)^{-1}\|_\beta\le(1-q)^{-1}$. Since $\|h\|_\beta\le\|h\|_\infty\le e^{\beta(b-a)}\|h\|_\beta$, the unweighted bound is $\|h\|_\infty\le e^{\beta(b-a)}(1-q)^{-1}\|g\|_\infty$. This is a bound for a fixed finite interval and fixed $f$, not a uniform bound over all $f$ or interval lengths.

pdf-item-theorem-3-5.Breakdown.RestrictStatement: The first assertion concerns any continuous inputs $f,h$, not necessarily solutions. The integral before $m$ is transported forward by the heat flow, as is its initial heat term. This is also the restart identity needed for a linearized trajectory with a free heat datum. `RestrictStatement` treats the quadratic case $f=h=u$.
pdf-item-theorem-3-5.Breakdown.restrict: Evolve the equation at $m$ by $e^{(t-m)\Delta}$. The free term becomes $e^{(t-a)\Delta}u(a)$ and the integral becomes $\int_a^m K(t-t')(f(t'),h(t'))dt'$ by (3.12). Subtract these terms from the equation at $t$. The only surviving integral is over $[m,t]$.
pdf-item-theorem-3-5.Breakdown.UniqueStatement: On a half-open interval the uniqueness assertion follows by comparing the two curves on $[a,t]$ for each $t<b$. The supremum norms needed for the proof are finite on these compact intervals, even if neither curve is bounded up to $b$. `UniqueStatement` includes both interval conventions.
pdf-item-theorem-3-5.Breakdown.mildUnique: Let $M=\max(\|u\|_C,\|v\|_C)$ on the closed interval. On a restarted interval of length $h\le1$, the difference with zero initial value is bounded in supremum norm by $8C_KMh^{1/4}$ times itself. Choose $h$ so this factor is less than one. In Lean one uses the same $h$ for a finite succession of restarts; the printed proof uses Lemma 3.4 on the whole interval.

pdf-item-equation-3-13.Breakdown.RestrictStatement: For $t'<m$, $e^{(t-m)\Delta}K(m-t')(f(t'),h(t'))=K(t-t')(f(t'),h(t'))$. This equality, with the arguments evaluated at the same earlier time $t'$, is why the past integral can be included in the new datum. At $t'=m$ the value of the integrand has no effect on the Bochner integral.
pdf-item-equation-3-13.Breakdown.restrict: To move the heat operator through the integral, one uses boundedness of $e^{(t-m)\Delta}$ on $\mathcal X$ and Bochner integrability from Lemma 3.3. The upper endpoint $t'=m$ of the earlier integral is a null set, so (3.12) is only needed at positive lag. `restrict` implements the identity when both inputs are the solution.

ns-3late-lemma-3-5-unique.Breakdown.UniqueStatement: For $d=u-v$, symmetry gives $K(\tau)(u,u)-K(\tau)(v,v)=K(\tau)(u+v,d)$. The free terms cancel when the initial values agree. Lemma 3.4 with $f=(u+v)/2$ and $g=0$ then gives $d=0$. In particular there is no smallness requirement on either solution.
ns-3late-lemma-3-5-unique.Breakdown.mildUnique: The inverse for the difference equation is used only to show that its kernel is zero. For the formal proof it suffices to choose a common step length from the supremum bounds of the two known solutions. The difference vanishes on the first step, and hence its datum on the second step is zero as well; no condition on the size of the original datum is needed.

ns-3late-restart-consequence.Breakdown.restrict: The datum after a restart is the value of the same solution, so both uniqueness and estimates can be applied on an interval chosen for the time of interest. In §7.10 one takes $m=2t-1$ for an ancient solution, making the heat interval have length $1-t$ and keeping the similarity scale comparable throughout it.

adapted.N2-07.2.Breakdown.Freq.mild_holds: The time integrals agree first for $t<b$ in distributions, hence in $X$. At $b$ the free heat term, the nonlinear Bochner integral and the given curve all have limits in $X$. Equality passes to those limits. `mild_holds` already states the closed-interval conclusion for its more restrictive weak-solution class.

ns-3late-weak-assumptions.Breakdown.Freq.IsWeakSolution: In the weak equation the pressure drops out against compact solenoidal tests. The paper assumes continuity in $X$ and (3.14). In `IsWeakSolution` one also requires smooth decaying slices and $u(t)-u(t')\in L^2$ for every pair of times, with $\|u(t)-u(t_0)\|_2\to0$ as $t\to t_0$ within the interval. The difference condition permits infinite energy of the slices themselves.
ns-3late-weak-assumptions.Breakdown.Freq.MildOfWeak: The weak equation gives the derivative of scalar test pairings, while (2.4) gives an equality of velocities in $X$. It is the latter that permits uniqueness against the mild trajectories of Lemma 3.5. `MildOfWeak` has the same type of conclusion on $[a,b]$, under the stronger hypotheses of `IsWeakSolution`.
ns-3late-weak-assumptions.Breakdown.Freq.mild_holds: Lean proves the identity by a backward heat test. Test the weak equation first with $-\Delta\psi$ to obtain an equation in the gradient pairing of $X$, then extend it by graph-norm density to heat-smoothed tests. For a fixed terminal time $t$ and $\varepsilon>0$, use $e^{(t-s+\varepsilon)\Delta}\psi$ at time $s$. Differentiation in $s$ produces $-\Delta$ on this test, cancelling the diffusion in the weak equation. The derivative of the pairing is then $\langle K(t-s+\varepsilon)(u(s),u(s)),\psi\rangle_X$. Integrate over $[a,t]$. The positive terminal lag permits all the test derivatives even at $s=t$. This proof uses the additional hypotheses of `IsWeakSolution`.

ns-3late-weak-equation.Breakdown.Freq.IsWeakSolution:
The linear term in (3.14) is $\int u\cdot\Delta\psi=-\int
abla u:
abla\psi$. For the nonlinear term integrate $\sum_{i,j}u_i u_j\partial_i\psi_j$ by parts; since $\operatorname{div}u=0$, the result is $-\int (u\cdot
abla)u\cdot\psi$. These are the two negative terms in `IsWeakSolution`, where the scalar derivative is required in the interior and the pairings are continuous up to both endpoints.

ns-3late-tensor-contraction.Breakdown.advectionPairing: Here $(u\otimes u):\nabla\psi=\sum_{i,j}u_i u_j\partial_i\psi_j$. In the integral move $\partial_i$ onto $u_i u_j$; the term with $\partial_i u_i$ vanishes on summation. The remaining term is the negative of `advectionPairing`, which integrates $(u\cdot\nabla)u\cdot\psi$. Compact support of $\psi$ removes the boundary term.

ns-3late-weak-to-mild.Breakdown.Freq.MildOfWeak: Once the scalar test identity gives (2.4), the same datum $u(a)$ and the same curve in $X$ can be used in the restart and uniqueness lemmas. No separate existence problem for a mild solution is being solved. The formal `MildOfWeak` makes this identification for the smooth-decay class with continuous $L^2$ differences.
ns-3late-weak-to-mild.Breakdown.Freq.mild_holds: Put $Z=u(t)-G(t-a)u(a)-\int_a^t K(t-s)(u(s),u(s))ds$. In `varConst_inner` take the terminal test $G(\varepsilon)Z$. Self-adjointness of $G$ and the heat-shift law identify the shifted nonlinear integral with the pairing of the ordinary Bochner integral against this test. Hence $\langle Z,G(\varepsilon)Z\rangle_X=0$. As $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, strong continuity gives $\|Z\|_X^2=0$. This argument includes $t=b$, under the hypotheses of `IsWeakSolution`.

pdf-item-equation-3-15.Breakdown.Periodic.V: Formula (3.15) has weight $4\pi^2|k|^2$ because differentiation multiplies the coefficient by $2\pi i k$; the factor $L^3$ restores the cell volume. `V` stores the coefficients for period one with weight $1+4\pi^2|k|^2$ in the squared norm. Its extra term measures $\|u\|_2^2$, so the zero mode is allowed.
pdf-item-equation-3-15.Breakdown.Periodic.weight: The additional $1$ in `weight` gives the velocity contribution $\|u\|_2^2$ to the squared $H^1$ norm. At $n=0$ this is the entire weight. It is for this reason that `V` can include constants whereas (3.15) defines a norm only with the mean-zero condition.
pdf-item-equation-3-15.Breakdown.Periodic.norm_sq_eq_tsum: The identity `norm_sq_eq_tsum` follows by cancelling the inverse square root in `coeff`: $\sum_k w(k)|a(k)/\sqrt{w(k)}|^2=\sum_k|a(k)|^2$. This is an identity for every element of the sequence space; identifying it with the integral of the physical $H^1$ norm of a smooth field uses the Fourier realization. In the paper the corresponding sum has only the gradient weight and includes the cell volume.

pdf-item-equation-3-16.Breakdown.Periodic.weight: For a nonzero unit-torus frequency $k$, the ratio of the inhomogeneous to the homogeneous squared weight is $1+(4\pi^2|k|^2)^{-1}\le1+(4\pi^2)^{-1}$. This proves (3.16) after removing $k=0$. The linked `weight` takes value one at that frequency; without mean zero the upper bound in (3.16) would fail even for a constant velocity.
pdf-item-equation-3-16.Breakdown.Periodic.norm_sq_eq_tsum: On a mean-zero torus of period $L$, Parseval gives $\|u\|_2^2\le L^2/(4\pi^2)\|\nabla u\|_2^2$. Thus the constant comparing the squared inhomogeneous and homogeneous norms is $1+L^2/(4\pi^2)$. The paper keeps the homogeneous norm until the period has been reduced to one, avoiding this growing factor. `norm_sq_eq_tsum` gives the inhomogeneous Fourier sum at that final period.

ns-3late-periodic-heat-multiplier.Breakdown.Periodic.heat: On the stored sequence, `heat` multiplies each coefficient by $e^{-4\pi^2t|k|^2}$ for $t\ge0$. The weight commutes with this multiplier, so ordinary Fourier coefficients evolve in exactly the same way. The zero frequency is unchanged. The formal definition uses $\max(t,0)$ for all real $t$.

ns-3late-periodic-force.Breakdown.Periodic.forceV: For $\tau>0$ the weighted coefficients of `forceV` are $\sqrt{1+4\pi^2|k|^2}\,e^{-4\pi^2\tau|k|^2}\mathbb P_k\hat f(k)$. Boundedness of $\hat f(k)$ for integrable $f$ and Gaussian decay make this an $\ell^2$ sequence. Unlike the paper’s homogeneous estimate for mean-zero sources, the formal source operator allows a constant source: its zero coefficient is unchanged at positive lag. Its value at nonpositive lag is set to zero, not the source itself.

pdf-item-equation-3-17.Breakdown.Periodic.kernel: The coefficient of $(u\cdot\nabla)v$ at $k$ is $\sum_j(2\pi i\,j\cdot\hat u(k-j))\hat v(j)$. At $k=0$ every summand vanishes by solenoidality of $\hat u(-j)$. This gives the mean-zero property directly in the Fourier representation, even though `V` allows constants. `kernel` adds the expression with the inputs reversed and multiplies its projected heat evolution by $-1/2$, as in (3.17).
pdf-item-equation-3-17.Breakdown.Periodic.kernel_symm: Because $K_{\mathbb T}$ is symmetric, the cross terms in $K_{\mathbb T}(u^{\mathrm a}+z,u^{\mathrm a}+z)$ combine to $2K_{\mathbb T}(u^{\mathrm a},z)$. The linearized operator in (6.6) contains this term with a minus sign; the term with both inputs $z$ is the quadratic remainder. `kernel_symm` follows directly from the symmetrized convolution.

ns-3late-periodic-mild.Breakdown.Periodic.IsMildOn: The formula (2.4) is imposed at every time in the half-open interval. The upper integration endpoint has zero heat lag; the kernel is only needed at positive lag almost everywhere in the integral. `IsMildOn` requires integrability and continuity of the trajectory on $[a,b)$, without prescribing a limiting velocity at $b$.
ns-3late-periodic-mild.Breakdown.Periodic.IsMildOnIcc: The endpoint value is needed in order to restart the mild equation. `IsMildOnIcc` requires the equation and continuity at both endpoints of an ordinary interval, whereas no value at the singular time is required by `IsMildOn`. When consecutive pieces of a physical curve are normalized by $\mu_n^{1/4}$ and $\mu_{n+1}^{1/4}$, their endpoint values must differ by $\lambda^{1/4}$, not be equal.

ns-3late-periodic-heat-laws.Breakdown.Periodic.heat_zero: At $t=a$ in (2.4) the integration interval has length zero. The free evolution must return the datum, which is precisely `heat_zero`: each Fourier multiplier is one, including at frequency zero.
ns-3late-periodic-heat-laws.Breakdown.Periodic.heat_add: To restart at $c\in(a,t)$, split the Duhamel integral at $c$. By `heat_add`, the contribution of the datum at time $a$ evolves as $e^{(t-c)\Delta}e^{(c-a)\Delta}u(a)$. With the kernel shift the part of the integral up to $c$ has the same factor $e^{(t-c)\Delta}$; together these terms equal $e^{(t-c)\Delta}u(c)$. The heat identity is required only for nonnegative lags.
ns-3late-periodic-heat-laws.Breakdown.Periodic.norm_heat_le: The squared norm is a sum of nonnegative weighted mode contributions; multiplying each mode by a number of modulus at most one cannot increase it. `norm_heat_le` proves contractivity in `V`; the paper uses the same argument with gradient weights. In Lean the identity extension at negative time is also contractive.
ns-3late-periodic-heat-laws.Breakdown.Periodic.heat_continuousOn: For $t\to t_0$ each Fourier multiplier converges, and the squared difference at frequency $n$ is bounded by $4|a(n)|^2$ for the stored sequence $a$. This majorant is summable. `heat_continuousOn` thus gives strong continuity at zero without additional smoothness of the datum.

s3-periodic-sobolev-proof-dependency.Breakdown.Periodic.kernelSharpBound_hold: The two factors of the advection have norms in $L^6$ and $L^2$, giving $1/6+1/2=2/3$. To bound their product in $L^{3/2}$ by two gradient norms uniformly in the period one needs precisely (3.18). A bound in terms of two inhomogeneous norms followed by Poincaré would not give such a uniform constant. The linked formal kernel estimate uses the full $H^1$ norm at unit period.

pdf-item-equation-3-18.Breakdown.Periodic.TrigHs: For (3.18) the exponent $6$ is the one for which scaling the cell and scaling the gradient have the same effect. The formal starting point `TrigHs` is different: it bounds finite complex Fourier sums in $L^6$ using the full weight $1+4\pi^2|k|^2$. In particular it applies without removing the constant coefficient.
pdf-item-equation-3-18.Breakdown.Periodic.trigHs: To prove the unit-cell bound in `trigHs`, multiply the periodically extended trigonometric polynomial by a fixed compact bump equal to one on the cell and apply the whole-space Sobolev inequality. The derivative of the bump costs a velocity $L^2$ term, while differentiating the polynomial costs its gradient. The integrals extend over only finitely many cells, giving the desired full $H^1$ bound with a fixed constant.

pdf-item-theorem-3-7.Breakdown.Periodic.ShellTorus.Internal.s: In `sourceOp_threeHalves` the source $A$ is inserted as $A((x-a)/\sqrt\mu)$, with no amplitude change. Its $L^{3/2}$ norm is multiplied by $\mu$, and the heat lag $\mu\tau$ costs $(\mu\tau)^{-3/4}$; the resulting factor is $\mu^{1/4}$. The interaction operator used below includes the inverse factor $\mu^{-1/4}$, so its bound is uniform in the scale. The formal estimate takes supported $L^2$ sources and $0<\mu\tau\le1$, unlike the unrestricted positive lags of (3.19).
pdf-item-theorem-3-7.Breakdown.Periodic.Forced.Internal.force: For a fixed source $f$, advancing its projected heat response at positive lag $\sigma$ by an additional $t\ge0$ gives the response at lag $t+\sigma$. In `forceV_eq_heat` the same Fourier coefficient is multiplied by two Gaussians whose exponents add. The restriction $\sigma>0$ matters: the formal response is set to zero at lag zero, where the source itself need not be an $H^1$ field.
pdf-item-theorem-3-7.Breakdown.Periodic.SourceCont.Internal.f: At a fixed positive lag $\tau_0$, each nearby coefficient is bounded by a constant times $\sqrt{w(k)}e^{-2\pi^2\tau_0|k|^2}$; its square is summable. Thus coefficientwise convergence implies convergence in `V`, giving `forceV_continuousOn`. No continuity at lag zero is needed for the mild integral, where the bound (3.19) controls the short-lag contribution.
pdf-item-theorem-3-7.Breakdown.Periodic.kernelSharpBound_hold: The nonlinear source has mean zero because it is the divergence of $v\otimes u+u\otimes v$. Its $L^{3/2}$ norm is bounded by $\|u\|_6\|\nabla v\|_2+\|v\|_6\|\nabla u\|_2$. Inserting this into (3.19) and using (3.18) gives (3.20), including the factor $1/2$ in (3.17). The formal proof uses a Fourier trilinear bound and polarization to give the analogous operator estimate on `V`, for $0<\tau\le1$.

ns-3late-periodic-force-bound.Breakdown.Periodic.ShellTorus.Internal.s: In the formal estimate the dual test is $(1-\Delta)e^{\mu\tau\Delta}z$, where $z$ is the projected heat response, since the norm includes the velocity square. The two bounds used to interpolate its $L^3$ norm are of orders $(\mu\tau)^{-1/2}$ and $(\mu\tau)^{-1}$ in $L^2$ and $H^1$ respectively, valid for $0<\mu\tau\le1$. The inserted source has $L^{3/2}$ norm $\mu\|A\|_{3/2}$; dividing the resulting pairing bound by $\|z\|_{H^1}$ gives the power $\mu^{1/4}$ in `sourceOp_threeHalves`.

ns-3late-periodic-force-shift.Breakdown.Periodic.Forced.Internal.force: For a source inserted at time $t\prime<c<t$, the two successive positive lags are $c-t\prime$ and $t-c$. The identity `forceV_eq_heat` says that their combined response is the one at lag $t-t\prime$. Thus the part of a Duhamel integral up to $c$ can be absorbed into the velocity at $c$ when restarting the equation.
ns-3late-periodic-force-shift.Breakdown.Periodic.SourceCont.Internal.f: The continuity statement concerns positive lag; a general source need not have a limit in $H^1$ at lag zero. For the mild integral it is enough to have continuity away from zero and the integrable bound $\int_0^h\tau^{-3/4}d\tau=4h^{1/4}$. `forceV_continuousOn` supplies the first of these properties.

ns-3late-periodic-kernel-bound.Breakdown.Periodic.KernelSharpBound: For bounded inputs on an interval of length $h\le1$, integrating (3.20) costs $\int_0^h\tau^{-3/4}d\tau=4h^{1/4}$. The mixed linear term therefore has operator norm at most $8C_{\mathbb T}h^{1/4}$ times the bound of the reference velocity on that interval. The same small-interval factor is available from `KernelSharpBound` after the time normalization in `stepFrame`.
ns-3late-periodic-kernel-bound.Breakdown.Periodic.kernelSharpBound_hold: Lean first estimates $K(\tau)(u,u)$ by pairing its weighted Fourier coefficients with the heat-smoothed advection. The trilinear bound gives a diagonal estimate $\|K(\tau)(u,u)\|\le D_\tau\|u\|^2$ with $D_\tau=O(\tau^{-3/4})$. Polarization, $4K(u,v)=K(u+v,u+v)-K(u-v,u-v)$, applied to unit inputs and then rescaled gives $\|K(\tau)\|\le2D_\tau$. Thus `kernelSharpBound_holds` controls all mixed terms, not just the diagonal Navier–Stokes term.

ns-3late-periodic-abstract-realization.Breakdown.Periodic.stepFrame: For a physical interval beginning at $t_0$ and of length $\mu(1-\lambda)$ set $U(s)=\mu^{1/4}u(t_0+\mu s)$. The time differential contributes $\mu$, the two velocities contribute $\mu^{-1/2}$, and normalization of the output contributes $\mu^{1/4}$. Thus the kernel in `stepFrame` is $\mu^{3/4}K_{\mathbb T}(\mu\tau)$. Since the factor $\mu^{3/4}$ cancels the power of $\mu$ in the smoothing estimate, one kernel constant suffices for every interval of the shrinking sequence.

pdf-item-equation-3-21.Breakdown.Periodic.TransplantNorm: For a test field $g$ of fixed support, transplant it by $g_\mu(x)=\mu^{-1/2}g((x-a)/\sqrt\mu)$ and periodize. If the support fits inside the cell, the two terms of the squared $H^1$ norm are $\mu^{-1/2}\|\nabla g\|_2^2$ and $\mu^{1/2}\|g\|_2^2$. Thus `TransplantNorm` gives $\|\mu^{1/4}\mathrm{toV}(g_\mu)\|^2=\|\nabla g\|_2^2+\mu\|g\|_2^2$. This is the identity used to recover the homogeneous whole-space norm in the limit $\mu\to0$.
pdf-item-equation-3-21.Breakdown.Periodic.stepFrame: The operator $D_\mu$ in (3.21) changes the spatial period to $L/\sqrt\mu$. `stepFrame` does not perform that spatial dilation. It keeps the space `V` fixed, changes the time to $s=(t-t_0)/\mu$, and multiplies the velocity state by $\mu^{1/4}$. The resulting heat operator and bilinear kernel are $e^{\mu s\Delta}$ and $\mu^{3/4}K_{\mathbb T}(\mu\tau)$; the latter has the uniform smoothing estimate for normalized lags at most one. The local spatial change of variables enters separately in `restrictTorus` and `transplantField`.

adapted.N2-10.1.Breakdown.Spectral.exists_dichotomy: The finite rank of the exterior projection is a statement about algebraic multiplicity. One need not compute a basis of eigenvectors: the formal dichotomy produces the projection, the two power bounds and surjectivity of the return on its range. These are exactly the hypotheses used by `DiscreteDichotomyStatement`.

adapted.N2-11.1.Breakdown.PeriodicSimilarityProfileExist: A positive return time $S$ and one isometry $R$ suffice for the whole argument in Section 4. Neither a least period nor the identity isometry is required. The choice fixes the length $1-e^{-S}$ of the first physical return interval and the free contraction $e^{-S/4}$ below.

ns-s4-003.Breakdown.physicalField: In $D_\mu$ the velocity factor is $\sqrt\mu$. For (4.1) the choice $\mu=(T-t)^{-1}$ therefore gives the spatial scale $\mu^{-1/2}=\sqrt{T-t}$ and the correct velocity prefactor $(T-t)^{-1/2}$. The argument of $W$ still uses its own logarithmic time.

ns-s4-004.Breakdown.IsSimilarityProfile: For fixed $t<1$ the dilation and phase are smooth and finite. The divergence of the physical field is $(1-t)^{-1}$ times the divergence of $W$ at the rescaled argument. Thus solenoidality is preserved before applying the decay estimates or invoking recurrence.
ns-s4-004.Breakdown.PhysicalMomentum: The local momentum calculation gives $\partial_t u^*=\Delta u^*-(u^*\cdot\nabla)u^*-\nabla p$ for all $t<1$. It is the input to the pressure-free test identity in Proposition 4.1. `PhysicalMomentum` states this equality for the rescaled field, while mildness and divergence are separate conditions.

pdf-item-equation-4-1.Breakdown.physicalField: Scaling the two bounds in (1.3) gives $(\sqrt{1-t}+|x|)^{-1}$ for the velocity and $(\sqrt{1-t}+|x|)^{-2}$ for its gradient. The inequalities on the right of (4.1) discard $\sqrt{1-t}$ to give bounds uniform in time away from zero. In the next paragraph the full denominators must be kept near zero, where $|x|^{-2}$ is not square integrable.
pdf-item-equation-4-1.Breakdown.IsSimilarityProfile: The $j=0,1$ clauses of the profile decay give (4.1) after scaling. The formal premise includes $j=2$ and $\nabla q$ with exponent three as well. For derivatives, the formal operator norm and the paper's square-sum norm are equivalent in fixed dimension; a decay constant may be enlarged when translating the estimates.
pdf-item-equation-4-1.Breakdown.embeddedProfileOrbit_holds: The formal orbit has values in $X$, with $w(s)$ the embedded slice $W(s,\cdot)$. Proposition 4.1 gives a physical mild solution from phase zero; applying it to the shifted profile $W(s_0+s)$ gives a mild solution from each phase $s_0$. Changing back to similarity time yields the two-time integral equation of `IsOrbit`, in addition to continuity, recurrence and nonvanishing.
pdf-item-equation-4-1.Breakdown.physicalMild_unconditional:
For the formal weak-to-mild argument one needs an $L^2$ estimate for a difference, not for a velocity slice. On $[0,b]$, $b<1$, the momentum equation and the additional formal bounds on $
abla^2W,
abla q$ give $|\partial_t u^*(t,x)|\lesssim_b(1+|x|)^{-3}$. Thus $\|u^*(t)-u^*(t')\|_2\lesssim_b|t-t'|$, even when $u^*(t)
otin L^2$. The mild identity itself is in $X$.

ns-s4-007.Breakdown.embeddedProfileOrbit_holds: To start from phase $s_0$ use the shifted profile $W(s_0+\cdot)$ and physical time zero. Inverting the change of variables at $t=1-e^{-\tau}$ gives the evolution from $w(s_0)$ to $w(s_0+\tau)$. The free term is $D_{e^{-\tau}}e^{(1-e^{-\tau})\Delta}w(s_0)$, which is the operator `S` in the formal similarity-time mild equation. This construction works for every $s_0\in\mathbb R$, not just nonnegative phases.
ns-s4-007.Breakdown.physicalMild_unconditional: The paper applies Lemma 3.6 after obtaining continuity in $X$ and the pressure-free test equation. The formal `physicalMild_unconditional` uses a different weak-to-mild lemma requiring continuity of differences of velocity slices in $L^2$ as well. The estimates on $\partial_tu^*$ from the stronger formal profile premise supply it; no bound on the energy of $u^*$ is assumed.

pdf-item-equation-4-2.Breakdown.MildFramework.IsOrbit: At $t'=1-\lambda(1-t)$ one has $s(t')=s(t)+S$ and $(1-t')^{-1}=\lambda^{-1}(1-t)^{-1}$. The orbit recurrence followed by the dilation composition law gives $u^*(t')=\rho_R D_{1/\lambda}u^*(t)$. This identity is in $X$ and includes the change of amplitude.
pdf-item-equation-4-2.Breakdown.MildFramework.selfSimilar: Use the definition of `selfSimilar` at the two times: the phase differs by $S$ and the dilation parameters by a factor $\lambda^{-1}$. Orthogonal covariance of the dilation permits $\rho_R$ to be taken outside. The return law for $w$, not the definition of `selfSimilar`, gives the equality of the two curves.
pdf-item-equation-4-2.Breakdown.ProfilePieceStatement: For the formal subdivision write $\mu=e^{-S/k}$ and $w_j(\sigma)=D_{(1-\sigma)^{-1}}W(jS/k-\log(1-\sigma))$, $0\le\sigma\le1-\mu$. At the right endpoint $D_\mu w_j(1-\mu)=w_{j+1}(0)$. Also $w_{j+k}=\rho_R w_j$, and $\sup_j\|w_j\|_{C X}\le\mu^{-1/4}\sup_s\|W(s)\|_X$. All three facts are in `ProfilePieceStatement`: matching, covariance and a uniform bound on the normalized backgrounds.
pdf-item-equation-4-2.Breakdown.orbitBound: Equation (4.2) implies that $(1-t)^{1/4}\|u^*(t)\|_X$ has period $S$ in $-\log(1-t)$. In fact it equals $\|W(s)\|_X$. `orbitBound` therefore takes the maximum of a continuous function on one compact period, not a supremum of the unscaled physical norm approaching one.
pdf-item-equation-4-2.Breakdown.orbitNorm: The formal lower bound uses a small-data estimate rather than the first-period minimum. If $\|W(s_0)\|_X\le c_{\rm small}$, the physical mild solution starting there satisfies $\|u(t)\|_X\le2\|W(s_0)\|_X$ up to time one. At its $n$th return, this gives $\|W(s_0)\|_X\le2e^{-nS/4}\|W(s_0)\|_X$. For large $n$ it forces the slice to vanish; uniqueness and recurrence then contradict the nonzero orbit.
pdf-item-equation-4-2.Breakdown.Freq.DilationAlgebra: The algebra used twice in iterating (4.2) is $D_\mu D_\nu=D_{\mu\nu}$ and $D_\mu\rho_R=\rho_R D_\mu$. The norm law gives $\|D_{1/\lambda}f\|_X=\lambda^{-1/4}\|f\|_X$. In particular the isometry introduces no additional norm factor.

ns-s4-016.Breakdown.physicalTime: The map $t\mapsto1-\lambda(1-t)$ reduces the remaining time by $\lambda$; indeed $-\log(\lambda(1-t))=-\log(1-t)+S$. It is a translation in similarity time. This makes the linear evolution on different physical periods comparable after rescaling.

ns-s4-017.Breakdown.MildFramework.gluePieces: In the formal gluing take $\mu=e^{-S/k}$, $t_j=1-\mu^j$ and $\sigma=(t-t_j)/\mu^j$. The physical field on that piece is $D_{\mu^{-j}}u_j(\sigma)$. The matching condition $u_{j+1}(0)=D_\mu u_j(1-\mu)$ makes the two formulas agree at $t_{j+1}$, since $D_{\mu^{-(j+1)}}D_\mu=D_{\mu^{-j}}$. Thus solutions on the same normalized interval join continuously at the physical endpoints.

ns-s4-018.Breakdown.ProfilePieceStatement: For the short-piece version of (4.3), take $\mu=e^{-S/k}$, $j=nk+r$ with $0\le r<k$. The $j$th piece samples the phase $jS/k-\log(1-\sigma)$ and its normalized profile equals $\rho_R^n$ of the $r$th piece. The additional $D_{\mu^{-j}}$ restores physical units. `ProfilePieceStatement` also verifies mildness and matching at the endpoints.
ns-s4-018.Breakdown.MildFramework.selfSimilar: Since $1-(t_n+\lambda^n\sigma)=\lambda^n(1-\sigma)$, the sampled phase is $nS-\log(1-\sigma)$. The physical dilation splits as $D_{\lambda^{-n}}D_{(1-\sigma)^{-1}}$. Substitution into `selfSimilar` and $n$ applications of recurrence prove (4.3).
ns-s4-018.Breakdown.stepData: For the short pieces set $\mu=e^{-S/k}$ and choose $\mu^{1/4}<\theta<1$. Write the normalized perturbation on piece $j$ as $\theta^j z_j$. A decay bound becomes a supremum bound on $z_j$, and matching requires the next weighted datum to be $\theta^{-1}D_\mu z_j(1-\mu)$. `stepData` solves the linear recursion with these factors and a freely chosen finite-dimensional correction on the first piece. The resulting decay rate is $-\log\theta/(S/k)$, between zero and $1/4$.
ns-s4-018.Breakdown.exists_section: The exterior projection $P_u$ will have finite-dimensional range $V$. The image $P_u C'$ of the dense test subspace is dense in $V$ and, being a linear subspace of $V$, is closed; hence it equals $V$. Lift a basis of $V$ to test fields. The restriction of $P_u$ to their span is an isomorphism onto $V$; its inverse gives the compactly supported lift, extended to a bounded map $J$ with $P_uJ=P_u$. The lift may have a stable component; no compact support of spectral vectors is required.

ns-s4-019.Breakdown.orbitBound: Taking the maximum of the continuous similarity norm on $[0,S]$ suffices for the upper bound: the isometry changes no norm. Equation (4.3) then restores the physical factor $(1-t)^{-1/4}$. In `orbitBound` the maximum need not be computed.
ns-s4-019.Breakdown.orbitNorm: Once the first-period norm has positive minimum, the scaling formula propagates it to all subsequent periods. `orbitNorm` gets positivity by another route: a similarity slice below the small-data threshold would have a physical evolution bounded through time one, incompatible with recurrence. The lower bound is used later in the reverse triangle inequality for the corrected flow.
ns-s4-019.Breakdown.Freq.DilationAlgebra: In (4.3) the isometry has norm one, and $D_{\lambda^{-n}}$ multiplies the gradient norm by $\lambda^{-n/4}$. Therefore $(1-t)^{1/4}\|u^*(t)\|_X=(1-\sigma)^{1/4}\|u^*(\sigma)\|_X$. The factor on the right lies in $[\lambda^{1/4},1]$ for $0\le\sigma<t_1$, giving the two constants in the proof.
ns-s4-019.Breakdown.monodromy: The dilation in (4.3) is undone when defining the return of a linearized perturbation. If $h_\chi$ solves (4.9), then $M\chi=\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda h_\chi(t_1)$. Without the interaction with $u^*$ this becomes $M_0\chi=\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda e^{t_1\Delta}\chi$, of norm at most $\lambda^{1/4}$. Lemma 4.4 makes $M-M_0$ compact. The growth rate of the reference itself in (4.4) is not the norm of $M$.
ns-s4-019.Breakdown.MonodromyStatement: For a subdivision into $k$ short intervals, $\mu=e^{-S/k}$. The linearized integral operator $A_j$ has norm at most $1/4$, so $(I-A_j)^{-1}$ has norm at most $4/3$. The short return $L_j$ evolves with this inverse and restores scale by $D_\mu$. The full return is $\rho_R^{-1}L_{k-1}\cdots L_0$. Each free short return has norm at most $\mu^{1/4}$, hence the product has norm at most $e^{-S/4}$. Compactness of the difference survives the finite composition: the difference of products is a finite sum with at least one compact factor in each summand.

ns-s4-020.Breakdown.ProfilePieceStatement: In the induction the normalized variable $\sigma$ is unchanged by the advance: $1-\lambda(1-t)=t_{n+1}+\lambda^{n+1}\sigma$. Every application contributes one $\rho_R$ and one $D_{1/\lambda}$. Their commutation gives the powers in (4.3); the short-piece theorem uses the same endpoint matching with step factor $\mu$.

ns-s4-021.Breakdown.MildFramework.gluePieces: The half-open intervals $[t_n,t_{n+1})$ cover $[0,1)$ without overlap. For the chosen $n$, $\sigma=(t-t_n)/\lambda^n\in[0,t_1)$ and $1-t=\lambda^n(1-\sigma)$. The same decomposition for short pieces in `gluePieces` leaves the normalized remainder $1-\sigma$ after rescaling, even as $1-t$ tends to zero. Matching supplies continuity at the common endpoints.

ns-s4-024.Breakdown.Piece: For $t=t_n+\lambda^n\sigma$, write $v_n=\rho_R^{-n}D_{\lambda^n}v(t)$. The exact expression under the supremum is $(1-\sigma)^{1/4-\kappa}\Theta^{-n}\|v_n(\sigma)\|_X$. Since $\lambda\le1-\sigma\le1$ on the first period, the phase factor is bounded away from zero. This is why a uniform bound on the divided pieces gives the global weighted estimate.
ns-s4-024.Breakdown.orbitSeq: The formal recurrence uses bounded sequences in place of decaying ones. For the full-period version put $z_n=\Theta^{-n}\chi_n$ and $c_n=\Theta^{-n}f_n$; then $z_{n+1}=\Theta^{-1}(\mathcal Mz_n+c_n)$. The inverse required in Proposition 4.3 is bounded for exactly this norm on the discrete states.
ns-s4-024.Breakdown.dichotomyHolds: One does not select $\kappa$ in advance. A faster desired rate corresponds to a smaller circle $\Theta=\lambda^\kappa$ and potentially a larger exterior space. Lemma 4.5 supplies a gap first, strictly outside the free radius $\lambda^{1/4}$ and strictly inside one. The exponent derived from that gap is automatically between zero and $1/4$.

ns-s4-025.Breakdown.Piece: On $[0,b]$ the weight in (4.5) lies between $(1-b)^{1/4-\kappa}$ and one; thus the ordinary and weighted supremum norms are equivalent there. The equivalence is not uniform as $b\uparrow1$. Subdividing in similarity time gives the same compact normalized interval on each step and puts all the dependence on the physical time into the scaling factors.

ns-s4-026.Breakdown.HeatBilinear.pieceBil: The singularity of the kernel at zero lag is integrable: $\int_0^L\tau^{-3/4}\,d\tau=4L^{1/4}$. Consequently $\|\mathcal B_L\|\le4C_KL^{1/4}$ on the space of bounded continuous curves. The mixed operator gains the same small factor, multiplied by twice the bound on the reference.
ns-s4-026.Breakdown.pieceOperator: The same estimate proves continuity at the moving upper limit: the last $\varepsilon$ of the integral has norm at most $4C_K\varepsilon^{1/4}$ times the two supremum norms. On the remaining part the heat lag is positive, where the kernel is continuous. `pieceOperator` packages the resulting continuous integral curves as a bounded bilinear map.
ns-s4-026.Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement: On one divided piece, let $x_n$ denote the incoming heat datum and put $U_n=(I-A_n)^{-1}$. The local solution is $U_n(\Gamma x_n+g_n)$. Its outgoing value gives $x_{n+1}=\theta^{-1}(M_nx_n+d_n)$, where $M_n=\operatorname{Ev}U_n\Gamma$ and $d_n=\operatorname{Ev}U_ng_n$. The source is first passed through the local inverse and only then evaluated at the endpoint.
ns-s4-026.Breakdown.orbitSeq: An additive source curve acts throughout a period. Its endpoint alone is insufficient to determine the discrete forcing: in (4.13) the relevant quantity is the endpoint of $(\mathcal U-I)g_n$, since the state is $v_n(0)-g_n(0)$. The bounded-sequence recurrence `orbitSeq` is obtained by dividing this state and forcing by $\Theta^n$.
ns-s4-026.Breakdown.StepDataStatement: Choose the subdivision before the spectral radius. With $\mu=e^{-S/k}$ and $M=\sup_s\|W(s)\|_X$, the mixed operator on each piece has norm at most $8C_K M(e^{S/k}-1)^{1/4}$. A sufficiently large $k$ makes this at most $1/4$ uniformly in the phase. Only the local equations are inverted at this stage; invertibility of the endpoint map is needed later, on its exterior spectral range over a full period.

ns-s4-027.Breakdown.PieceOperatorStatement: In (4.8), $e^{t\Delta}\gamma$ means the entire heat curve. Its evaluation at time zero is $\gamma$, whereas its value at the end of a period is the freely evolved datum. `pieceFree` is the operator $\Gamma:X\to\mathrm{Piece}$ giving this curve on one short interval; it has norm at most one.

ns-s4-028.Breakdown.orbitSeq: For $v\in C_\kappa$, the norm of its endpoint after returning to the first period is at most $\Theta^n\|v\|_\kappa$. Since $g$ belongs to the same space, subtracting its normalized endpoint changes the bound to $\Theta^n(\|v\|_\kappa+\|g\|_\kappa)$. Thus one may impose the same decay on the propagated variable $v-g$.
ns-s4-028.Breakdown.MildFramework.selfSimilar: `selfSimilar` uses a phase $s_0$ and local time $t$: the physical field is $D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(s_0-\log(1-t))$. Applying the gradient scaling gives $(1-t)^{-1/4}$ times the profile norm. The norm (4.5) consequently measures the rescaled error with the additional factor $e^{\kappa s}$.

ns-s4-029.Breakdown.PiecePerturbationStatement: The error equation retains the two mixed terms as $2\mathcal B(u^*,v)$ and the entire quadratic term as $\mathcal B(v,v)$. Since $u^*$ is an exact solution, its pure term cancels. Solving (4.7) is therefore equivalent to solving the mild equation for $u^*+v$, with its shifted initial value; no approximation is made at this step.

pdf-item-equation-4-7.Breakdown.piecePerturbation: At $t=0$ both integrals vanish and the heat operator is the identity. Hence a solution of the perturbation equation with prescribed heat input $e^{t\Delta}x$ has initial value $v(0)=x$. Adding the exact reference equation yields a solution with datum $u^*(0)+x$, as in `piecePerturbation`.
pdf-item-equation-4-7.Breakdown.varConstIntegral: Equation (4.7) makes sense on every $[0,b]$ with $b<1$, since the inputs are bounded there and $(t-t')^{-3/4}$ is integrable. `varConstIntegral` gives this local assertion. Control of the quadratic term in the weighted norm on all of $[0,1)$ is a further estimate, proved in (4.18)–(4.19).
pdf-item-equation-4-7.Breakdown.PieceOperatorStatement: The short-interval estimate gives $\|2\mathcal B_L(u^*,\cdot)\|\le8C_K L^{1/4}\sup\|u^*\|_X$. Inverting $I-2\mathcal B_L(u^*,\cdot)$ for small $L$ gives a solution for each incoming datum and source. By restarting the equation one can then cover a whole period of arbitrary length; there is no smallness condition on the full-period mixed operator.

adapted.N2-16.1.Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.tail: The finite recurrence gives $P_{\mathrm u}\chi_0=-\sum_{m<N}\mathcal M_{\mathrm u}^{-m-1}P_{\mathrm u}f_m+\mathcal M_{\mathrm u}^{-N}P_{\mathrm u}\chi_N$. For a decaying solution the last term is $O((\Theta/r_2)^N)$ and must vanish in the limit. The negative infinite sum is thus necessary, not just a possible choice for the initial exterior value.

ns-s4-032.Breakdown.stepData: `stepData` constructs a right inverse on bounded sequences of divided pieces. It first makes each local linear equation invertible by choosing $k$, then uses the spectral splitting of the $k$-step return to choose the initial coefficient in a finite-dimensional range. This avoids trying to invert the mixed operator on the entire half-open interval by a Neumann series.
ns-s4-032.Breakdown.exists_section: For a fixed $g$, any two admissible data in (4.12) differ by an element of $\ker P_{\mathrm u}$: their difference evolves homogeneously, and the inverse power bound forces its exterior projection to vanish. Conversely an interior displacement has the required decay. Taking the datum in the complementary space $E$ selects exactly one point of this affine space.

pdf-item-equation-4-8.Breakdown.StepDataStatement: At zero (4.8) gives $v(0)-g(0)=\gamma$. For the later source $g=e^{t\Delta}\chi+\mathcal B(v,v)$, this reads $v(0)=\chi+\gamma$. The two terms should not be confused: the prescribed displacement is part of the source, whereas the correction comes from the first component of the inverse.
pdf-item-equation-4-8.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: The right inverse of Proposition 4.3 is for the exact whole-space reference. For a field $u^{\mathrm a}$ that does not solve the equation, its residual must also enter the source. The sequence perturbation lemma assumes that a suitable inverse about $u^{\mathrm a}$ has already been constructed; small residual alone is not enough to give such an inverse.
pdf-item-equation-4-8.Breakdown.ContractionStatement: The use of (4.8) in the nonlinear problem is to insert $g=e^{t\Delta}\chi+\mathcal B(v,v)$. At a fixed point of its second component, the resulting pair solves (4.7) with $v(0)=\chi+\gamma$. One does not first solve the nonlinear equation and then choose the correction.

ns-s4-034.Breakdown.MonodromyStatement: The operator $\mathcal U$ solves the mixed equation for every continuous source on the full first period. One obtains it by solving on short intervals and restarting. Lean bounds each short-interval inverse by $4/3$ after making the mixed operator norm at most $1/4$; a product of these short inverses need not have that bound.

ns-s4-035.Breakdown.stepMap: For the local homogeneous equation, $\Gamma\chi$ is the heat curve and $(I-A_n)^{-1}\Gamma\chi$ the solved curve. The endpoint is dilated by $D_\mu$ via $\operatorname{Ev}=D_\mu\operatorname{ev}_L$. Thus `stepMap` maps one normalized starting field to the next, not to a trajectory.

pdf-item-equation-4-9.Breakdown.MildFramework.stepOp: Here the operator depends linearly on $h_\chi$, with $u^*$ a known time-dependent field. `stepOp` uses the restriction of the reference to the $n$th normalized interval as that fixed argument, including its phase. `stepFree` supplies the independent heat input; the inverse is applied to the sum of heat input and additive source.
pdf-item-equation-4-9.Breakdown.MonodromyStatement: To recover (4.9) from the short-interval construction, solve the homogeneous linear equation on each successive normalized piece and pass $D_\mu h(L)$ into the next. After $k$ steps, the product has applied total dilation $D_{\mu^k}=D_\lambda$. The remaining operation is $\rho_R^{-1}$, returning the last field to the orientation of the first.

ns-s4-037.Breakdown.iterProd: Let $M_j$ be the short endpoint maps and $Q=M_{k-1}\cdots M_0$. On the next block the product is $\rho_R Q\rho_R^{-1}$, since all intermediate conjugations cancel. In coordinates rotated back by $\rho_R^{-n}$ at block $n$, the homogeneous block update is always $\rho_R^{-1}Q$. This is the formal period map.
ns-s4-037.Breakdown.MonodromyStatement: The recurrence of the background multiplies it by $\rho_R D_{1/\lambda}$ over one period. Both operations are invertible and commute, so undoing them on the final perturbation gives exactly $\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda h_\chi(t_1)$. This is why there is no forward rotation in (4.10).

ns-s4-038.Breakdown.stepMap: The bound $(4/3)\mu^{1/4}$ on a short endpoint map need not be below one. In fact $\mu^{1/4}\to1$ as the pieces are shortened. The smallness estimate gives a bounded solution operator on each piece; decay over an entire period must come from the free comparison and the subsequent spectral argument.
ns-s4-038.Breakdown.MonodromyStatement: The bound on $\mathcal U$ proves that $\mathcal M$ is a bounded operator. It gives no useful estimate for $\mathcal M^n$ at a specified decay rate. The free part, rather than the full return, has norm at most $e^{-S/4}$; the compact difference permits the subsequent spectral splitting.

ns-s4-039.Breakdown.monodromy: Write $Q_m=M_{m-1}\cdots M_0$ for the product of the actual short returns and $B$ for the free step. Then $Q_{m+1}-B^{m+1}=(M_m-B)Q_m+B(Q_m-B^m)$. Compact operators form a two-sided ideal, so compactness of each $M_m-B$ suffices by induction; one does not need compactness of $Q_m$ or of the free heat operator.
ns-s4-039.Breakdown.MonodromyStatement: A free step is $B=D_\mu e^{(1-\mu)\Delta}$, with norm at most $\mu^{1/4}$. The Lean proof only needs $\|B^k\|\le\mu^{k/4}$. To identify it with the paper’s free map, use (3.5): $B^2=D_{\mu^2}e^{(1-\mu^2)\Delta}$, since the heat times add as $(1-\mu)+\mu(1-\mu)$. Hence $B^k=D_\lambda e^{t_1\Delta}$ and $\rho_R^{-1}B^k$ is the desired return.

ns-s4-040.Breakdown.Freq.DilationAlgebra: The free comparison uses the exact same change of coordinates as the true return. Its three factors give $\|\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda e^{t_1\Delta}x\|_X=\lambda^{1/4}\|e^{t_1\Delta}x\|_X\le\lambda^{1/4}\|x\|_X$. Neither the amplitude of $u^*$ nor its spectrum enters this bound.

ns-s4-042.Breakdown.dichotomyHolds: Lean states the backward estimate without introducing inverse notation: $\|P_{\mathrm u}x\|\le Kr_2^{-n}\|\mathcal M^nP_{\mathrm u}x\|$. Taking $n=1$ gives injectivity on the exterior range, and the separate surjectivity hypothesis gives an inverse there. Taking $P_{\mathrm u}x=\mathcal M_{\mathrm u}^{-n}y$ recovers the inverse-power bound. No inverse of the full operator is needed.

ns-s4-043.Breakdown.DichotomyHolds: The preceding argument gives bounds in operator norm, including for generalized eigenvectors. A radius at which one had only bounded divided homogeneous powers would not suffice: summing $n$ equally sized divided source contributions can give growth proportional to $n$. The gap gives summability of these powers.

adapted.N2-17.1.Breakdown.monodromy: A free step is $B=D_\mu e^{(1-\mu)\Delta}$ with $\mu=e^{-S/k}$. The product law for the heat and dilation gives $B^k=D_{\mu^k}e^{(1-\mu^k)\Delta}$; its norm is at most $\mu^{k/4}=e^{-S/4}$. Thus subdivision of the period has not changed the free spectral bound. The final inverse isometry has norm one.

ns-s4-049.Breakdown.DichotomyHolds: For the restriction to the interior, choose $r_1$ strictly between its spectral radius and $\Theta$; for the inverse restriction to the exterior choose $r_2^{-1}$ strictly between its spectral radius and $\Theta^{-1}$. The spectral radius formula bounds sufficiently large powers at these rates; finitely many earlier powers are absorbed into the constant. In particular the argument does not require the projections to be orthogonal or the operator to be normal.

ns-s4-051.Breakdown.StepDataStatement: From $\Theta=\lambda^\kappa$ one has $\kappa=-\log\Theta/S$. The interval $\lambda^{1/4}<\Theta<1$ is exactly $0<\kappa<1/4$. If there are $k$ steps in one period, $\theta=\Theta^{1/k}$ is the decay weight per step and $\theta^k=\Theta$; one should not use the full-period weight on every short step.

ns-s4-052.Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement: The normalized reference on short interval $j$ is the physical solution started at phase $jS/k$. Recurrence changes this reference by $\rho_R$ after $k$ intervals, so the corresponding local endpoint maps are conjugate. Within one period their phases generally differ. At full-period boundaries one can undo the accumulated rotation, reducing all the homogeneous block updates to the same operator (4.10).

ns-s4-053.Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement: Put $a_n=g_n(0)$ and let $y_n=\chi_n+a_n$ be the full rescaled endpoint. The recurrence (4.14) then gives $y_{n+1}=\mathcal M y_n+f_n+a_{n+1}-\mathcal Ma_n$. The two additional terms are exactly the change in source response caused by restarting with the full endpoint. The formal short-interval inverse uses the full endpoint and locally restarted sources.

ns-s4-054.Breakdown.orbitSeq: The exponent $n$ in $D_{\lambda^n}$ removes the physical scale of the $n$th interval; the exponent $-n$ in $\rho_R^{-n}$ removes its orientation. After taking the difference of the two rescaled curves at zero one obtains $\chi_n$. The subsequent division by $\Theta^n$ is a decay normalization, distinct from both changes of coordinates.

ns-s4-055.Breakdown.orbitSeq: In the full-endpoint convention, a global heat input $g=e^{t\Delta}\eta$ is accounted for by adding $\eta$ to the initial datum; it supplies no new local source on later intervals. In (4.13) the same heat curve can produce a nonzero $f_n$ because the propagated endpoint is that of $v-g$. The difference is bookkeeping of the heat input, not a different linearized equation.
ns-s4-055.Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement: Write $d_n=\operatorname{Ev}(I-A_n)^{-1}g_n$, $M_i=\operatorname{stepMap}(i)$ and $\Theta=\theta^k$. In the first block, iteration of $y_{i+1}=\theta^{-1}(M_i y_i+d_i)$ gives $y_k=\Theta^{-1}(M_{k-1}\cdots M_0y_0+\sum_{i<k}\theta^i M_{k-1}\cdots M_{i+1}d_i)$, with the empty product equal to $I$. The factors $\theta^i$ are needed because the local sources are already divided. Rotating back at block boundaries gives the constant monodromy in the divided recurrence.

ns-s4-056.Breakdown.StepDataStatement: The equality $1-t=\lambda^n(1-\sigma)$ gives the bound directly: $\|g_n(\sigma)\|_X\le\Theta^n(1-\sigma)^{\kappa-1/4}\|g\|_\kappa$. The largest phase factor is $\lambda^{\kappa-1/4}$, attained at the end of the period. The endpoint map of $(\mathcal U-I)g_n$ multiplies this by at most $\lambda^{1/4}(1+\|\mathcal U\|)$, independently of $n$.

ns-s4-057.Breakdown.orbitSeq: The key point of the second identity in (4.14) is that $f_n$ is independent of $\chi_0$. Thus the datum can be chosen using the entire sequence of $f_n$, computed from the prescribed $g$. For the nonlinear equation we first fix a trial quadratic source, apply this linear selection, then use the resulting trajectory to update the source.

ns-s4-059.Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement: Splitting the integral at $t_n$ and using (3.12), the part before $t_n$ is the heat evolution of $2\mathcal B(u^*,v)(t_n)$. Adding the original heat term yields the heat evolution of $v(t_n)-g(t_n)$. The remaining integral begins at $t_n$; this is the exact restart identity even when $g$ has no time derivative.

ns-s4-060.Breakdown.Freq.DilationAlgebra: Writing $\mu=\lambda^n$, the identity $D_\mu e^{\mu\sigma\Delta}=e^{\sigma\Delta}D_\mu$ moves the normalized heat operator outside the change of coordinates. Together with commutation with the isometry, the incoming heat curve becomes $e^{\sigma\Delta}\chi_n$. There is no extra power of $\lambda$ in this term.

ns-s4-061.Breakdown.MildFramework.stepOp: Upon setting $t'=t_n+\lambda^n\sigma'$, the factor $dt'=\lambda^n d\sigma'$ cancels the inverse time-scaling factor of $K$. In formulas, for $\mu=\lambda^n$, $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(a,b)=K(\tau)(D_\mu a,D_\mu b)$. Isometry equivariance and (4.3) then return the mixed kernel to $K(\sigma-\sigma')(u^*(\sigma'),v_n(\sigma'))$.

ns-s4-062.Breakdown.stepMap: Linearity of $\mathcal U$ separates $v_n$ into the solution driven by the incoming heat datum and that driven by the local additive curve. The monodromy is obtained from the first part alone. The second part contributes the source response to the recurrence; it must not be included in the definition of the homogeneous step map.

ns-s4-063.Breakdown.orbitSeq: At the common physical endpoint of periods $n$ and $n+1$ the two normalized values differ by $\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda$. Applying this map to $v_n(t_1)-g_n(t_1)$ gives $\chi_{n+1}$. With $v_n=h_{\chi_n}+\mathcal U g_n$, its homogeneous term is $\mathcal M\chi_n$ and its source is precisely the difference in (4.13).

adapted.N2-21.1.Breakdown.exists_section: The lift is a bounded map on the finite-dimensional exterior range, and extending it by first applying $P_{\mathrm u}$ gives a map $J$ on $X$ satisfying $P_{\mathrm u}J=P_{\mathrm u}$. In the proof of `exists_section` this is the composition of `J₀` with the range restriction of the projection. The map $J$ selects a datum; it need not commute with $\mathcal M$.

ns-s4-069.Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.step: Multiplication of the future sum at $n$ by $\mathcal M_{\mathrm u}$ gives a first term $-P_{\mathrm u}f_n$; adding the current forcing cancels it. All later summands have the exponents of the sum at $n+1$. This checks the recurrence itself, not only the bound on its solution.
ns-s4-069.Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.rec_: The forward formula has a homogeneous term $\mathcal M^n(I-P_{\mathrm u})\gamma$ as well as the past sources. One must retain this term: the compact lift of the prescribed exterior datum need not itself lie in the exterior range. A source at index $m$ enters the state at $m+1$ and undergoes exactly $n-1-m$ further returns.

ns-s4-070.Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyStatement: The estimate for past forcing is $KF\Theta^n/(\Theta-r_1)$, and that for future forcing is $AF\Theta^n/(r_2-\Theta)$, if $\|f_m\|\le F\Theta^m$ and the two projected power bounds have constants $K,A$. For the past sum the exponent of a power is $n-1-m$; for the future sum the inverse exponent is $m-n+1$. The remaining homogeneous term has norm at most $Kr_1^n\|\gamma\|$.

ns-s4-071.Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement: The decay of the endpoint $\chi_n$ must be converted to a bound on the whole normalized period. Use $v_n=\mathcal U(e^{\sigma\Delta}\chi_n+g_n)$ and heat contractivity to obtain $\|v_n\|_\infty\le\|\mathcal U\|(\|\chi_n\|+\|g_n\|_\infty)$. This step has one fixed constant for all periods, so it loses no decay rate.

ns-s4-072.Breakdown.MildFramework.gluePieces: Undoing the change of scale gives the exact norm relation $(1-t)^{1/4-\kappa}\|v(t)\|_X=(1-\sigma)^{1/4-\kappa}\Theta^{-n}\|v_n(\sigma)\|_X$. The phase factor is at most one and at least $\lambda^{1/4-\kappa}$ on a period. Thus bounded divided pieces give the claimed physical-time estimate, and conversely the physical-time estimate bounds all divided pieces.

ns-s4-073.Breakdown.StepDataStatement: For this fixed choice of $E$, the linear inverse (4.8) is in fact unique. The difference of two solutions has zero source and initial datum in $E$. Its exterior projection must vanish by the backward power bound, whence the datum is zero because $E\cap\ker P_{\mathrm u}=\{0\}$. Local uniqueness gives zero trajectory. The resulting linear map is bounded by the preceding estimates.
ns-s4-073.Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement: In the sequence inverse the first component is an exterior vector; applying the fixed lift makes it a physical datum correction. Its second component solves the local equations for arbitrary additive curves. Matching the full endpoints also requires the local sources to vanish at each noninitial left endpoint; the residual and quadratic Duhamel term have this property in the nonlinear application. Thus the gluing assertion concerns the corrected mild trajectory, not arbitrary inputs to the abstract inverse.

ns-s4-074.Breakdown.HeatBilinear: The construction of the torus inverse is postponed to Section 6; the contraction uses only its trajectory estimate, as in (4.22). Neither compactness of the kernel nor the spectral splitting is required again here. This separation allows the same lemma to correct an approximate field that is not recurrent on the torus.

ns-s4-075.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: The residual is the difference between the proposed curve and the mild formula with its own initial value. It is zero at the left endpoint whether or not the curve solves the equation. The sign in (4.17) is negative because the error must cancel this defect; in the piece version this also makes the residual contribution zero at each restart.

ns-s4-076.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: The defect in (4.16) is a mild-equation residual, so its norm is measured after the heat evolution and time integration, in the same space as the velocity error. This is the norm estimated in Lemma 6.2. In the formal sequence setting the analogous local defect is divided by $\theta^n$; its smallness is a bound uniform in $n$.

ns-s4-077.Breakdown.PiecePerturbationStatement: Expanding $\mathcal B(u^{\mathrm a}+v,u^{\mathrm a}+v)$ gives the reference term, two equal mixed terms and the quadratic error. Subtracting the heat input of the prescribed datum separates $F^{\mathrm a}$ and $\mathcal L(\gamma,v)$ from the remaining two terms. For an exact background this reduces to the compact-interval implication `PiecePerturbationStatement`.

ns-s4-078.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: On piece $n$ write the actual normalized error as $\theta^nz_n$. Its quadratic term after division is $\theta^n N_n(z_n,z_n)$, while the given residual is $-\theta^{-n}r_n$. The prescribed datum contributes a heat curve on piece zero only. Later heat curves are those of the propagated corrected endpoints, so the initial perturbation is not counted again.

ns-s4-080.Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_sma: The contraction treats $e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}$ as a known curve and $\mathcal B(v,v)$ as a trial-dependent one. A linear inverse bound $C_{\mathcal R}$ makes the trial ball of radius twice the norm bound for the known response. The quadratic term is small relative to this radius when the known source is sufficiently small; no smallness of the mixed term is assumed.

ns-s4-081.Breakdown.varConstIntegral: Write $r=1-t$ and $\tau=t-t'$. Then $1-t'=r+\tau$, and the change $\tau=r\theta$ yields the factor $r^{-3/4+\kappa-1/2+1}=r^{\kappa-1/4}$. The remaining dimensionless integral is bounded independently of $t$; this is precisely the factor canceled by the weight of $C_\kappa$.

ns-s4-083.Breakdown.varConstIntegral: The two products have different time dependence: the quadratic product has exponent $2\kappa-1/2$, and the interaction of a bounded field with a $C_0$ field has exponent $-1/4$. On $0<1-t'\le1$ both are bounded by $(1-t')^{\kappa-1/2}$. The common integral (4.18) therefore controls both (4.19) and the cutoff estimate (4.21).
ns-s4-083.Breakdown.PieceOperatorStatement: On a compact interval the kernel estimate gives the factor $4C_KL^{1/4}$ times two ordinary supremum norms. These norms need not be bounded as the interval approaches time one. Substitution in (4.18) keeps the pointwise time-dependent input powers inside the integral and gives an output bound uniform in the weighted norm.

pdf-item-equation-4-19.Breakdown.PieceOperatorStatement: The estimate loses some of the decay of a product of two errors: their product has the power $(1-t')^{2\kappa-1/2}$. In fact (4.18) with $\eta$ in place of $\kappa$ bounds $\mathcal B(v,v')$ in $C_\eta$ whenever $\eta\le2\kappa$ and $0<\eta<1/4$. For the fixed point it is enough to take $\eta=\kappa$, without changing the spectral circle used for the inverse.

pdf-item-equation-4-20.Breakdown.HeatBilinear: By heat contractivity and $(1-t)^{1/4-\kappa}\le1$, the weighted norm of the heat curve is at most $\|\chi\|_X$. The value at $t=0$ attains this bound, so in fact equality holds. This is why smallness of the prescribed datum in $X$ suffices to make its heat input small in $C_\kappa$.

ns-s4-086.Breakdown.varConstIntegral: The bounded input in (4.21) need not decay in physical time. In Section 6 it is the difference $\bar u-u^*$, whose ordinary supremum norm is $O(L^{-1/2})$ by (6.4). The other factor is allowed the reference rate in $C_0$. This estimate makes their mixed Duhamel term small in the stronger $C_\kappa$ norm required by the inverse.

ns-s4-087.Breakdown.varConstIntegral: Fix $b<1$. Both inputs have finite ordinary supremum norms on $[0,b]$, so removing a lag shorter than $\varepsilon$ costs $O(\varepsilon^{1/4})$ uniformly there. The truncated integral varies continuously with its endpoint; passing to the limit proves continuity on $[0,b]$. Since $b$ is arbitrary, no field at time one is needed.

ns-s4-088.Breakdown.HeatBilinear: The lag $t-t'$ controls smoothing, while the time to the singularity $1-t'$ controls the size of the inputs. Their relation is $1-t'=(1-t)+(t-t')$. The substitution in (4.18) separates out the current remaining time $1-t$ and leaves a dimensionless integral, whose finiteness is what makes the bound uniform in $t$.

ns-s4-089.Breakdown.PieceOperatorStatement: At a fixed short interval the kernel gives a bound by $4C_K L^{1/4}$ times the two supremum norms. The global proof must instead keep the powers of $1-t'$ inside the time integral; a supremum over all physical times could be infinite. The rescaled piece proof handles the same issue by keeping the factor $\theta^n$ in its quadratic term.
ns-s4-089.Breakdown.HeatBilinear: Only the heat contraction and the singular bilinear kernel bound are used here. These are the relevant fields of `HeatBilinear`. No recurrence or compactness is required for the nonlinear estimates once a bounded right inverse has been supplied.

ns-s4-090.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: The lemma assumes a right inverse of the mixed equation about the chosen reference, whether or not the reference is exact. It does not need that reference to be small. In `SeqPerturbation` the analogous given inverse acts on divided pieces, and the residual and prescribed heat input are small together. The hard part on the torus is constructing that inverse, not proving a second contraction principle.
ns-s4-090.Breakdown.ContractionStatement: For an exact reference the residual is zero. The source of the sequence inverse is $\Gamma\xi$ on the first interval, plus $\theta^nN(z_n,z_n)$ on every interval. The heat effect of $\xi$ is carried into later intervals by the preceding endpoints. The approximate-reference theorem adds the negative divided residual on each interval.

pdf-item-equation-4-22.Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement: The inverse is applied to trial right-hand sides, and only its second component is iterated. The parameter space $E$ therefore needs no norm in Lemma 4.8. A bound for the parameter is available if the inverse has one, as in (4.8) or the bounded sequence inverse, and is needed for the Lipschitz estimate of the selected datum in Section 5.2.

ns-s4-092.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: Let $a=\|e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}\|_\kappa$. The radius is $\delta=2C_{\mathcal R}a$, and on this ball the Lipschitz constant of the inverse applied to the quadratic term is at most $2CC_{\mathcal R}\delta=4CC_{\mathcal R}^2a$. The square in (4.23) thus comes once from the size of the solution and once from applying the inverse to a difference.

ns-s4-093.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: With $a=\|e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}\|_\kappa$, (4.24) gives a trajectory of size at most $2C_{\mathcal R}a$. If the known input vanishes then the selected fixed point is zero. In the formal sequence estimate the bound is $2\|R\|(\rho+\|\xi\|)$ on the divided pieces; the actual normalized error has the additional factor $\theta^n$.

ns-s4-094.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: The endpoint condition in `SeqPerturbation` follows by evaluating the corrected mild formula at zero of each piece: the mixed and quadratic integrals and the local residual vanish there. Thus for $n>0$ the divided incoming error is $(c/\theta)z_{n-1}(L)$, where $c$ is the endpoint scaling. Multiplying by $\theta^n$ and adding the matching reference gives the required matching of corrected fields.

ns-s4-095.Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_sma: For the generic fixed-point lemma take $b=C_{\mathcal R}a$ and $K=CC_{\mathcal R}$, with $a=\|e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}\|_\kappa$. Its hypothesis $8Kb\le1$ is exactly (4.23) for $\varepsilon_1=(8C)^{-1}$. It gives a fixed point in the closed ball of radius $2b$.

ns-s4-096.Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_sma: For a trial velocity $v$ use the second component of $\mathcal R[e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}+\mathcal B(v,v)]$. If that component equals $v$, the first component of the same pair gives the datum parameter. There is no separate iteration of the datum, and no norm of the parameter is required to establish the contraction.

ns-s4-097.Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_sma: On the ball of radius $\delta$ the contribution of the known source is at most $\delta/2$ and that of the quadratic term at most $CC_{\mathcal R}\delta^2\le\delta/4$. Their sum is at most $3\delta/4$. The self-map property of the ball is thus established separately from the contraction estimate.

ns-s4-098.Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_sma: Bilinearity gives $\mathcal B(v',v')-\mathcal B(v'',v'')=\mathcal B(v'-v'',v')+\mathcal B(v'',v'-v'')$. Each term contains the difference once and an unchanged factor of norm at most $\delta$. With (4.19) and the bound for the inverse this gives Lipschitz constant $2CC_{\mathcal R}\delta\le1/2$.

s1-outline-contraction.Breakdown.ContractionStatement: On $\mathbb R^3$ the cutoff is applied to the datum, not to the reference in the equation. Thus the reference has zero mild residual, and the heat curve of the initial mismatch is the small input to the contraction. The mixed interaction with $u^*$ is handled by the linear inverse, however large $u^*$ becomes.

ns5.cutoff.solenoidal.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffDivergenceFree: Where the cutoff varies, $\operatorname{div}(\eta(\cdot/r)u^*)=r^{-1}\nabla\eta(\cdot/r)\cdot u^*$. The additional term from the curl has exactly the opposite divergence, by $\operatorname{curl}A=u^*$. `cutoffDivergenceFree` establishes this cancellation without estimating the size of the added term.

ns5.cutoff.scalar.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceApprox.stdBu: The same bump is used at every radius, so the first and second spatial derivatives of $\eta(\cdot/r)$ cost $r^{-1}$ and $r^{-2}$. The formal `stdBump` has radii $1$ and $2$; its rescaling by $2/r$ gives the inner and outer radii $r/2$ and $r$.

pdf-item-equation-5-1.Breakdown.Periodic.homotopyPotential: The formula uses the field along the segment from the centre to $x$ at one fixed time, so it requires no solution of a spatial elliptic equation or boundary condition for the potential. The order $u^*(t,\sigma x)\times x$ gives $\operatorname{curl}A=u^*$, not its negative. `homotopyPotential` allows the centre to be translated, which is useful in placing the cutoff inside the unit cell.
pdf-item-equation-5-1.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffField: In (5.1) the product rule gives $\bar u=\chi u^*+\nabla\chi\times A$, with $\chi=\eta(\cdot/r)$; this is the formula of `cutoffField`. Since $|A|\lesssim1$ and $|\nabla\chi|\lesssim r^{-1}$, the correction has the same order $r^{-1}$ as the velocity in the transition annulus. This is why enforcing zero divergence does not increase the order of the mass estimate.
pdf-item-equation-5-1.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceApprox.cutof: The theorem `cutoff_isTestField` gives the three properties of the cutoff curl needed for membership of $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$: smoothness, compact support and zero divergence. Its fixed bump at scale $r/2$ gives the paper's support radius. Equality with $u^*$ on the inner ball requires the separate curl identity for $A$.

ns5.cutoff.parameter.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffField: The radius is held fixed during each evolution. On $\mathbb R^3$ the cutoff changes only the datum; on the torus it changes the reference at every time. In the latter case $r=L/8$ makes the support a fixed ball, which is why the entire mixed advection in (6.9) is determined by the perturbation restricted to that ball.

ns5.lemma5.1.geometry.Breakdown.Periodic.approxFieldProperties: Lean also localizes the pressure, in order to estimate the differential residual. Write $p_T^*(t,x)=(T-t)^{-1}q(s,(x-a)/\sqrt{T-t})$ for the physical pressure and $x_0$ for the fixed point of the transition annulus. The pressure used is $\chi(x)(p_T^*(t,x)-p_T^*(t,x_0))$. Its gradient agrees with the original gradient in the inner ball. The subtraction eliminates dependence on a time-dependent pressure gauge and allows the extra cutoff term to be bounded using differences of pressure, hence $\nabla p_T^*$.
ns5.lemma5.1.geometry.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceApprox.cutof: The support and smoothness of the potential multiplied by a bump pass to its curl, and the divergence of a smooth curl vanishes. `cutoff_isTestField` packages these facts for each fixed nonzero scale. Neither equality on the inner ball nor a bound uniform in time follows from membership of the test-field class alone.
ns5.lemma5.1.geometry.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffGradientClose: In similarity coordinates, $f(y)=\sqrt\ell\,\bar u(t,a+\sqrt\ell y)$, $\ell=T-t$, agrees with $W(s,y)$ on $B_{1/(16\sqrt\ell)}$. The identity $\|\nabla_y(f-W)\|_2^2=\sqrt\ell\,\|\bar u-u_T^*\|_{\dot H^1}^2$ is on the whole space before periodization. `cutoffGradientClose` chooses the threshold on $\ell$ uniformly in the phase. A choice of $T$ below that threshold works also at all later times.
ns5.lemma5.1.geometry.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffMassBound: Increasing $r$ improves the gradient approximation but need not bound the mass uniformly in $r$: the radial integrals of the squared gradient bound outside $r$ and of the squared velocity bound inside $r$ are of orders $r^{-1}$ and $r$. In the formal cutoff the physical radius is fixed, so the latter growth occurs only in the similarity-coordinate mass; `cutoffMassBound` compensates it by the physical volume scaling.

pdf-item-equation-5-2.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffGradientClose: The paper gives an explicit physical norm estimate for every $r>0$. With remaining time $\ell$ and fixed physical $r$, squaring and changing to similarity variables gives $\|\nabla(f-W)\|_2^2\lesssim\sqrt\ell/r$. `cutoffGradientClose` proves the needed smallness of the squared similarity gradient by an integrable majorant, with a weaker power of $\ell$ in its proof and a fixed physical radius. Its tolerance is a squared norm, not the norm in (5.2).
pdf-item-equation-5-2.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffMassBound: The normalized inhomogeneous norm has two terms. If $\ell=T-t$, $f(y)=\sqrt\ell\,\bar u(t,a+\sqrt\ell y)$ and $\mu$ is the remaining time at the start of the current interval, its square is $(\mu/\ell)^{1/2}\|\nabla f\|_2^2+\sqrt{\mu\ell}\|f\|_2^2$. Here $\lambda\mu\le\ell\le\mu$ and `cutoffMassBound` bounds the second term by $K\sqrt\mu$. The gradient term is bounded above and away from zero by the first estimate of (5.2) and the profile norm bounds. This is why both estimates are used in `ApproxSizes`.

ns5.proof.curlintegrand.Breakdown.Periodic.Cutoff.Internal.poten: For a smooth field $g$, differentiation gives $\operatorname{curl}_x[\sigma g(\sigma x)\times x]=2\sigma g(\sigma x)+\sigma^2 Dg(\sigma x)x-\sigma^2x\operatorname{div}g(\sigma x)$. The zero-divergence hypothesis eliminates the last term. The first two constitute a derivative in $\sigma$, so there is no spatial inversion left to perform. `potential_pointwise` proves the componentwise identity with a translated centre as well.

ns5.proof.curlpotential.Breakdown.Periodic.homotopyCurl: `homotopyCurl` proves the same curl identity at an arbitrary centre and also gives smoothness of the potential. The vanishing of the lower endpoint uses smoothness at the centre, not decay at infinity. Hence the potential construction itself needs neither compact support nor a decay estimate.

ns5.proof.productformula.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffField: Writing $\chi(x)=\eta(x/r)$, the two derivatives of the cutoff satisfy $|D\chi|\lesssim r^{-1}$ and $|D^2\chi|\lesssim r^{-2}$.
