This resembles one step with a prescribed inverse Jacobian, but its proof neither bounds the derivative of $\Phi$ nor asserts convergence of iterates.

ns7-data-s038.Breakdown.extended_certificate_orbit_pro: For an arbitrary trial field $g$ in (7.57), the linear solve need not satisfy the adjoint bound (7.32) with $g$ in place of $(v\cdot\nabla)v$. Hence the paper projects the parameter update to keep the joint iteration in $K$. At the fixed point this discrepancy is gone; (7.35) and (7.37) give the enclosure before projection, which is what implies zero total force. Lean uses a fixed-parameter contraction first, so its finite-dimensional map is already formed from nonlinear solutions.

sec7-nonlinear-008.Breakdown.Cert.extendedExistsZeroHeldHol: At each parameter the fixed-pin nonlinear correction generally has a nonzero auxiliary force. The formal proof first constructs that correction in the class (7.59), then applies a finite-dimensional zero theorem to the continuous total coefficient map. Only at the selected parameter is $\beta=-\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)$. The two bounds survive unchanged from the held solve; the zero-selection step does not make the correction smaller.
sec7-nonlinear-008.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.IsHeld: The two bounds are part of the definition of the class in which the fixed-parameter solve is unique, not consequences of merely satisfying its projected equation. `IsHeldSolution` also records the prescribed pin gap and invariance. It permits nonzero $\beta^{\mathrm a}+\beta$; (7.60) is the additional condition imposed by the parameter theorem.
sec7-nonlinear-008.Breakdown.Cert.extendedHeldMapsToHolds_o: The self-map closes two bounds for a reason. After (7.52), the residual and prescribed pins consume at most $\varepsilon$, and (7.25) bounds the energy cost of a quadratic trial by another $\varepsilon$. Then (7.55) and (7.27) bound the gradient supremum by $M$, which is needed to control the next quadratic trial by (7.49). The linked maps-to theorem closes this loop for the held iteration.

sec7-nonlinear-009.Breakdown.Cert.extendedBorderedInvertibl: The uniqueness at this step is uniqueness for the linear trial problem, with both the forcing $-\mathbb P(F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+g)$ and the pin vector $\bar\ell(\alpha)$ prescribed. The inverse does not yet impose $g=(v\cdot\nabla)v$. This allows the paper to define the joint map on the entire forcing ball rather than just on nonlinear solutions.
sec7-nonlinear-009.Breakdown.Cert.extendedInvarianceHolds_o: Membership of $g$ in $\mathcal Z$ gives its invariance; (7.58) gives invariance of the projected residual. Since $\mathbb P$ preserves symmetry, their sum is an admissible projected forcing for Proposition 7.8. The linked result supplies the residual invariance and the symmetry of the projected terms, not the inverse itself.

adapted.N4-40.1.Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedHeldMaps: The useful way to read the smallness conditions is in the order of a single update. The defect and pins cost at most $\varepsilon$ in the joint norm; an input product of norm at most $2c_w\varepsilon M$ costs at most $c_L(2c_w\varepsilon M)\le\varepsilon$. The output therefore has joint norm at most $2\varepsilon$. Condition (7.27) then gives its gradient supremum bound $M$ through (7.55), so its own product again has norm at most $2c_w\varepsilon M$. `step_bounds` gives the two estimates on the output.

adapted.N4-41.1.Breakdown.Held.convexCompactFixedPoint: Projection keeps the parameter in $\mathcal K$ during the joint iteration, when the quadratic trial is still independent of the output correction. Once the enclosures are established it can be removed from the fixed-point identity. The linked theorem uses projection in proving the finite-dimensional compact convex fixed-point theorem; it is not the infinite-dimensional Schauder–Tychonoff theorem applied in the paper.

adapted.N4-43.1.Breakdown.Cert.extendedHeldLimitHolds_of: Uniform bounds on the corrections do not directly bound the free residual, since the drift and time derivative enter an unbounded operator. The projected equation instead writes $f_k$ as a sum of four bounded fields. In the formal proof the bound for convection follows from operator-norm continuity along the convergent parameter sequence and the common derivative bounds. This places all $f_k$ in one bounded Hilbert-space ball before the subsequences of force, multiplier and local product are extracted.

adapted.N4-44.1.Breakdown.Cert.extendedHeldLimitHolds_of: Passing the equation and pins to the limit is not enough for the formal argument: its uniqueness statement is restricted to (7.59). The last two steps of `extendedHeldLimitHolds_of` recover the joint weighted radius by weak lower semicontinuity, and the gradient supremum by weak closedness of the slice bound. This makes the limiting coefficient the same one selected at the limiting parameter. In the paper the independent limiting $g$ instead fixes a linear problem, so these two extra steps are unnecessary for uniqueness.

adapted.N4-45.1.Breakdown.Cert.heldExistsUniqueHolds_of: At each fixed parameter the formal iteration uses the current correction to form the quadratic forcing and the bordered inverse to obtain a new correction with its multiplier. Unlike the paper's product-space fixed point, the contraction also bounds the difference of two such outputs; (7.26) is used in this difference estimate. The result is uniqueness in the two-radius class, not global uniqueness of nonlinear profiles. Only the later parameter theorem cancels the total multiplier.

adapted.N4-46.1.Breakdown.Cert.extendedExistsZeroHeldHol: Projection alone could conceal an outward step at the boundary: on an interval, for example, projecting a point beyond the right endpoint returns that endpoint. After quadratic consistency is known, the two enclosures in (7.61) show that the proposed point itself lies in $\mathcal K$, and projection fixes it. Then the fixed-point equation forces $V^T(\beta^{\mathrm a}+\beta)=0$. The formal argument obtains an unprojected self-map directly because the nonlinear solve has already been performed at every parameter.

adapted.N4-47.1.Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedExistsZe: Set $p_j=\langle F_\alpha^{\mathrm a},\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}+(Y(\alpha)\bar\ell(\alpha))_j$. The offset estimate bounds $V_j\cdot\beta^{\mathrm a}-p_j-d_j\alpha_j$. The correction estimate bounds $V_j\cdot\beta+p_j$. Their sum cancels $p_j$ before the triangle inequality, leaving exactly the discrepancy in (7.61). `box_split` is this addition of the two enclosures.

adapted.N4-48.1.Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedExistsZe: The complementary coordinates are controlled collectively, not one at a time. For $j\notin\mathcal J$ put $x_j=V_j\cdot\beta^{\mathrm a}-d_j\alpha_j$ and $z_j=V_j\cdot\beta$. Their Euclidean norms are bounded by $o_*$ and $2\varepsilon a_*/\omega$. Expanding $\|x+z\|_2^2$ and using Cauchy–Schwarz gives at most $(o_*+2\varepsilon a_*/\omega)^2\le\varrho_*^2$. This is the squared ellipsoid enclosure, which can be substantially sharper than independent coordinate bounds.

pdf-item-theorem-7-11.Breakdown.FarField.periodicLerayProfileE: The edition `proposition_7_11` retains the given period and the phasewise equality of spatial representatives. Its premise includes square integrability of the weak Hessian over a period, not imposed separately in the printed proposition. The open Hessian bridge concerns the hypothesis; under the stronger premise the phasewise conclusion is proved.
pdf-item-theorem-7-11.Breakdown.FarField.smoothFieldOfOrbit_ho: The reconstruction retains the continuous mild orbit it starts from. To prove (7.62), the edition wrapper first identifies that orbit with the rescaled continuous representative of the given weak field and then applies `regularizeKeeping`. Equality with the given curve is therefore obtained before the far-field estimates, not deduced merely from existence of a smooth solution.
pdf-item-theorem-7-11.Breakdown.FarField.IsVelocityOf: The norm on $X$ is the gradient norm of an $L^6$ velocity. If two slices have equal gradients, their difference is constant; only the zero constant belongs to $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$. Thus equality in $X$ in (7.62) identifies the velocities almost everywhere, with no additive constant. In the application to the certificate, subtracting $W_\alpha^{\rm a}(s/S,\cdot)$ recovers the correction bounded in Proposition 7.10.

pdf-item-equation-7-62.Breakdown.FarField.smoothFieldOfOrbit_ho: An almost-everywhere equality in phase first identifies the weak representative with the constructed mild curve. Both are continuous in $X$, so equality extends to every phase. The smooth reconstruction preserves that curve, giving (7.62) without making a new choice of phase or period.
pdf-item-equation-7-62.Breakdown.FarField.IsVelocityOf: `IsVelocityOf` means $\forall s,\ W(s,\cdot)=w(s)$ almost everywhere in space. The time quantifier is outside the spatial almost-everywhere quantifier. The proof first identifies continuous $X$-valued curves, so a possible exceptional set of phases from the weak reconstruction disappears. No common exceptional spatial set for all phases is required to obtain pointwise equality of two continuous spatial representatives.
pdf-item-equation-7-62.Breakdown.WeakProfile.weakOrbitOfParts_h: The given continuous $X$-valued representative and the constructed mild orbit agree almost everywhere in time after converting $\theta$ to $s=S\theta$. Their difference is continuous, and the set on which it vanishes is dense. Thus the two agree at every phase, as used in the edition theorem.

adapted.N4-50.1.Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedSigmaPro: The continuity needed here is continuity in $X$, hence of the gradient in $L^2$, not uniform spatial convergence. For $\theta_k\to\theta$, the gradient difference tends to zero pointwise and its square is bounded by $4C_{\mathrm a}^2(1+|y|)^{-4}$. The radial integral $\int_0^\infty r^2(1+r)^{-4}\,dr$ is finite, so dominated convergence applies. `profile_grad_sq` supplies the majorant.

adapted.N4-51.1.Breakdown.Cert.extendedHeldNonzeroHolds_: If the sum vanished, its gradient would vanish in $\mathcal H$, hence the gradients of the approximate field and the correction would be negatives of one another. But the former has norm strictly greater than $2\varepsilon/\sqrt{w_*}$ by (7.28), whereas the latter has norm at most this number by (7.59). This strict separation is why the weak orbit obtained by the formal construction is nonzero.

sec7-nonlinear-044.Breakdown.WeakProfile.physicalCurve: The normalized period-one curve $\mathcal W$ must be evaluated at $s/S$. Thus with $x(s)=\mathcal W(s/S)$ and phase offset zero, `physicalCurve` is $D_{1/(1-t)}x(-\log(1-t))$. Since each $t<1$ gives a positive finite dilation, joint continuity of dilation on $X$ yields continuity of $u$ on the entire physical interval $(-\infty,1)$.

sec7-nonlinear-045.Breakdown.WeakProfile.physicalCurve: Write $r=1-t$. For the velocity the scaling factor in $L^6$ is $r^{-1/2}r^{3/12}=r^{-1/4}$; for the gradient in $L^2$ it is $r^{-1}r^{3/4}=r^{-1/4}$. Thus (7.63) is an equality of rescaled velocity norms. As $t$ runs over $(-\infty,1)$, $\theta$ runs over all of $\mathbb R$; continuity and period one bound the supremum by that on $[0,1]$.

adapted.N4-54.1.Breakdown.WeakProfile.constOfWeakDeriv_h: Call the two scalar pairings $A(t)$ and $B(t)$, so the identity is $\int\phi'A=-\int\phi B$. The formal primitive theorem has sign convention $\int\phi'A=\int\phi b$, with $b=-B$ here. It gives $A(t)=c+\int_{t_0}^t B$ almost everywhere on an interior interval. Both sides are continuous, so the equality holds everywhere and $A'=B$.

adapted.N4-55.1.Breakdown.FarField.lerayKernel: The formula for `lerayKernel` is $\delta_{ij}\partial_k G_\tau+\int_\tau^\infty\partial_i\partial_j\partial_k G_\rho\,d\rho$, where $G_\rho$ is the heat kernel. The integral comes from $(-\Delta)^{-1}e^{\tau\Delta}=\int_\tau^\infty e^{\rho\Delta}\,d\rho$ in the Leray projection. Both terms scale as $\tau^{-2}$ with spatial argument $x/\sqrt\tau$, so the $L^p$ norm has power $\tau^{-2+3/(2p)}$. This yields $-7/8$ and $-3/4$ for $p=4/3$ and $p=6/5$, respectively; the nonlocal projection changes the kernel but not its parabolic scaling.

adapted.N4-56.1.Breakdown.FarField.smoothFieldOfOrbit_ho: For a fixed starting time $a$, the bounded mild theory gives bounds on $(t-a)^{k/2+l}\nabla_x^k\partial_t^l u$. The weights are harmless on a compact interval strictly after $a$. Since the field is defined for every $t<1$, one can always start the mild formula earlier than that interval; all finite phases are thus covered by the regularization. The linked formal theorem reconstructs the smooth field from the mild orbit and retains its $X$-valued slices.

adapted.N4-57.1.Breakdown.FarField.IsSmoothOrbitField: For each fixed $t$, testing the smooth momentum residual $G$ against curls gives $\operatorname{curl}G=0$. The radial primitive has gradient $-G$, yielding the pressure of (1.1). `IsSmoothOrbitField` asks in addition for the gradient of the *similarity* pressure to belong to $L^2$ at each phase. This integrability is not a consequence of the radial primitive formula alone; it is established by the formal regularity argument.

sec7-nonlinear-057.Breakdown.WeakProfile.physicalCurve: The inverse physical change of variables is $D_{e^{-s}}u(1-e^{-s})$. Since the normalized weak field was read at $\theta=-S^{-1}\log(1-t)$, this gives $W(s,\cdot)=\mathcal W(s/S)$ in $X$. Advancing $s$ by $S$ advances the normalized phase by exactly one. The pressure rescaling uses the square of the velocity amplitude.
sec7-nonlinear-057.Breakdown.FarField.IsVelocityOf: The inverse rescaling gives $D_{e^{-s}}u(1-e^{-s})=\mathcal W(s/S)$ in $X$ at every $s$. At $s+S$ the right side is the same element as at $s$. Therefore the two smooth velocity slices agree almost everywhere in $y$ and, by spatial continuity, everywhere. This is the passage from periodicity of the original weak field to the pointwise return law of the profile.
sec7-nonlinear-057.Breakdown.FarField.IsSmoothOrbitField: The inverse change of variables stays in the smooth region for every finite $s$, since $1-e^{-s}<1$. It gives the similarity equations and the return law pointwise. For `IsSmoothOrbitField` the smoothness and recurrence are supplemented by uniform spatial derivative bounds through order three, a uniformly vanishing velocity tail and a square-integrable pressure gradient. Weighted inverse-distance decay is proved in the next stage.

sec7-nonlinear-058.Breakdown.FarField.farFieldDecay_holds: The formal far-field proof also uses the whole-past integral equation. Put $\delta=1-t$ and $\tau=(t-t')/\delta$ in (7.64). The earlier similarity phase is $s-\log(1+\tau)$ and its spatial argument is $z/\sqrt{1+\tau}$ in the current spatial units. The squared velocity amplitude gives the factor $(1+\tau)^{-1}$ in `profileBilin`. Starting at $t-A(1-t)$, the rescaled heat term is bounded by $C(1+A)^{-1/2}$ because the heat kernel has mass one and the earlier velocity has smaller amplitude. It tends to zero as $A\to\infty$. Thus the profile is determined by the quadratic integral itself, to which the weighted decay estimates apply.
sec7-nonlinear-058.Breakdown.FarField.DecayBounds: The extra pressure-gradient bound in `DecayBounds` needs more than the velocity derivative estimates of Remark 1.2. The formal argument takes the divergence of (1.2), giving $-\Delta q=\sum_{i,j}\partial_i\partial_j(W_iW_j)$. In the Newton potential for $\nabla q$, away from the kernel singularity, two integrations by parts move the two derivatives onto the cut-off kernel. The second derivatives of this cut-off gradient kernel are bounded uniformly by $O(r^{-4})$, where $r=\max(1,|y|)$, and $\int_{|z|<2r}|W(z)|^2dz=O(r)$, giving $O(r^{-3})$ for this part. The complementary tail and the local source give the same bound; the square-integrability of $\nabla q$ is used to identify it with the Newton field.

sec7-nonlinear-059.Breakdown.FarField.periodicLerayProfileE: The edition `proposition_7_11` gives an identity-return profile at the input period, agreeing with the weak field at every phase in the sense of spatial almost-everywhere equality. Its `IsIdentityProfile` also includes the extra velocity-Hessian and pressure-gradient decay. These are precisely the properties used by the edition Theorem 7.1 and its whole-space consequence, under the stronger formal weak-profile hypotheses.

adapted.N5-01.1.Breakdown.VarConstIntegralInternal.conti: For positive lags near $\tau_0$ the norms of the bilinear maps are uniformly bounded. Add and subtract the value with the limiting inputs at the varying lag, use bilinearity for the input differences, and then use continuity at fixed inputs for the remaining lag difference. `continuousOn_K` proves precisely this joint continuity away from zero; integrability, rather than continuity at zero, controls the time endpoint.

adapted.N5-02.1.Breakdown.pieceOperator: For `pieceOperator` the bound is $4C_KT^{1/4}$ on the bilinear integral map for $T\le1$. The paper is estimating the operator linear in $h$ with $f$ fixed on an arbitrary finite interval. With its exponential norm the bound becomes $2C_K\|f\|_C\Gamma(1/4)\beta^{-1/4}$, as the ratio of the weights at $t$ and $t'$ is $e^{-\beta(t-t')}$. Taking $\beta$ large replaces the formal restriction to a short step.

adapted.N5-03.1.Breakdown.restrict: After applying the heat flow from $m$ to $t$ to the equation at $m$, the free term and all the earlier contributions have exactly the lags of the corresponding terms at $t$. Subtracting leaves the integral over $[m,t]$. The linked `restrict` proves this for the mild equation with $f=h=u$; the printed identity also holds for distinct inputs.

ac-015.Breakdown.Periodic.heat_add: The projected evolution of a fixed mean-zero source has coefficients $e^{-4\pi^2\tau|k|^2}\mathbb P_k\hat f(k)$. Multiplication by the heat factor at $t$ gives the coefficient at $t+\tau$; there is no new estimate of a Fourier sum. The formal `heat_add` is the heat law on the inhomogeneous space at period one, including the zero mode.

ac-017.Breakdown.Periodic.kernelSharpBound_hold: The mean of $(u\cdot\nabla)v$ vanishes: as a periodic distribution it is $\operatorname{div}(v\otimes u)$, whose integral is its pairing with the constant test. Thus (3.19) applies to both advections in (3.17). Hölder with (3.18) bounds their $L^{3/2}$ norms by a constant times $\|u\|_{\dot H^1}\|v\|_{\dot H^1}$, independent of $L$. The linked bound is in the unit-torus inhomogeneous norm for lags at most one.

adapted.N5-11.1.Breakdown.mildRegular_realization: All Sobolev orders are finite initially for a compact smooth datum, and persistence of these orders gives smoothness up to time zero. This is different from the interior smoothing of the ancient, possibly infinite-energy field in §7.10. The linked whole-space realization supplies the smooth velocity and pressure on a closed slab; the paper's energy calculation supplies the bound $\|u_0\|_2$ independently of its endpoint.

adapted.N6-36.1.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.CellSystemCond: The cell conditions specify a single set of represented fields and compatible local quadratic forms. In particular the local unknowns used to prove coercivity are measurements of arbitrary perturbations, not a restriction of the perturbation to the splines. The join and pressure conditions allow the local inequalities to be summed for that same global field. The analytic proof of Sections 7.5–7.9 then uses their consequences rather than the mesh itself.

ns7-data-s004.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.coercive: Appendix B proves the inverse estimate by combining two inequalities. In (B.20) and (B.21) the integrals of the mode density and the stretching term, as well as the pairing of the unknown force with $\mathsf Mv$, disappear when the inequalities are combined. Lemma B.2 then has the scalar form $P^2\le c_M\|F\|_{\mathcal H}P+Q^2$, with $P^2$ containing $\frac3{50}\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}^2$ and $Q^2=\frac3{50}[F]^2+1000|\ell(v)|^2$. Bounding the positive root by $c_M\|F\|_{\mathcal H}+Q$ and using $\sqrt{3/50}\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}\le P$ gives (7.18). The cell computations thus bound an inverse on the full domain, not the smallest singular value of the discretization alone.
ns7-data-s004.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.gap_tran: Lemma B.9 estimates the change $G=(\mathcal C_\alpha-\mathcal C_\alpha^{\mathrm r})v$ in the convection operator by $c_{\mathrm r}\|v\|_w$. Applying the reference estimate to $F-G$ costs at most $(c_1+c_0)c_{\mathrm r}\|v\|_w$ in addition to the cost of $F$. Hence (7.21) makes the extra cost absorbable into the left side of (7.52).
ns7-data-s004.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.adjoint_: Lemma B.10 permits either a slice $L^3$ or a slice $L^2$ bound on $\psi_j$. In the first case estimate the velocity factors in $L^6$ and $L^2$; in the second use $L^\infty$ and $L^2$. Both products are bounded by constants times $|v(\theta)|_w^2$, which can be integrated over one period. This is why the adjoint error is quadratic in $\|v\|_w$, rather than requiring a separate bound on the maximum gradient in time.

The adjoint defect is an estimate for a linear functional of $v$, not an $L^2$ norm of an adjoint residual. Lemma B.11 uses Hardy's inequality to bound $|\int v\cdot R|$ by $2\||y|R\|_{\mathcal H}\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H}$ for the unstructured part of a defect field $R$; its azimuthal decomposition improves the estimate for nonzero wave numbers. This is suited to the homogeneous space, in which $v$ itself need not belong to $\mathcal H$. Lemma B.12 then incorporates the constraint fields and the remaining terms of the adjoint identity.
ns7-data-s004.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.frozen_f: The transfer of the frozen form is a second use of the same convection difference. If $G(u)=(\mathcal C_\alpha-\mathcal C_\alpha^{\mathrm r})u$ at a phase, the change in the form is $-\langle G(u),\Delta u\rangle_{L^2}$. Lemma B.9 controls this pairing from below; its contribution adds to the reference lower-bound constant rather than being absorbed as in (7.52). This gives the constant $c_3$ for the energy-growth estimate.

b12-rotation-coordinate.Breakdown.axialRot: At $r>0$, the frame at $R_{\phi_0}y$ is the image under $R_{\phi_0}$ of the frame at $y$. Thus $R_{-\phi_0}v(\theta,R_{\phi_0}y)$ has the cylindrical components of $v$ at the shifted angle, expressed in the frame at $y$. This is the operation averaged in (B.12); averaging the Cartesian components without that rotation would give different mode labels.

b12-halfturn-coordinate.Breakdown.CertCell.flipPoint: The rotation $R_*$ sends $(r,\phi,z)$ to $(r,-\phi,-z)$. At the reflected point the radial basis vector is $R_*e_r$, whereas the other two basis vectors are $-R_*e_\phi$ and $-R_*e_z$. This is why the cell vectors below have two minus signs, and the cell tensors a minus sign exactly when one of their indices is radial.

b12-order.Breakdown.CertCell.CellHypothesis: The lower bound three is on the spacing of the angular Fourier lattice, not on the number of harmonics retained. In particular the first nonzero angular frequency has modulus at least three. In Lemma B.5, this makes both $|k|-1$ and $|k|-2$ positive for every nonaxisymmetric mode (where $k$ is that mode's angular Fourier integer).

b12-two-generators.Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.IsModeClass: The mode-class predicate asks for these two particular group elements and an order at least one. This suffices to infer Fourier support and reflection of an invariant field. To apply the later certificate construction one also imposes order at least three and the generation condition, the latter being used to establish invariance of the represented data.
b12-two-generators.Breakdown.CertCell.Instance.GeneratedByC: To prove invariance of a represented field, it suffices to prove the identities for the two pairs in (B.1). The identity for a product follows by applying the two identities successively; period one accounts for the remaining integer time translation. This is the use of the generation condition, as opposed to membership of the two pairs, which is sufficient for restricting the modes of an already invariant perturbation.
b12-two-generators.Breakdown.CertCell.CellHypothesis: The restriction on $\Gamma$ ensures that the symmetry of the finite data and the symmetry assumed of the unknown perturbation are the same. Membership of the first pair also implies that the gradient energy has period $1/2$, by rotation invariance of the spatial integral. Thus the same choice of symmetries has a second use in Proposition 7.9, besides its use for the Fourier lattice here.

b12-allowed-symmetries.Breakdown.CertCell.Instance.GeneratedByC: A rotation through $a$ times the generating angle has time translation $a/2$ modulo integers. The reflection-type element with the same angle is obtained by composing it with $(R_*,0)$. These are exactly the products whose invariance follows from the two generator identities and period one.

pdf-item-equation-B-2.Breakdown.CertCell.labelPhase: The integer lattice may be read in terms of the two traveling phases of C.1: with $j=2\iota_2-\iota_1$ and $m$ the angular integer, the phase change under the combined shift is $\pi(j+m/k)=2\pi\iota_2$, where $k$ is the angular order. In particular a purely time-dependent mode has even $j$, but a mode with odd $m/k$ must have odd $j$.

b12-harmonic-parity.Breakdown.CertCell.labelPhase: Under the simultaneous half-period and half-angle shifts, the scalar phase acquires the factor $e^{i\pi(j+j'/k_{\mathrm{rot}})}$. It is one precisely for the lattice (B.2). Thus (B.12) can project onto that lattice without a Fourier truncation of the unknown perturbation.

b12-first-symmetry.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.fieldClass: The scalar components are unchanged under the combined shift, whereas the cylindrical frame rotates by the angle of the generator. Reassembling the components gives precisely the vector transformation in (7.5). The linked theorem proves it for the admissible fields (B.6), including points on the axis.

b12-label-reflection.Breakdown.CertCell.labelFlip: The time integer $2\iota_2-\iota_1$ is unchanged by $\iota^\flat$, whereas the angular integer is negated. In particular the two travelling families $\iota_2=0$ and $\iota_2=\iota_1$ of C.1 are exchanged. Applying the map twice gives the original label. Conjugation instead negates both integers (and, in (B.5), the radial index).

pdf-item-equation-B-3.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.chartCoord: A single polynomial interval ending at $\sigma=1$ describes the entire exterior of the sphere corresponding to its left endpoint. In particular $(1-\sigma)^h=\mathsf L^h/(R+\mathsf L)^h$ imposes the desired power of decay without an infinite sequence of radial cells.
pdf-item-equation-B-3.Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.heightRat: The value assigned to $\eta$ at the origin is only a convention for the total coordinate function. Limits taken along different rays still give different height ratios; the amplitude factors in (B.7) and (B.8) must remove this dependence when the full velocity is assembled.

pdf-item-equation-B-4.Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.polarVecQ: For $R=|y|>0$, $\mathbf p=\eta y/R-e_z$ is perpendicular to $y$ and has squared length $1-\eta^2$. It is minus the tangential projection of $e_z$ onto the sphere, and hence vanishes at both poles. One can therefore use $\mathbf p$ rather than the unit polar vector when writing a field with a regular axis. Its value at $y=0$ is immaterial to this calculation; the origin expansion is separate.
pdf-item-equation-B-4.Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.azimVecQ: The azimuthal vector is $e_z\times y/|y|$. In particular it is already multiplied by $r/|y|$, which removes the unit azimuthal vector's directional ambiguity on the nonzero axis. The total formal definition gives zero also at the origin.

b12-weighted-unit-vectors.Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.polarVecQ: Near a nonzero point of the axis, the factor $r/R$ in the length of $\mathbf p$ removes the singular unit polar vector. In (B.8) this allows the axisymmetric radial amplitude $u_0$ to be nonzero on the axis while the tangential amplitude contributes zero there. The nonaxisymmetric construction instead makes all three amplitudes vanish to fourth order in $r$.
b12-weighted-unit-vectors.Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.azimVecQ: Since $|e_z\times y|=r$, the length of $\mathbf a$ is $r/|y|=(1-\eta^2)^{1/2}$ away from zero. The amplitude multiplying it in (B.8) can therefore describe an axisymmetric swirl without a singular unit vector on the axis.

b12-phase-condition.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsRadialPh: For $R=|y|$, the first two radial derivatives of $f(R^2)$ are $2Rf'(R^2)$ and $2f'(R^2)+4R^2f''(R^2)$, of orders $R^{-1}$ and $R^{-2}$ at infinity; the third is of order $R^{-3}$. The third derivative is needed because (B.7) and (B.8) already differentiate the phase once in the velocity amplitudes, before the equation differentiates the velocity twice. A bound on the phase itself is unnecessary.

pdf-item-equation-B-5.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.keyPhase: For a fixed $\iota$, all the indices $l$ have the same factor $E_\iota(\theta,\phi)$. Their amplitudes, multiplied by $e^{ilf(R^2)}$, add before any norm of $\hat v_\iota$ is taken. The orthogonality used in B.2 is in $\iota$, not in the radial phase index $l$.
pdf-item-equation-B-5.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.shiftedSca: The scaled radial derivative $R\partial_R$ acts on $e^{ilf(R^2)}u$ by the product rule. On dividing out the exponential its two terms are $\sigma(1-\sigma)\partial_\sigma u$ and $2ilR^2f'(R^2)u$, namely $\mathcal V_l u$. Differentiating the amplitude alone would omit the second term, including in the divergence equation.

pdf-item-equation-B-6.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.shapeInfoF: The three terms are the radial, polar and azimuthal parts of a single velocity harmonic. Only two scalar splines are free: for a nonzero azimuthal frequency the third component is determined by divergence, whereas for zero frequency the first two are determined by a stream function.
pdf-item-equation-B-6.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.keyDiverge: The divergence calculation is performed on the complex summand, before taking its real part. In (B.7) the azimuthal derivative cancels the divergence of the meridian components; in (B.8) the meridian components already have zero divergence. Thus changing the coefficients within the admissible amplitude spaces preserves solenoidality without a further linear constraint in the numerical solve.
pdf-item-equation-B-6.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsTimeFiel: The finite list of keys and the two scalar splines for each key determine a field by (B.6)–(B.8). The data predicate imposes the further conditions on the exponents, joins, origin values and paired keys. It is these conditions, not the finite-sum formula alone, that give a periodic solenoidal $C^1$ field with the stated decay.

b12-finite-mode-data.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.shapeInfoF: For each nonzero angular integer the two free splines prescribe the radial and polar amplitudes, and the angular amplitude is obtained by dividing the meridian divergence by the angular derivative in (B.7). At angular integer zero this division is unavailable: one instead prescribes a stream function and a swirl, with the extra origin coefficient in the stream function. These are the independent coefficients of the velocity representation.
b12-finite-mode-data.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.keyDiverge: For each key $(\iota,l)$ the divergence identity holds before taking a real part or adding any other key. Thus the coefficients can be varied independently subject to the spline and symmetry conditions without solving a new equation for divergence. Finiteness is needed for the data representation, not for this cancellation.

b12-nonzero-exponents.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsTimeFiel: The factors have different jobs: near the origin $\sigma^{h_0}=O(R^{h_0})$, at infinity $(1-\sigma)^h=O(R^{-h})$, and near a nonzero point of the axis $(1-\eta^2)^2=r^4/R^4$. The last factor compensates for the angular derivatives, while $h_0\ge2$ ensures that the nonaxisymmetric summands have zero first derivative at the origin.

pdf-item-equation-B-7.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.reducedCom: The azimuthal velocity is $u_2\mathbf a$, with $\mathbf a=(r/R)e_\phi$. Its divergence is therefore $E_{\iota,l} i k_{\mathrm{rot}}\iota_1 u_2/R$, so the coefficient of $u_2$ in the divergence equation is nonzero. Solving this algebraic equation gives the third amplitude from the two meridian amplitudes, without an integration constant or an additional boundary condition.
pdf-item-equation-B-7.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsTimeFiel: The joins are imposed on the free splines, rather than separately on the three resulting amplitudes. In $u_2$ the radial derivative of $\mathsf A$ and the height derivative of $\mathsf B$ must themselves have continuous first derivatives. Thus $\mathsf A$ needs order two in $\sigma$ and order one in $\eta$, and $\mathsf B$ the reverse.

b12-zero-stream.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.reducedCom: For $\iota_1=0$ an azimuthal velocity has zero divergence regardless of its radial and height dependence, so it cannot be used to cancel the divergence of the other two components. Instead (B.8) imposes the cancellation between those components by a stream function, and leaves the swirl free.

pdf-item-equation-B-8.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.reducedCom: Here $\iota_1=0$ is only a restriction on the angle: the term can still oscillate in time and radius. The operator $\mathcal V_l$ is therefore retained in the stream-function formula. In contrast, $\mathsf T$ can be chosen independently because the axisymmetric swirl contributes no divergence.
pdf-item-equation-B-8.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsOriginPr: The coefficient $\gamma$ supplies the only possible nonzero first derivative at the origin. Indeed $\mathsf S,\mathsf T=O(\sigma)$ there, and the additional factor $\sigma$ makes their contributions $O(|y|^2)$. The leading $\gamma$ term is of order $|y|$ and yields the axisymmetric trace-free linear field described below.

b12-origin-function.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsOriginPr: At an interior join $\sigma_g$ the polynomial must have zero first and second derivatives, since it is followed by a constant. This ensures two derivatives of $g$ agree there: $u_1$ in (B.8) already contains one radial derivative of $g$.

b12-zero-divergence.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.keyDiverge: The cancellation in the calculation applies away from the coordinate singularities. The linked statement has no such exclusion: it is about the divergence of the represented Cartesian vector field at every spatial point, under the shape and field-data hypotheses.

b12-field-data-description.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.shapeInfoF: Changing $f$ leaves the spline data unchanged, but it changes two places in the field: the scalar factor $E_{\iota,l}$ and the radial derivative $\mathcal V_l$ used to construct the dependent amplitudes. The latter change is essential for retaining the divergence identity when the phase is varied in (B.9).

adapted.N5-20.1.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsJoinedSp: The traces to be matched along a spline edge are polynomials in the tangential variable. Equality of these polynomials implies equality of their tangential derivatives, so matching the indicated normal derivatives also matches the mixed derivatives required after applying $\mathcal V_l$ or $\partial_\eta$. This is why the free splines in (B.7) and (B.8) need different join orders.

b12-c1-periodic.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.FieldJoint: The $C^1$ assertion includes the axis and the origin, not only points at which the cylindrical coordinates are smooth. On the axis the explicit angular factors remove the singularity of the angular basis; at zero the axisymmetric $\gamma$ term supplies a Cartesian linear field and the other terms have vanishing first derivative. The joins give the same first derivatives on both sides of each sphere and cone.

b12-second-derivatives.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.FieldWeakH: In the formal statement the weak derivative is taken of each vector $D_yW\,e_j$ separately. The join conditions allow the piecewise Hessian to serve as that derivative: boundary terms from the two neighboring regions cancel. Its values on the interfaces themselves do not affect this identity.
b12-second-derivatives.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.fi: The decay estimate for the represented Hessian can be established using the formulas on the polynomial pieces. To use its trace as $\Delta W$ in a weak equation requires the distinct assertion that the represented Hessian is the weak derivative of $D_y W$. The latter follows from the matching first derivatives and is the content of `FieldWeakHessian`.

b12-conjugation.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsTimeFiel: Conjugation negates the radial index as well as the harmonic label, so that $\overline{\mathcal V_l u}=\mathcal V_{-l}\overline u$. In (B.7) the simultaneous negation of the azimuthal integer conjugates the purely imaginary prefactor of $u_2$ as well. The two constructed vector terms are thus conjugate, and a pair of distinct keys contributes twice the real part of one term.

b12-reflection-data.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsTimeFiel: Write $D_l=\mathcal V_l+2$ and $L_\eta u=\partial_\eta((1-\eta^2)u)$. Under the half-turn $u_0$ is reflected without a sign and $u_1$ with a minus sign, so $D_lu_0-L_\eta u_1$ is reflected without a sign. The angular integer changes sign, giving the required minus sign of $u_2$ in (B.7). In (B.8) the stream function and swirl are odd in $\eta$, which yields the same vector transformation.

b12-both-symmetries.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.fieldClass: The proof uses two different facts: the frequency lattice gives the half-period rotation and the reflected amplitudes give the half-turn at fixed time. Applying the first transformation twice also gives invariance under a spatial rotation by twice its angle, since the time period is one.

b12-gamma-invariant.Breakdown.CertCell.Instance.GeneratedByC: The generating transformations are invertible, so an identity $W(\theta+t,Ry)=RW(\theta,y)$ also gives the identity for the inverse pair. Iterating and using period one proves invariance for each product in the generation condition. No finiteness assumption on $\Gamma$ is needed for this argument.

b12-axis-factors.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.reducedCom: The factor in $u_1$ is $(1-\eta^2)^2$, so the height derivative in (B.7) differentiates a factor $(1-\eta^2)^3$ and leaves at least $(1-\eta^2)^2$. Thus the dependent amplitude has the same fourth-order vanishing in $r$ as the free amplitudes at a nonzero point of the axis. At the origin the common factor $\sigma^{h_0}$ persists as well, since $\mathcal V_l$ uses the scaled derivative $R\partial_R$.

b12-axis-zero-mode.Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.polarVecQ: Write $R=|y|$. Since $\sigma=R/\mathsf L+O(R^2)$, (B.8) gives $u_0=\gamma R(3\eta^2-1)/\mathsf L+O(R^2)$ and $u_1=-3\gamma R\eta/\mathsf L+O(R^2)$. Substitution of $\mathbf p=\eta y/R-e_z$ cancels the two terms proportional to $3\eta^2y$. The remaining vector is $-(\gamma/\mathsf L)(y_1,y_2,-2y_3)$, to be multiplied by the phase at zero. In particular the linear term is independent of the direction used to approach zero.
b12-axis-zero-mode.Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.azimVecQ: The swirl is a multiple of $e_z\times y/R$. On the nonzero axis this vector vanishes; at the origin the additional vanishing of $\mathsf T$ at $\sigma=0$ makes the entire swirl $O(R^2)$. Hence it does not contribute to the linear field at zero.

b12-decay-orders.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.fi: Near infinity put $s_1=1-\sigma=\mathsf L/(R+\mathsf L)$. The operator $R\partial_R=-\sigma s_1\partial_{s_1}$ preserves the factor $s_1^h$, as does multiplication by $2ilR^2f'(R^2)$, which is bounded. Thus even the dependent amplitudes retain their decay order. Ordinary spatial derivatives cost a further $R^{-1}$ each; time derivatives of a fixed harmonic merely multiply by its time frequency.

b12-decay-one.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.fi: The order-one tail is compatible with the homogeneous energy space: $R^{-1}\in L^6(R>1)$, $R^{-2}\in L^2(R>1)$ and $R^{-3}\in L^2(R>1)$. It need not be in $L^2$ itself. For the residual, the combination $S^{-1}\partial_\theta W+W/2+(y\cdot\nabla)W/2$ must also be in $\mathcal H$; order-one decay alone does not establish this. The phase choice in C.1 and C.4 cancels the leading transport of the oscillatory tail.

b12-profile-dependence.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Pr: The field has two parameter dependences: the explicitly affine sum of coefficients and the common change of phase. For a key with radial index $l$ the latter gives a factor $e^{il(\mathsf k\cdot\alpha)f_*}$ and changes the dependent amplitude through $\mathcal V_l$. Both changes vanish on the cutoff ball. Outside, even the field indexed by $0$ depends on the parameter.

b12-phase-cutoff.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.st: The cutoff is identically zero near the lower endpoint of the integral, where $d\rho/\rho$ would be singular. Near infinity the integrand is exactly $d\rho/\rho$. The $C^2$ join of $\chi$ gives a $C^3$ radial phase, including at the transition radii, as required for differentiating (B.7) and (B.8) twice in space.

pdf-item-equation-B-9.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Pr: The function $f_*$ allows the logarithmic slope of the radial phase at infinity to change while leaving the field on the interior ball unaffected by the phase change. Thus the same parameter can enter the interior residual polynomially and alter the leading similarity transport of an oscillating tail. The split between these two calculations is used in B.4.
pdf-item-equation-B-9.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.mo: Writing $a=\mathsf k\cdot\alpha$, the operation changes only the phase parameter from $f$ to $f+a f_*$. The compactification length and angular order stay fixed, so the same harmonic labels and amplitude meshes can be used for all trials.
pdf-item-equation-B-9.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.st: The integral is a function of squared radius, although it is integrated in the ordinary radius. If $R>0$, differentiation with respect to $R$ gives $R\partial_R f_*(R^2)=\chi(R/(R+\mathsf L))$. This explains both the interior agreement and the logarithmic tail.
pdf-item-equation-B-9.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.af: On the cutoff ball $f_*$ and its radial derivatives vanish, so the exponential and the differential construction of the amplitudes both agree with their values at $\alpha=0$. This gives an exact affine identity for the velocity, also for its first derivatives and almost everywhere its second derivatives. It is this identity on the ball that is used in the expansion (B.57).
pdf-item-equation-B-9.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.st: For $R\le r_\chi$, the whole interval $0\le\rho\le R$ in (B.9) has $\rho/(\rho+\mathsf L)\le\sigma_\chi$. Not only is the integral zero, but its radial derivatives vanish at the transition as well, to the orders implied by $\chi\in C^2$. This matters because $\mathcal V_l$ in the velocity formulas differentiates the phase.
pdf-item-equation-B-9.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.In: Beyond the last transition of $\chi$, the difference $f_*(R^2)-\log R$ has zero derivative in $R$. The resulting addition to the phase changes its logarithmic slope by $\mathsf k\cdot\alpha$, while leaving the power $(1-\sigma)^h$ unchanged. In the squared-radius variable the tail is $\tfrac12\log\rho+C$.

b12-independent-amplitudes.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Pr: Each $W^i_\alpha$ has its own amplitude data; only the common phase varies. The formula therefore does not require identical spline meshes for the different fields. In particular a derivative with respect to $\alpha$ outside the cutoff ball also differentiates the radial phase.

b12-period-affine.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is: The operator $\mathcal T_S$ contains $S^{-1}\partial_\theta$, so affine dependence of $S^{-1}$ makes this part of the interior residual a quadratic polynomial in $\alpha$. Affine dependence of $S$ itself would introduce a denominator. In the exterior the matching change of the logarithmic radial phase cancels the leading time and similarity transport terms as in C.4.

b12-forcing-affine.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is: The force coefficient of the approximate equation is prescribed by $\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)$, whereas $\beta$ is solved for in the correction equation. The force of the corrected field is zero only when $\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)+\beta=0$. This is the finite-dimensional equation addressed by the parameter bounds (7.35)–(7.37), after the linearized inverse has controlled $\beta$.

adapted.N5-22.1.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Pr: `PressureShapeEntry.pressure` represents the scalar pressure by a center plus parameter-weighted tangent pressures, all evaluated using the phase data at the chosen parameter. The shift by half the squared speed in this passage is the paper's convention for the residual after rewriting convection; the definition evaluates the represented pressure and does not itself establish the pressure-shift identity.

If the prescribed join order in one variable is $d$, identifying the endpoint derivatives through order $d$ gives equality of the corresponding traces on adjacent pieces. In a Hermite basis the free coefficients for higher endpoint derivatives and interior polynomials remain available to fit the field. For two variables the traces are themselves polynomials in the other variable, so their equality also supplies the necessary tangential derivative matches.

b12-forcing-data.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsCompactT: Multiplying an arbitrary solenoidal field by a scalar cutoff would produce the extra divergence $\nabla\chi\cdot b$. Here support is imposed instead on the free amplitude splines before (B.7) and (B.8) construct the dependent components. With the zero origin coefficient the field is compactly supported and the divergence cancellation is unchanged.

b12-forcing-smooth.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.FieldJoint: The support is imposed on the free splines, not by multiplying the resulting field by a discontinuous characteristic function. At the last support sphere their joined traces also vanish to the orders required in (B.7) and (B.8). This is consistent with the global $C^1$ assertion for $b_i$ even at that sphere.

b12-forcing-divergence.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.keyDiverge: No projection is needed to make the represented force divergence-free: each harmonic is constructed by (B.7) or (B.8), and the divergence of each term vanishes under the shape hypotheses. The cutoff is built into the amplitudes, rather than applied afterwards to a solenoidal vector field.
b12-forcing-divergence.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.fieldClass: The force uses its own length and radial phase, but the same angular order and reflection rules. Since these are precisely the hypotheses for generator invariance of the represented fields, each force respects the common symmetries. Full $\Gamma$-invariance additionally uses the generation condition.

b12-forcing-support.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.compactFie: The last possible nonzero radial coordinate is $\sigma_i$, whose inverse image is the sphere of radius $\mathsf L_i\sigma_i/(1-\sigma_i)$. All terms, including the origin term, are zero beyond it: the free polynomials vanish there, and $\gamma=0$. The meridian square in B.3 encloses this ball, so no forcing term is omitted in treating the complement.

b12-adjoint-data.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is: The choice $h\ge3$ makes $\psi_j$ itself square integrable over the period, since its square is $O(R^{-6})$, and $y\cdot\nabla\psi_j$ has the same decay. In (7.33) the period and linearized operator can vary with $\alpha$ even though the field used to test the equation is fixed. The error in the adjoint equation is accordingly estimated uniformly.

b12-adjoint-rows.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Ad: The adjoint conditions of (7.32)–(7.34) use only $j\in\mathcal J$. For those rows the stored entries are the same for every parameter; the approximate adjoint fields are fixed as well. These identities specify the chosen rows, not the invertibility of the matrix appearing in the parameter argument.

b12-cell-rectangle.Breakdown.CellCert.CellAnalysis.IsCellBo: Revolving the rectangle and including its reflection gives the spatial set on which the cell integrals are taken. For a scalar depending only on $(r,z)$ the three-dimensional integral over the upper part is $2\pi\int_Q f(r,z)r\,dr\,dz$; if the reflected integrand is equal, the lower part contributes the same amount. The measure factor $r$ is essential in the local Gram matrices.

b12-mesh-cover.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.ActuatorSu: The square contains the meridian image of each actuator support ball: $|y|<r_*$ implies $r<r_*$ and $|z|<r_*$. Thus no actuator remains in the exterior region used in B.3. The support condition and the disjoint-interior mesh coverage are separate hypotheses.

b12-tensor-polys.Breakdown.CertCell.CellMatField.field: The displayed coefficient indexed by $(a,b)$ tests the $b$ component of $(e_a\cdot\nabla)v$. Lean's `CellMatField.frameMap` instead enumerates the matrix entries by output component then input component, so its entry `(b,a)` is the coefficient in the displayed convention. The distinction disappears on the diagonal but not for the mixed derivatives.

pdf-item-equation-B-10.Breakdown.pinValue: Each $\ell_i$ measures a direction of the first derivative, not a value of the perturbation or of its Laplacian. In particular $|\ell_i(v)|\le\|\Xi_i\|_{\mathcal H}\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H}$. The pairing is therefore defined on the weak perturbation space even though the cell tensor has jumps.
pdf-item-equation-B-10.Breakdown.CertCell.CellMatField.field: Write $G=\nabla v$ as the linear map $G e_a=(e_a\cdot\nabla)v$. Then $\langle e_b\otimes e_a,G\rangle=e_b\cdot G e_a$. In the Lean `frameMap`, $x_{ab}$ multiplies $e_a\otimes e_b$; hence the polynomial in (B.10) with indices $(a,b)$ corresponds to the stored entry $(b,a)$. With this convention the assembled tensor gives exactly the pairing in (7.11).

b12-tensor-reflection.Breakdown.CertCell.CellMatField.field: The signs come from the half-turn on the cylindrical frame: radial has sign $+$ and the other two directions sign $-$. A tensor entry acquires the product of its two signs, so it changes sign exactly when one index is radial. The label flip accounts separately for $\phi\mapsto-\phi$.

b12-tensor-support.Breakdown.CertCell.CellMatField.field: The cell boundaries can be assigned values without affecting the integral in (B.10), since they have zero volume. The test tensor is bounded with bounded support, so it belongs to $\mathcal H$; the linear constraint only uses the weak first derivative of $v$.

b12-zero-pin-gap.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is: The paper prescribes zero pins on the correction: $\ell(v)=0$. In the formal data `target` is instead the prescribed pin value of the corrected velocity. The equation `target_eq` sets it equal to the pin of $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$, so `targetGap` is identically zero and subtraction gives precisely the paper's constraint. The general linear estimate (7.18) is still proved for arbitrary $\ell(v)$.

b12-phi-representation.Breakdown.PotentialShape.cylField: The constraint potential is represented in physical meridian coordinates rather than $(\sigma,\eta)$. Its coefficients multiply $r$ and cylindrical harmonic vectors; the factor $r$ forces the represented value to vanish on the axis. The linked definition does not establish the required weak-gradient and support properties by itself.

b12-phi-error.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectBou: For a vector $x$ of coefficients, the error in the combined constraint is $\langle\nabla v,\sum_i x_i(\Xi_i-\nabla\Phi_i)\rangle_{\mathcal H}$. It is bounded by $c_\Xi |x|\|v\|_w/\sqrt{w_*}$. In B.12 one uses $x=(Y_{ji})_i$; hence the whole rounding error costs $\mathsf n_Y c_\Xi/\sqrt{w_*}$ in (B.53), without a factor counting the constraints. The separate replacement of $\Phi_i$ by a solenoidal field is estimated there in a different norm.

b12-row-polynomial-data.Breakdown.CertCell.Instance.IsRowValues: For a fixed cell and label, if the polynomial triples are $\varphi_j$ and their Hermitian Gram matrix is $H$, then $c^*Hc=\int_Q|\sum_j c_j\varphi_j|^2r\,dr\,dz$. Positivity means that no nonzero linear combination vanishes in this integral. This is the independence needed for (B.11), not an assumption that the triples are already orthogonal.

b12-row-divergence.Breakdown.CertCell.Instance.IsRowValues: The polynomial identity is the cylindrical divergence equation after multiplication by $r$: the derivative in the azimuthal direction contributes $ik_{\mathrm{rot}}\iota_1\varphi_\phi$. This is a local condition; zero extension across a cell face need not preserve distributional divergence. The row tests in (7.17) belong to $\mathcal H$, not necessarily $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{div}}$.

b12-row-gram.Breakdown.CertCell.Instance.IsRowValues: For a nonzero harmonic the average of the product of two real parts is half the real part of the Hermitian product. Angular integration gives a factor $2\pi$ and reflection doubles the upper-half integral. The resulting real Gram block is $2\pi$ times the realification of the local Hermitian matrix; at zero harmonic its factor is $4\pi$. Hence positive definiteness is inherited block by block, without a comparison between distinct cells or harmonic pairs.

b12-row-realfields.Breakdown.CertCell.RowValues.rowFieldOf: For a nonzero label the identity $\operatorname{Re}((a-ib)E_\iota\varphi)=a\operatorname{Re}(E_\iota\varphi)+b\operatorname{Im}(E_\iota\varphi)$ explains the two real generators and the factor $-i$ in `rowPartFactor`. The negative label gives their complex conjugates and adds no direction. At the zero label the triple is real and there is no imaginary generator.

pdf-item-equation-B-11.Breakdown.CertCell.RowValues.rowFieldOf: The two factors in (B.11) serve different purposes: $G^{-1/2}$ changes coordinates to an orthonormal basis of the row space, while $\sqrt{\tau_k}$ determines how strongly the corresponding component of $F$ is measured. The implementation stores the unit row and the weight separately.
pdf-item-equation-B-11.Breakdown.CertCell.RowValues.rowWeightOf: With $c=3/50$, `testWeight` stores $c\tau_k$ and `rowWeightOf` divides it by $c$, giving the weight $\tau_k$ in (7.17). For one block of common weight $\tau$, if $m$ denotes the pairings with the real generators and $G$ their Gram matrix, its contribution to $[F]^2$ is $\tau m^{\mathsf T}G^{-1}m=\tau\|P_E F\|_{\mathcal H}^2$, where $E$ is their span. This also explains why the local row matrices in B.3 can use the original polynomial generators.
pdf-item-equation-B-11.Breakdown.CertCell.Instance.rowFieldsOrt: The local Hermitian Gram matrices establish independence of the real generators after reflection. The linked orthonormality theorem takes positive definiteness of the full real Gram matrix as a hypothesis and applies the inverse-square-root identity to that matrix. It gives unit rows; multiplication by $\sqrt{\tau_k}$ in (B.11) is a separate operation.

b12-row-cap.Breakdown.CertCell.RowValues.rowWeightOf: The bound $400(1+2^{-18})$ applies to `testWeight`, namely $c\tau_k$ for $c=3/50$, because the form in (B.21) contains $c[F]^2$. Dividing by $c$ gives the bound on `rowWeightOf`, the squared length of the corresponding paper row $e_k$. Confusing these two weights would lose the factor $50/3$ in (B.22).

b12-row-orthogonality.Breakdown.CertCell.Instance.rowFieldsOrt: It is precisely orthogonality, not just the bound on each row, that yields $[F]\le c_0\|F\|_{\mathcal H}$ in (7.17). In the unit-row convention this follows by pulling the largest $\tau_k$ out of the sum of squared pairings and applying Bessel's inequality.

adapted.N5-26.1.Breakdown.PieceWeights.IsMultiplierField: The ordinary mode time derivative is imaginary, so it contributes no real part when tested against the mode itself. The multiplier instead tests the vorticity or velocity against $i\operatorname{sgn}_p$ times that mode in a rotating frame. The resulting real part is $|\Omega_p|$ times a square. The gain acts on the modes of the unknown perturbation, including those absent from the finite reference field.

adapted.N5-15.1.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.extendedCoerciveC: The coefficient energy enters from (B.21), not from the construction of the multiplier. This distinction is important for the bordered problem of Section 7: a bound for $v$ alone would leave the force coefficients uncontrolled. The assembled estimate controls the pair $(v,\beta)$ in the norm (7.14).

pdf-item-equation-B-12.Breakdown.modeVel: At a fixed $(r,z)$, write the velocity in the cylindrical frame. The components of $R_{-\phi_0}v(\theta+\theta_0,R_{\phi_0}y)$ in the frame at $y$ are precisely those of $v$ at the shifted time and angle. Thus (B.12) is ordinary Fourier projection of those three component functions; the radial and height arguments are untouched. The conjugate exponential in the average selects the stated label.
pdf-item-equation-B-12.Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.ClassSupportHo: A rotation acts on derivative tensors as well as on the argument. For the gradient the projected integrand is $R_{-\phi_0}(\nabla v)(\theta+\theta_0,R_{\phi_0}y)R_{\phi_0}$; the Hessian has two rotated input arguments. The formal mode derivatives use these averages of the supplied weak derivatives. Thus differentiation preserves the allowed label, even though the Fourier integers of individual Cartesian entries can change.

b12-harmonic-support.Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.ClassSupportHo: Applying the half-period generator twice gives invariance under rotation through twice the angle of the generator. This restricts the ordinary angular frequencies to multiples of the rotation order. One application then imposes the parity condition in (B.2). These identities hold also for the weak derivative tensors, with the rotation acting on their derivative indices. This removes forbidden Fourier labels, not the large allowed ones.

pdf-item-equation-B-13.Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.modeShiftRotat: For a fixed $r,z$, (B.13) gives $\hat v_\iota(\theta,R_\phi(r,0,z))=E_\iota(\theta,\phi)R_\phi\hat v_\iota(0,(r,0,z))$. The gradient and Hessian transform by rotating their values and inversely rotating their arguments. Thus all five squared norms in (B.16) are independent of time and angle, and their space-time integrals reduce to $2\pi\int |\cdot|^2 r\,dr\,dz$. The products in $J$ do not separately have this property; their time and angle mean is formed in B.3.

adapted.N5-27.1.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.IsAdmissibleWeak: There are two partitions or selections with different purposes. The conversion weights $\mathsf D,\mathsf Z$ are assigned to disjoint classes covering the whole lattice; the sets $\mathcal N_p$ select modes for a skew test in a particular rotating frame. ns-b3-modified-stretch-constant.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.PointCoef.wi: In (B.25) the factor $\sqrt{7/2}$ multiplies the mean-gradient product $\mathsf s_2|G||u|$ and the two Young terms with $\mathsf s_3$. Replacing it by $\mathsf c^*$ leaves the curl-square cost $\mathsf s_1$ alone. The larger constant is therefore allowed at the expense of a smaller lower bound for the unresolved density.

ns-b3-rectangle-region.Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.IsCreditPatch: The rectangle does not introduce a second copy of the trace. Its vector consists of selected axial trace moments already present in the cells along $z=0$. The energy for their estimate comes from the reflected harmonic, which is neither resolved nor eliminated, so that it can be reserved in its velocity charge in (B.28).

ns-b3-rectangle-test.Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.IsCreditPatch: For a combination $\psi_c$ of the rectangle tests, divergence of the reflected mode $u$ gives the bottom trace pairing (up to sign) as $\int_\Pi u\cdot\overline{\nabla\psi_c}\,r\,dr\,dz$, where the gradient includes the angular derivative. With the positive reserved weight $a$, put $E=\int_\Pi a|u|^2r\,dr\,dz$. Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz and the Dirichlet matrix bound give $|c^*m|^2\le E c^*Mc$ for the vector $m$ of these trace pairings. Taking $c=M^{-1}m$ gives $m^*M^{-1}m\le E$, including the trivial case $m=0$. The credit is bounded by this inverse form.

ns-b3-regional-test.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.IsOffModeCon: The polynomial comparison (B.26) acts on finitely many coordinates. For a mode not resolved in a cell we instead estimate a quadratic form on its five derivative norms. The angular relations (B.35) reduce this comparison to two norms, $|\nabla u|$ and $|u|$, with $u=\hat v_\iota$. One scalar test can then cover every perturbation and many harmonic labels at once.

ns-b3-region-coefficient-data.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.IsOffModeCon: The labels in a regional set must share the enclosures for the multiplier pieces. Membership in $N_p$ and lower bounds on $|\Omega_p(\iota)|$ determine the contributions from (B.14)–(B.16); $|k_{\mathrm{rot}}\iota_1|\ge k_0$ supplies a separate angular derivative bound. A large time frequency with $\iota_1=0$ can benefit from the multiplier but gives no positive angular gain in (B.35).
ns-b3-region-coefficient-data.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.IsExteriorCo: At infinity the four numbers replace the pointwise choice of $\mathsf t$, not the bounds on the original five coefficients. We still need the lower Hessian coefficient and the charged coefficients throughout the region. The additional bounds compare the effective gradient term with losses of orders $\rho^{-2}|u|^2$ and $\rho^{-1}|\nabla u||u|$, where $\rho=|(r,z)|$.

ns-b3-regional-cover.Breakdown.CertCell.rowRestClause_closed: For a fixed label $\iota$, a finite cover of a cell suffices: the conclusions there hold almost everywhere, and are preserved on the union. On the complement the exterior inequality concerns an integral over an entire region. Summing inequalities for overlapping regions would count some parts of the density more than once, so the cover there is a partition up to null sets.

ns-b3-charged-coefficients.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.PointCoef.wi: Subtract (B.25) with $\mathsf c^*$ and the three charges in (B.28) from the five lower coefficients of (B.16). No term being subtracted contains a second derivative of the mode, so $\mathsf f_2$ and $\mathsf f'_2$ are unchanged. The sixth coefficient $\mathsf f_{01}$ bounds a loss, not a square, which is why it is an upper bound and enters (B.36) with a minus sign.

If $b<0$, the cost of the curl terms is at most $2|b||\nabla u|^2$; if $b\ge0$, their lower bound is zero. The Hessian term supplies $\mathsf f_2(k_0-2)_+^2/r^2$ to the gradient coefficient. Thus $\mathsf f_1^*$ includes the angular gains from the second derivatives, but not yet the gain from the first derivative of $u$.
ns-b3-effective-coefficients.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.PointCoef.ve: Put $q=(k_0-1)_+^2/r^2$. For $\mathsf t\ge0$, $\mathsf t|\nabla u|^2\ge q\mathsf t|u|^2$. Transferring this part of the gradient coefficient increases the velocity coefficient by $q\mathsf t$. Taking too much would leave too little of $\mathsf f_1^*$ to bound the mixed term in (B.29).

ns-b3-b29.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.PointCoef.Pa: With $A=\mathsf f_1^*-\mathsf t$, $B=\mathsf f_0^*$ and $c=\mathsf f_{01}$, the last inequality says that the matrix with diagonal entries $A,B$ and off-diagonal entries $-c/2$ is positive semidefinite. ns-b3-exterior-shapes.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.IsExteriorCo: The square exterior is a ray exterior with inner radius $a/\max(r/\rho,z/\rho)$ in the direction $(r,z)/\rho$. The constant $2$ in place of $1/4$ in (B.31) reduces the velocity cost in (B.30) by a factor of eight and the mixed cost by $\sqrt8$.
ns-b3-exterior-shapes.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.IsDirectionR: Fixing a direction fixes a single inner radius. ns-b3-exterior-coefficient-bounds.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.IsExteriorCo: The factors $\rho^2$ and $\rho$ remove precisely the powers of radius controlled by (B.31). The velocity loss is bounded by a constant times the integral of $|u/\rho|^2$; the mixed loss is bounded by a constant times the integral of $|\nabla u||u/\rho|$. Any faster decay of the adverse coefficients can be incorporated into smaller upper bounds on the chosen exterior.

pdf-item-equation-B-30.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.IsExteriorCo: Use measure $r\,dr\,dz$ on $Z$, and put $D=\int_Z|\nabla u|^2r\,dr\,dz$, $V=\int_Z|u|^2\rho^{-2}r\,dr\,dz$. By (B.31), $V\le D/\Lambda_0$, and Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the mixed integral by $\sqrt{DV}$. Substitution into (B.36) gives a lower bound of $(\mathsf f_1^\infty-\mathsf f_0^\infty/\Lambda_0-\mathsf f_{01}^\infty/\sqrt{\Lambda_0})D$. Equation (B.30) makes this nonnegative.

ns-b3-b31.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.modeSquareIn: For the zero angular wave number the cylindrical coefficients are independent of $\phi$, but $\partial_\phi\mathbf e_r=\mathbf e_\phi$ and $\partial_\phi\mathbf e_\phi=-\mathbf e_r$. pdf-item-theorem-B-4.Breakdown.CertCell.formNegFinite: The first conclusion of B.4 precedes any calculation with the finite matrix: it ensures that the density integral can be defined as $\mathcal I^+-\mathcal I^-$. ns-b3-b4-finite.Breakdown.CertCell.formNegFinite: The conclusion concerns the sum of the negative parts of the modal and stretching terms. ns-b3-b4-global-state.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.TreeRowCondi: The condition $x_p=0$ at $v=\beta=F=0$ is essential, even though we are interested in nonzero perturbations. ns-b3-b33-error-quantifiers.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsCellFo: The numbers $\mathsf r_{\mathsf Q,j}$ are witnesses to an inequality for the chosen extension $x_{\rm g}$, not new certificate constants required to work for all perturbations. Keeping this combination avoids charging the same error twice.

pdf-item-equation-B-33.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsCellFo: There are two operations still to perform on (B.33): drop the unresolved residual integrals using (B.29), and move $\mathsf r_{\mathsf Q,0}$ to the right. ns-b3-b33-absolute-convergence.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsCellFo: The complement of the resolved set is taken separately in each cell. This justifies discarding their nonnegative sum after (B.29), even though infinitely many harmonics have no coordinates.

ns-b3-b34.Breakdown.CertCell.rowSharesOfInstance: Put $f_k=e_k/\sqrt{\tau_k}$. By (B.11) the $f_k$ are orthonormal, whereas $[F]^2=\sum_k\tau_k|\langle F,f_k\rangle_{\mathcal H}|^2$. The weights are therefore part of the row calculation in (B.34); replacing it by an unweighted projection norm would in general change the coercive estimate.
ns-b3-b34.Breakdown.CertCell.InstancePair.pairShar: The actuator term in (B.34) is a gradient pairing. ns-b3-b34.Breakdown.CertCell.creditLeavesBound_clo: One trace estimate uses the charged velocity square of $\iota^\flat$. This accounts for the factor $2$ in (B.34); it is not the factor of two from the reduction of the meridian to the quarter plane.

ns-b3-square-final-claim.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.modeSquareIn: For $\iota_1=0$ the reflected label is the original one. At $z=0$ the axial component changes sign in (B.24), so its trace is zero. These are the boundary conditions on the coordinate planes; none is imposed on the two inner sides of the square exterior.

ns-b3-negative-finite-proof.Breakdown.CertCell.formNegFinite: One need not first prove that the full signed density is integrable. This establishes $\mathcal I^-<\infty$ independently of the sign of the finite form.

adapted.N6-10.1.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.exteriorPoin: The zero harmonic of $\mathbb V$ in the rotating frame gives diagonal pairings in the perturbation labels. The fluctuation instead is estimated on the full fields before averaging: the trace-zero contraction bound and Young give separate squared gradient and velocity terms. This is why (B.25) can be summed over all harmonics without retaining a matrix of their couplings.

ns-b3-resolved-energy-bound.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsLeafVa: The Hessian and curl-gradient floors apply to the actual derivatives of the perturbation. After separating the part measured by the coefficients, the remainder of those integrals is still available. Thus the error in a model of the reference field and the truncation of the perturbation are controlled by different estimates.

ns-b3-coupling-label-rule.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.meanStretchT: The rule for the blocks is addition of the two labels: a coefficient of label $\eta$ multiplying a mode of label $\iota$ can pair with the conjugate of a mode of label $\iota+\eta$. In particular a finite harmonic model of the coefficient supplies only finitely many label differences, even though the perturbation has infinitely many harmonics.

ns-b3-resolved-model-coupling.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.EliminationC: The displayed error calculation is in the physical measure. Off the axis the basis is orthonormal for $dr\,dz$; hence $\int_Q|P|^2r\,dr\,dz\le r_2\sum_{j,l}|P_{jl}|^2$. This converts the constant coefficient error allowance into an explicit diagonal bound in the measured coordinates. On an axis cell the radial basis already includes $r$.

ns-b3-eliminated-mode.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.EliminationC: The inverse used by `turnedSource` exists for $k\ne0,\pm1$. A velocity source $s_v$ is changed to a source in the angular gradient slot by the adjoint of $r(ikI+e_z\times)^{-1}$. This is a change in the source of the pairing, not an approximation that sets the eliminated velocity to zero.

ns-b3-unresolved-absorption.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsLeafVa: After computing the resolved-polynomial couplings and treating the eliminated band, the remaining products contain at least one factor not measured by the cell vector. For a resolved harmonic their costs must be absorbed by the lower pointwise comparison for $A^{\mathsf Q,\iota}$ and the derivative-tail bounds. For an unresolved harmonic the costs are deducted from $\mathcal I_\iota$ in defining $\mathcal I_\iota^\circ$.
ns-b3-unresolved-absorption.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.offModeDensi: The residual in (B.28) is not the original energy of an unresolved mode. The stretching loss and the three extra charges have already been deducted from it. Its nonnegativity therefore leaves the deducted energy available to pay for the products and measurements assigned to that harmonic.

ns-b3-forcing-rows.Breakdown.CertCell.rowSharesOfInstance: The axial formula below is just one term of the pressure pairing. When the radial and azimuthal terms are included, the interior factor multiplying the pressure is $-\overline{\partial_r(r\varphi_r)+ik\varphi_\phi+r\partial_z\varphi_z}=0$. The remaining side pairings generally do not vanish, so only the pressure moments on the sides, not an interior expansion of pressure, are needed.

ns-b3-row-and-pairing-errors.Breakdown.CertCell.rowSharesOfInstance: The forcing term $\mathsf r_{\mathsf Q,1}$ is a form of the squared test pairings; $\mathsf r_{\mathsf Q,2}$ contains the signed actuator and pinning pairings. The latter sign is essential. Replacing that pairing by its absolute value would not recover the cancellation with the multiplier inequality and the pinning expression in (B.44).
ns-b3-row-and-pairing-errors.Breakdown.CertCell.InstancePair.pairShar: For an actuator-gradient error $e_i$, a mixed term of the form $\beta_i\langle e_i,\nabla v\rangle$ can be estimated by a positive multiple of the gradient square plus a coefficient of $|\beta_i|^2$ proportional to the weighted square of $e_i$. The former spends energy in the cell and the latter contributes to $n_b$. This explains why (B.43) deducts $n_b|\beta|^2$ from the global leaf.

ns-b3-rectangle-absorption.Breakdown.CertCell.creditLeavesBound_clo: The bottom normal trace of the absent reflected harmonic equals, up to sign, the measured axial trace of the resolved harmonic. The rectangle bound therefore uses a velocity energy that was already reserved in $a_0$ of the absent harmonic. The conjugate reflected harmonic supplies the same estimate, yielding the coefficient two in front of $\mathsf C_\Pi$.

ns-b3-b34-sum.Breakdown.CertCell.rowSharesOfInstance: For each cell and harmonic group, the pairings with the given triples are normalized by the inverse square root of the Gram matrix in (B.11), then weighted by $\tau_k$ in the squared norm. The groups have disjoint supports or orthogonal harmonics. Adding their contributions gives $[F]^2$; the normalization of (B.33) requires the factor $(3/50)/(4\pi)$.
ns-b3-b34-sum.Breakdown.CertCell.InstancePair.pairShar: The actuator and pinning pairings reassemble to the global pairings once their cellwise profile errors are included. In particular $n_b|\beta|^2$ bounds the remaining actuator error rather than multiplying the forcing measurement. The $4\pi$ factor is the conversion from the quarter-plane form to the original space-time integral.
ns-b3-b34-sum.Breakdown.CertCell.creditLeavesBound_clo: Add the rectangle forms to the sum of the cell forms, moving $\mathsf r_{\mathsf Q,0}$ to the right in (B.33). The resulting right-hand side contains precisely the left-hand side of (B.34), which is bounded by the global row and pairing terms. This is why the rectangle forms are added in (B.38), although they are paid for by energy deducted from unresolved harmonics.

ns-b3-square-component-argument.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.squareExteri: The boundary contribution on the inner square is $rg^2\partial_n\log h$ with $n$ pointing into the square. For $h=z/\rho^2$ its logarithmic derivative is $(a^2-r^2)/(a\rho^2)$ on $z=a$, $r<a$, and $2a/\rho^2$ on $r=a$, $z<a$. Interchanging $r$ and $z$ gives the signs for $h=r/\rho^2$. Thus the square completion works even for a component which is nonzero on the inner boundary.
ns-b3-square-component-argument.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.modeSquareIn: For weak modes the scalar boundary conditions are obtained by approximation, not by choosing pointwise traces of the original field. Radial convolution preserves both symmetries. For a kernel of support sufficiently small compared with $\eta$, apply the estimate on $r>a+\eta$ or $z>a+\eta$, with $z>0$. The smoothed gradient there is bounded in integral by the original gradient on the exterior extended down to $z> -\eta$. First pass to the smoothing limit, then let $\eta$ decrease to zero; the two domains tend to the required exterior up to null sets.

pdf-item-theorem-B-5.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.angularModeB: These derivative inequalities use the spatial transformation law (B.13), at fixed $\theta$. In particular their frequency is the angular wave number, independent of the rates $\nu_p(\alpha)$ used in (B.15). They apply to all the harmonics of $v$, including those not chosen in a cell or acted on by a skew multiplier.

ns-b3-b35.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.angularModeB:

abla u|^2\ge324|u|^2/r^2$ and $|

ns-b3-b36-hypotheses.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.pointwiseQua: Two different sign hypotheses are needed to turn the second-derivative energies into first-derivative energies. In the Hessian term it is the lower coefficient $\mathsf f_2$ that must be nonnegative. In the curl-gradient term it is the actual coefficient $\mathsf I'_{2,\iota}$, nonnegative by admissibility. A negative enclosure $\mathsf f'_2$ is therefore allowed, even though multiplying the angular inequality directly by that enclosure would reverse its sign.

pdf-item-equation-B-36.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.PointCoef.gr: Equation (B.36) retains all the Hessian gain in $\mathsf f_1^*$ while discarding any positive remainder in the curl square. pdf-item-equation-B-36.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.Internal.Ext: In `quad_lower` the exterior expression $\mathsf f_1^\infty|\nabla u|^2-\mathsf f_0^\infty|u|^2/\rho^2-\mathsf f_{01}^\infty|\nabla u||u|/\rho$ is subtracted from the actual form. By the exterior coefficient bounds the resulting lower form has nonnegative effective gradient and velocity coefficients and zero mixed coefficient. It passes the same scalar test with $\mathsf t=0$. This yields the pointwise lower bound used in B.6, without requiring pointwise nonnegativity of the exterior density.

ns-b3-b5-conclusion.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.offModeCondi: The regional test is independent of the unknown field. To apply it, the actual mode must satisfy the derivative inequalities, which hold almost everywhere for the weak perturbation. Thus the conclusion is almost-everywhere nonnegativity for each $\iota$ in the region's set, including on its intersection with the cell when the region is larger than that cell.

ns-b3-curl-differences.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.AngularRelat: For each pair of indices $j<l$, the estimate $|\partial_ju_l-\partial_lu_j|^2\le2(|\partial_ju_l|^2+|\partial_lu_j|^2)$ holds also for complex components. The angular derivative acts on a vector as $ikI+J$, rather than $ikI$: on the axial and circular transverse components its eigenvalues are $ik,i(k+1),i(k-1)$. Each transverse component can lose at most one unit of $|k|$. Keeping the directional derivative in this estimate will also give the extra term in (B.31).

ns-b3-gradient-commutator.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.angularModeB:
With $G=
abla u$ in Cartesian coordinates, differentiating the two rotations of $G$ gives $r(\mathbf e_\phi\cdot
abla)G=ikG+JG-GJ$, where $Jx=\mathbf e_z	imes x$. In the Frobenius norm, $|JG|,|GJ|\le|G|$. Hence $r|

ns-b3-lower-coefficients.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.pointwiseQua: The five square coefficients of the actual mode dominate the corresponding lower enclosures. ns-b3-discriminant.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.pointwiseQua: One can choose $\mathsf t$ independently of the perturbation. With $q=(k_0-1)_+^2/r^2$, $F=\mathsf f_1^*$, $B=\mathsf f_0$, maximize the concave quadratic $(F-t)(B+qt)$ on $[\max(0,-B/q),F]$ when $q>0$ and this interval is nonempty. pdf-item-theorem-B-6.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.modeRayInver: The first assertion of B.6 is an inverse-square inequality for the ray geometry and the angular mode, with no multiplier coefficients in it. pdf-item-theorem-B-6.Breakdown.CertCell.exteriorConditionSoun: We first need to know that the signed integral of $\mathcal I_\iota^\circ$ is defined, even if its positive part is infinite. ns-b3-b6-ray-claim.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.modeRayInver: The inner boundary of the ray integral may vary from ray to ray, but on each ray the boundary term is $-a|U(a)|^2$ and has the same sign. ns-b3-b6-integrated-claim.Breakdown.CertCell.exteriorConditionSoun: After (B.31) is available, the shape of $Z$ no longer enters the coefficient calculation. ns-b3-ray-density-class.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.radialRay: The harmonic projection (B.12) is an average of time translates and spatial rotations with factors of modulus one. Equation (B.13) then reduces the full spatial integrals of the squared norms to $2\pi$ times the corresponding meridian integrals.
