Integrating $(\rho|U|^2)'$ gives the boundary term $-a|U(a)|^2\le0$. The inner radius can vary with direction; no vanishing trace at that radius is required.

ns-b3-angular-radial-combination.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.modeRayInver: At a point off the axis the radial unit vector is $(r\mathbf e_r+z\mathbf e_z)/\rho$, perpendicular to $\mathbf e_\phi$. Thus $|\partial_\rho u|^2+|\mathbf e_\phi\cdot\nabla u|^2\le|\nabla u|^2$. The angular estimate has the weight $r^{-2}$, which is at least $\rho^{-2}$; after this weakening it has the same weight as the radial estimate and the constants add.

ns-b3-exterior-coefficient-signs.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.Internal.Ext: Set $s=\sqrt{\Lambda_0}$, $G=\mathsf f_1^\infty-\mathsf f_{01}^\infty/(2s)$ and $A=\mathsf f_0^\infty+s\mathsf f_{01}^\infty/2$. ns-b3-exterior-lower-bound.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.Internal.Ext: The lower bound from `quad_lower` contains only $|\nabla u|^2$, $|u|^2/\rho^2$ and their geometric mean. The first integral is finite by the perturbation hypothesis and the second by (B.31); Cauchy–Schwarz then gives finiteness of the mixed integral. This is sufficient even if some of the original higher-derivative terms have infinite positive integral.

Young's inequality with a free parameter $s>0$ gives a cost of at most $\mathsf f_{01}^\infty(1/(2s)+s/(2\Lambda_0))$ in units of the gradient integral. The minimum is at $s=\sqrt{\Lambda_0}$, the choice in the proof. It agrees with the constant obtained by applying Cauchy–Schwarz directly to the two integrals.

adapted.N6-16.1.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.signedTre: For a nonroot node its passed form occurs once on the outgoing side of its own inequality and once on the incoming side of its parent’s. Adding the inequalities cancels these forms exactly. The remaining root form is nonnegative and can be dropped, leaving the signed pivot and column lower bound.

ns-b3-attached-matrices.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.TreeStateInt: Partitioning a cell matrix into blocks does not partition its coordinates into independent problems. Off-diagonal blocks join two coordinate groups, and a block and its adjoint must be kept together to account for the real cross term. The additional matrices attached at two nodes with opposite signs are permitted because their sum in (B.38) is zero.

ns-b3-b38.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.TreeStateInt: This identity is a sum of the attached forms, not a new inequality: every cell block is included, the rectangle forms have their factor two, the global form occurs once and the auxiliary pairs cancel. Thus the later tree estimates are estimates of exactly the form used in (B.44).

ns-b3-node-data.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesRea: Let $S_\xi=\mathsf N_\xi+\sum_{\xi'}\mathsf V_{\xi'}$. The node need only certify a lower bound for $S_\xi-\mathsf V_\xi$. The simpler matrices $\mathsf H_\xi$ and $\mathsf K_\xi$ approximate its two terms from opposite sides, with separate allowances for errors. They need not be equal to the incoming and outgoing matrices.

ns-b3-b39.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesRea: The two comparisons are in opposite directions. Thus, on subtracting the outgoing bound from the incoming one, both error forms are deducted and the nonpivot $m_jx_j^2$ are added. It is the latter terms that will cancel the row errors on nonpivots.

ns-b3-b40.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesRea: Write $C=|B|+\mathsf H^\prime+\mathsf K^\prime$ for the entrywise error bound in (B.40) and put $a_j=1/\mathsf w_j$. The row test is $(Ca)_i\le m_i a_i$. By symmetry and $2|x_i x_j|\le (a_j/a_i)x_i^2+(a_i/a_j)x_j^2$, it gives $|x|^{\mathsf T}C|x|\le\sum_i m_i x_i^2$. The positive weights redistribute the required diagonal margins: for an error joining only two coordinates, making one margin smaller makes the other larger.

ns-b3-pivot-diagonal-and-slack.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesRea: At a pivot the error allowance must be paid out of the proposed positive diagonal: $p_j-m_j\ge p_{\xi,j}>0$. At a nonpivot it is paid by deducting $m_jx_j^2$ from the outgoing form, as in (B.39). Thus a variable need not have a positive margin at every node where it appears; the sum of the node estimates will require one positive pivot somewhere.

ns-b3-complex-coordinates.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesCom: At a complex pivot, $z_l=x_j\pm ix_{j\prime}$ with $j\ne j\prime$ when both components occur. Hence $|z_l|^2=x_j^2+x_{j\prime}^2$; if one component is absent, only its remaining square is present. After multiplying by $t_\xi$, each such coordinate contributes the stated amount to the real pivot coefficients. Nonpivot coordinates need not have this normalization.

ns-b3-complex-matrices.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesCom: The Hermitian residual need not be nonnegative: entrywise modulus gives $|z^*Bz|\le\sum_{l,m}|B_{lm}||z_l||z_m|$. This is a real symmetric error form in the moduli, so the weighted row bound applies exactly as for a real node. No order comparison between the complex entries themselves is used.

ns-b3-complex-node-enclosures.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesCom: Apply the two enclosures at $z=X_\xi x$ and subtract. Since $t_\xi\ge0$, the weighted row error estimate still applies after multiplication by $t_\xi$. The outgoing nonpivot deduction cancels the nonpivot part of this error, leaving scaled complex pivot and column squares, which are then expressed in the real coordinates.

ns-b3-complex-residual.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesCom: The complex analogue of a real column square is the Hermitian form $yy^*$, whose value is $|y^*z|^2$. Thus $Y^\prime Y^{\prime *}$ contributes nonnegative squares and $-YY^*$ contributes negative squares. The residual, after removing these and the proposed pivot diagonal, is estimated entrywise by moduli in (B.40).

ns-b3-complex-pivot-transfer.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesCom: For a complex column $y$ write $a+ib=\sqrt{t_\xi}\mathsf X_\xi^*y$, with $a,b$ real. Since the global vector $x$ is real, $t_\xi|y^*\mathsf X_\xi x|^2=(a^{\mathsf T}x)^2+(b^{\mathsf T}x)^2$. Killing a complex pairing generally requires two real equations. Both columns must be included in the count used to bound the codimension in Proposition B.8.

pdf-item-theorem-B-7.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.signedTre: Summing the node inequalities cancels each nonroot form against its copy at the parent. Lean retains the root form and the pivot terms and subtracts the squared column pairings. The paper assumes the root form is nonnegative, so it can drop that term in (B.41). On the common column kernel all column losses vanish. Positive pivot weights and coverage of every coordinate then give strict positivity for each nonzero vector in that kernel.
pdf-item-theorem-B-7.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.pivotCoun: The column-count condition and the pivot condition are used for different conclusions. If there are $f$ free coordinates, the common kernel of the real negative-column pairings has codimension at most $f$. The positive pivot coefficients make the root lower form strictly positive there, and the signed-tree bound transfers this to the total form. B.8 supplies the additional fact that the kernel meets the free-coordinate subspace only at zero.

ns-b3-b41.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.signedTre: With $D$ the diagonal of the accumulated positive pivots and $Y$ the matrix of negative columns, (B.41) reads $x^{\mathsf T}\mathsf N x\ge x^{\mathsf T}D x-|Y^{\mathsf T}x|^2$. In particular on any subspace orthogonal to the columns, $\mathsf N$ is strictly positive away from zero. This is the lower bound to be combined with the zero-perturbation test in Proposition B.8.

ns-b3-column-kernel-positive.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.pivotCoun: For a vector in the common kernel the only surviving terms in (B.41) are the positive pivot squares. Each coordinate has at least one strictly positive coefficient, so the sum can vanish only at zero. The formal positivity assertion is for the root lower form, which bounds the total form from below by the preceding lemma.

ns-b3-residual-matrix-identity.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.signedSla: The definition of the residual gives an exact decomposition of $H-K$ into the proposed pivot diagonal, $Y^\prime(Y^\prime)^{\mathsf T}$, $-YY^{\mathsf T}$ and $B$. The positive column squares may be dropped in a lower bound; the negative ones must be retained. Rather than assigning a sign to $B$, the proof bounds its loss by the diagonal row allowances.

ns-b3-weighted-row-proof.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.signedSla: The row-sum argument controls the residual $B$ and the two enclosure errors together. Their combined contribution to the lower estimate is at least $-|x|^{\mathsf T}(|B|+\mathsf H^\prime+\mathsf K^\prime)|x|$, hence at least $-\sum_jm_j x_j^2$ by (B.40). It is not necessary for either enclosure-error matrix to be positive semidefinite; their entries are nonnegative and the estimate is on $|x|$.

ns-b3-complex-pivot-proof.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.complexNo: The pullback of a complex squared column pairing is $t_\xi|y^*X_\xi x|^2=|a^{\mathsf T}x|^2+|b^{\mathsf T}x|^2$, with $a+ib=\sqrt{t_\xi}X_\xi^*y$. At pivots the real and imaginary parts are distinct real coordinates with coefficients of modulus one, so the squared modulus also splits into the required real pivot squares. This is why the same real tree inequality applies.

ns-b3-tree-cancellation.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.signedTre: When the inequalities (B.42) are added, a nonroot $\mathsf V_\xi$ occurs on the right at its own node and on the left at its unique parent. Only the root form remains on the right; dropping it uses its nonnegativity. The sum of all the $\mathsf N_\xi$ is the assembled form (B.38), not the matrix of a single cell.

ns-b3-strict-positivity-proof.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.pivotCoun: On the column kernel the lower bound is a sum of positive multiples of coordinate squares, and every coordinate has a pivot at some node. A nonzero vector therefore gives a strictly positive term. Strict positivity, not just nonnegativity, is needed below to exclude a nonzero free vector from the kernel.

ns-b3-b43.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.TreeRowCondi: The normalization of the global leaf is the same as that of the cell inequalities. The coefficient $-\mathsf n_b$ on $|\beta|^2$ cancels the allowance of (B.34), while the remaining two penalties become $-3\omega^2|\beta|^2/50$ and $-|\zeta|^2/1000$ on multiplication by $4\pi$. The inequality for $\mathsf A_0$ must hold on every extension of the prescribed vector.
ns-b3-b43.Breakdown.CertCell.globalForm: `globalForm` is the scalar penalty $-(c\omega^2/(4\pi)+e)|\beta|^2-|\zeta|^2/(4\pi t)$, giving (B.43) for $c=3/50$, $e=n_b$, $t=1000$. Its definition fixes the signs and normalization. The inequality that the actual global leaf is no greater than this penalty is a separate condition.

ns-b3-error-budget.Breakdown.CertCell.InstancePair.pairShar: The error from replacing $\nabla b_i$ by a surrogate is paired with the actual perturbation gradient and multiplied by $\beta_i$. Young’s inequality bounds such a product by a derivative-energy cost and a squared surrogate-error integral times $|\beta|^2$. The latter integrals, with their specified weights and the other nonnegative allowances, form the lower bound required of $\mathsf n_b$. They need not be evaluated on the perturbation.

pdf-item-theorem-B-8.Breakdown.CertCell.rowRestClause_closed: Proposition B.8 is the passage from finitely represented data and their inequalities to a bound on every admissible perturbation. It supplies (B.21), not yet (7.18); the latter follows by Lemma B.2 together with (B.20). The Lean implication has the cell, region, tree and field-data conditions as hypotheses. Neither the statement nor its proof is an enclosure of the numerical matrices of a particular certificate.

ns-b3-b8.Breakdown.CertCell.rowRestClause_closed: Fix any $\alpha\in\mathcal K$. The same supplied conditions give the lower density bound for every solution of the reference linearized equation at that parameter. Lemma B.2 combines this with the multiplier estimate to obtain (7.18); only afterwards are the bounds (7.19)–(7.21) used to transfer the estimate to the approximate profile.

ns-b3-b8-finiteness-proof.Breakdown.CertCell.rowRestClause_closed: The negative integral is finite by B.4. If the positive integral is infinite, the left side of (B.21) is $+\infty$ while its right side is finite for the given $v,\beta,F$. It is therefore enough to prove the remaining inequalities in the case where both contributions are finite.

ns-b3-finite-signed-integrals.Breakdown.CertCell.modeDensityBridge_clo: Finiteness of both sign integrals implies summability of the absolute modal integrals and integrability of the stretching term. In particular the quarter-plane expression in (B.23) can now be restricted to the cells and their complement and added back as an ordinary integral. This is the reason for disposing of the infinite-positive case first.

ns-b3-free-state-choice.Breakdown.CertCell.stateEnclosureCertifi: At this point the same prescribed vector $x_{\rm p}$ is held fixed throughout the calculation. Keeping $x_{\rm f}$ arbitrary proves (B.44) on the entire affine space of extensions. Only after this uniform bound is available will the tree select an extension; choosing the pinning variable or other free coordinates beforehand would restrict the space available to that argument.

ns-b3-cell-off-modes.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.offModeCondi: The finite cover makes the negative-part integral of the unresolved density zero for each unresolved label. The formal cover can use larger regional curl, gradient and velocity charges, with the same stretching constant, than those subtracted in the cell: this only decreases the tested form. The sum of unresolved negative-part integrals is therefore zero (`OffModesVanish`), which leaves the absolutely convergent nonnegative remainder in (B.33).

ns-b3-exterior-loss-comparison.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.offModeDensi: The original stretching loss uses $\sqrt{7/2}$; (B.28) enlarges it to $\mathsf c^*\ge\sqrt{7/2}$ and subtracts further nonnegative charges on the complement. Consequently $\mathcal I_\iota-\mathcal L_\iota\ge\mathcal I_\iota^\circ$. On bounded regions the latter is nonnegative pointwise by (B.29), whereas on unbounded regions only its integral need be nonnegative. Either estimate suffices to show that the exterior makes no negative contribution after summing the modal integrals.

ns-b3-exterior-sum-positive.Breakdown.CertCell.exteriorConditionSoun: For a fixed label, sum the regional inequalities over the partition of the complement. Since $\mathsf c^*\ge\sqrt{7/2}$ and the three exterior charges are nonnegative, (B.28) is no greater than $\mathcal I_\iota-\mathcal L(\nabla\hat v_\iota,\hat v_\iota)$. It follows that the integral of $\mathcal I_\iota$ pays for the integral of the stretching majorant for this label.
ns-b3-exterior-sum-positive.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.exteriorPoin: We are now in the case $\mathcal I^+<\infty$ and $\mathcal I^-<\infty$. By B.3, the sum of the integrals of $|\mathcal I_\iota|$ is finite. The nonnegative $\mathcal L_\iota$ on the complement has integral at most that of $\mathcal I_\iota$ for each $\iota$, so its sum is integrable as well. This permits (B.32) to be integrated and gives the nonnegative exterior contribution to (B.21).

ns-b3-sum-before-b44.Breakdown.CertCell.initialState_closed: After dropping the nonnegative unresolved residuals, add the cell bounds and move the four error terms to the right. Add the rectangle forms; (B.34) bounds the resulting error by the forcing rows, actuator and pin pairings, and $\mathsf n_b|\beta|^2$. The last term cancels with (B.43). Multiplication by $4\pi$ now puts both the density and the pairings back in their original normalization. The exterior can be included because its integral is nonnegative.

pdf-item-equation-B-44.Breakdown.CertCell.initialState_closed: Put $D$ equal to the left side of (B.21) minus its right side. By completing the square, (B.44) reads $4\pi\langle\mathsf N x_{\rm g},x_{\rm g}\rangle\le D-|\zeta-1000\ell(v)|^2/1000\le D$. It is enough to find one extension of the prescribed vector on which the form is nonnegative. The bound is available on all extensions, which is crucial for the following dimension argument.
pdf-item-equation-B-44.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.TreeStateInt: By (B.38) the cell forms, twice the rectangle forms and the global form constitute the same real quadratic form that is bounded by Lemma B.7. The auxiliary matrices used in the tree have zero total contribution. Thus no further matrix approximation is needed between the analytic inequality (B.44) and the signed tree bound.

ns-b3-find-free-coordinate.Breakdown.CertCell.stateEnclosureCertifi: The subspace $H$ from the preceding finite-dimensional argument is determined by the tree. It does not depend on the prescribed measurements. To use it for the present perturbation we must show that projecting $H$ onto the prescribed-coordinate space is onto. The zero-perturbation inequality supplies the other half of this dimension argument.

adapted.N6-20.1.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.pivotCoun: In the notation of the preceding completion argument, the count of real columns gives $\dim H\ge p$ for $p$ prescribed coordinates. The zero-input estimate gives $H\cap E_{\mathrm f}=\{0\}$, so projection onto $E_{\mathrm p}$ is injective and $\dim H\le p$. Equality makes this projection an isomorphism. The unique completion is in this particular kernel, not necessarily unique among all vectors of nonnegative form.

ns-b3-final-nonnegativity.Breakdown.CertCell.stateEnclosureCertifi: All negative column pairings vanish on the chosen extension, so its form is nonnegative. Inequality (B.44) bounds it above by the desired gap divided by $4\pi$. The choice was made only in the auxiliary coordinates; there has been no change to the perturbation or its equation. This proves (B.21) even if $\mathsf N$ is indefinite.

pdf-item-equation-B-45.Breakdown.sixthPowerGradientBound_four_t: The linked inequality is the squared vector estimate, with coefficient $4/3$. Its hypotheses are $u\in L^6$ and a weak gradient in $L^2$; neither zero divergence nor the symmetries in (7.5) are required. In B.10 it is applied at a fixed time, before integration over the period.

pdf-item-equation-B-46.Breakdown.CertReduction.energyBoundsHold: The constant in the last bound uses the same product inequality as the third: (7.48) gives $\|u\|_{L^\infty}^2\le(2\pi)^{-1}\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}\|\Delta u\|_{L^2}$. Bounding the product, instead of bounding each factor separately, gives $c_w^2=(4\pi\sqrt{w_*})^{-1}$. This saves a factor of two in the squared estimate.

pdf-item-theorem-B-9.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.ShiftNumbersBo: There are two fields associated with the centre of the parameter set: $W_0^{\mathrm a}$ is the member used in (B.9), while $W^{\mathrm r}$ is the field used to prove the inverse estimate in B.2–B.3. The latter can be chosen for ease of certification and need not be a member of the approximate family. Its difference from the centre is estimated once, and the additional variation from the centre is estimated uniformly on $\mathcal K$.
pdf-item-theorem-B-9.Breakdown.CertReduction.FrozenFormBounde: There are two contributions to the reference convection form. The one in which $W^{\mathrm r}$ differentiates $u$ reduces by incompressibility to a quadratic form in $\nabla u$ with the strain as coefficient. Only its lower bound is needed. The term in which $u$ differentiates $W^{\mathrm r}$ is bounded in absolute value with the $L^3$ norm of the full reference gradient.
pdf-item-theorem-B-9.Breakdown.CertReduction.gapTransferBridg: In (7.52) the use of the reference estimate costs $(c_1+c_0)c_{\mathrm r}\|v\|_w$ because the change of forcing is measured in both the norm and the seminorm (7.17). Thus $c_{\mathrm r}<1/(c_1+c_0)$ is needed when $c_1+c_0>0$. The inverse constant for zero constraints is then bounded by $(c_1+c_0)/(1-(c_1+c_0)c_{\mathrm r})$. The first bound of (B.48) must be sufficiently small for the chosen $c_L$ in (7.21).
pdf-item-theorem-B-9.Breakdown.CertReduction.formShiftBridgeH: A bound for the period norm in (7.19) by itself gives no bound on the supremum of the gradient energy over time. For the latter, Proposition 7.9 uses the energy identity and integrates from a phase of minimum energy. The spatial form (7.22) controls the increase between phases, so its estimate is required for each $\theta$, before time integration.
pdf-item-theorem-B-9.Breakdown.CertReduction.frozenFormBridge: The reference-form bound applies to the given model field before using any of the difference estimates. The formal statement permits the reference field to depend on the parameter; its strain and $L^3$ gradient bounds must then hold uniformly. Appendix B makes that field fixed, and a separate estimate bounds the cost of replacing it by $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$.

pdf-item-equation-B-47.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.ShiftNumbersBo: Both differences enter the transport term through their supremum norms. For the derivative term the two alternatives are $\|u\|_\infty\||\nabla Z|_{\rm op}\|_2$ and $\|u\|_6\||\nabla Z|_{\rm op}\|_3$. The paper uses the first for the fixed centre error and the second for the family variation. The choice concerns the products after the Sobolev constants are included, not a comparison of the two unweighted gradient norms.
pdf-item-equation-B-47.Breakdown.CertReduction.FrozenFormBounde: The condition $\mathbb S\ge-\mathsf s_- I$ is a lower bound for a quadratic form, not an absolute bound on its entries. In the transport pairing it is exactly the condition on the derivative of the reference field acting twice on the same vector. A bound on the full gradient in $L^3$ is required for the other pairing, with two different vectors $u$ and $\Delta u$.

ns-b4-006.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.ShiftNumbersBo: The supremum in $\theta$ of the spatial norm is taken separately for each parameter, and the same bound must hold for all parameters in $\mathcal K$. It cannot be replaced by an $L^3$ norm in space-time: the product involving $u$ is to be estimated also for a single time slice in (7.22). For the fixed centre error the parameter quantifier is redundant.
ns-b4-006.Breakdown.CertReduction.FrozenFormBounde: For a real vector $g$, $g\cdot(\nabla W^{\mathrm r})g=g\cdot\mathbb Sg$, since the skew part has zero quadratic form. Consequently $\mathbb S\ge-\mathsf s_- I$ gives exactly the derivative form bound required in the formal reference certificate. An upper bound on the strain is unnecessary for this part of the estimate.

pdf-item-equation-B-48.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.ShiftNumbersBo: Group the first budget as $A+B$, where $A=c_w\mathsf n_0^{(2)}$ and $B=(\mathsf n_0^\infty+\mathsf n_1^\infty+2\mathsf n_1^{(3)}/\sqrt3)/\sqrt{w_*}$. The third budget is $A+B/2$. Its terms multiplying $\|\nabla u\|_2\|\Delta u\|_2$ gain the factor $1/2$ from (B.46); the term $\|u\|_\infty\|\Delta u\|_2$ has already used the mixed product in the derivation of $c_w$ and is bounded by $c_w|u|_w^2$.
pdf-item-equation-B-48.Breakdown.CertReduction.FrozenFormBounde: The middle budget concerns only $W^{\mathrm r}$. The strain loss is at most $\mathsf s_-\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}^2\le(\mathsf s_-/w_*)|u|_w^2$. The remaining convection term has one gradient and one Laplacian norm, so (B.45) and the product estimate in (B.46) give the coefficient $\mathsf n_{\mathrm r}^{(3)}/\sqrt{3w_*}$.

ns-b4-008.Breakdown.CertReduction.gapTransferBridg: At fixed $\alpha$, the reference equation and the approximate-field equation use the same $S(\alpha)$, constraints and forcing fields. Hence the change in the equation is exactly the two convection terms with $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-W^{\mathrm r}$. There is no estimate of a time derivative of this difference in (7.19).
ns-b4-008.Breakdown.CertReduction.formShiftBridgeH: The form (7.22) is obtained after the contribution of the free operator has been evaluated. Its diffusion and dilation terms have the same coefficients for either convection field. Subtracting the forms thus leaves only the pairing with $-\Delta u$ of the change of convection, which can be bounded in absolute value.
ns-b4-008.Breakdown.CertReduction.frozenFormBridge: The middle inequality of (B.48) is a bound at $W^{\mathrm r}$ alone. The first and last inequalities involve the difference of the profiles, whereas this middle one requires a bound on the strain and on the full $L^3$ gradient of the reference. It is not necessary for $W^{\mathrm r}$ itself to be small.

ns-b4-009.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.ShiftNumbersBo: Here both profiles are evaluated at the same $\theta=s/S(\alpha)$ in period-one coordinates. The centre error $Z_0$ is fixed as a function of these coordinates. By (B.9), $Z_1$ is affine in $\alpha$ inside $B_{r_\chi}$ (and vanishes at $\alpha=0$); outside the ball the radial phase varies as well. The gradient norm in (B.47) must enclose the derivative of that phase, not just the affine coefficient variation.

pdf-item-equation-B-49.Breakdown.CertReduction.gapSupTermHolds_: For the transport part of the difference the pointwise bound is $|(Z\cdot\nabla)u|\le |Z||\nabla u|$. The supremum bounds on $Z_0,Z_1$ give a coefficient $(\mathsf n_0^\infty+\mathsf n_1^\infty)/\sqrt{w_*}$ in units of $|u|_w$. In the formal period estimate this coefficient is squared along with the norm.
pdf-item-equation-B-49.Breakdown.CertReduction.gapGradTermHolds: In the second inequality of (B.49), the prescribed $L^2$ gradient is multiplied by a perturbation bounded in $L^\infty$; in the third, the prescribed $L^3$ gradient is multiplied by a perturbation in $L^6$. These are the two cases of `gapGradCoeff`. The former uses both spatial derivative norms in $|u|_w$, while the latter uses only its gradient term.
pdf-item-equation-B-49.Breakdown.CertReduction.cubicWeightProdu: To obtain the squared norm bound, apply Hölder to $|\nabla Z_1|_{\mathrm{op}}^2|u|^2$ with exponents $3/2$ and $3$. The resulting factors are $\||\nabla Z_1|_{\mathrm{op}}\|_{L^3}^2$ and $\|u\|_{L^6}^2$, respectively. The latter gives the constant $4/3$ by (B.45), which becomes $2/\sqrt3$ in (B.49).

ns-b4-014.Breakdown.CertReduction.convectionIdenti: For a component $u_i$, the product rule applied to $W\cdot g$, $g=\nabla u_i$, gives the two terms $(\partial_kW_j)g_jg_k$ and $W_j(\partial_k g_j)g_k$. The equality $\partial_k g_j=\partial_jg_k$ changes the second to $\tfrac12 W_j\partial_j|g|^2$ after summation in $k$. This uses that $g$ is a gradient, and remains valid for its weak derivatives.

ns-b4-015.Breakdown.CertReduction.convectionIdenti:
The cutoff calculation applies to $g=
abla u_i$ even if $u_i
otin L^2$. Indeed $g,
abla g\in L^2$ suffice for $|g|^2\in W^{1,1}$. The vanishing integral eliminates the transport of the gradient energy; the term with the derivative of $W$ remains and gives the strain contribution.
ns-b4-015.Breakdown.CertReduction.FrozenFormBounde:
For each $i$ the remaining integral is at least $-\mathsf s_-\|
abla u_i\|_{L^2}^2$. Summation over the three components gives $-\mathsf s_-\|
abla u\|_{L^2}^2$. Since the skew part of $
abla W$ has zero quadratic form on $g$, no estimate on that part is needed for this pairing.

ns-b4-016.Breakdown.CertReduction.frozenFormBridge: The transport pairing has a signed lower bound from the negative strain. Hölder bounds the other pairing in absolute value using the spatial $L^3$ norm of $|\nabla W|_{\mathrm{op}}$. With the convection identity and the standing bounds, Lean combines both convection estimates with the nonnegative viscous and dilation terms to bound the full frozen form from below.
ns-b4-016.Breakdown.CertReduction.shiftGradTermHol: Hölder bounds the second pairing in magnitude by $\mathsf n_{\mathrm r}^{(3)}\|u\|_{L^6}\|\Delta u\|_{L^2}$. Use (B.45), then $2\sqrt{w_*}\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}\|\Delta u\|_{L^2}\le|u|_w^2$. Its cost is thus at most $\mathsf n_{\mathrm r}^{(3)}|u|_w^2/\sqrt{3w_*}$.

ns-b4-017.Breakdown.CertReduction.frozenFormBridge: In (7.22) we may discard $\|\Delta u\|_2^2+\|\nabla u\|_2^2/4$ when obtaining a lower bound. The remaining two terms are the strain contribution and the term estimated by Sobolev. The resulting bound may be negative; Proposition 7.9 controls the increase of the energy over an interval, without requiring the form to be coercive at every phase.

ns-b4-018.Breakdown.CertReduction.shiftSupTermHold: The supremum terms of (B.49), paired with $\Delta u$, give $(\mathsf n_0^\infty+\mathsf n_1^\infty)\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}\|\Delta u\|_{L^2}$. The third inequality of (B.46) gives the coefficient $(\mathsf n_0^\infty+\mathsf n_1^\infty)/(2\sqrt{w_*})$ in the form-shift estimate.
ns-b4-018.Breakdown.CertReduction.shiftGradTermHol: The $L^2$ gradient error is bounded using $\|u\|_{L^\infty}\|\Delta u\|_{L^2}\le c_w|u|_w^2$. For the $L^3$ error, apply (B.45) and the third inequality of (B.46) to get $\|u\|_{L^6}\|\Delta u\|_{L^2}\le |u|_w^2/\sqrt{3w_*}$. These give the remaining two terms in the third budget of (B.48).
ns-b4-018.Breakdown.CertReduction.formShiftBridgeH: Pairing the operator-norm bound (7.19) with $-\Delta u$ at the slice level would give the first budget of (B.48) as a sufficient coefficient. The proof instead keeps the separate terms in (B.49) until multiplying by $\|\Delta u\|_2$. It thereby gains a factor of two in the costs of transport and of the $L^3$ gradient error, but not the $L^2$ gradient error.

ns-b4-019.Breakdown.CertReduction.formShiftBridgeH: For each $u$ and $\theta$ the form at the reference is at least $-c'_3|u|_w^2$, and the change to $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ is at least $-c''_3|u|_w^2$. Adding proves (7.22). In Lean the two assertions are combined in `ExtendedFrozenBridge.profile_form`, using the inequality for the declared total form bound.

In contrast to B.11 below, the estimate does not use cancellation between angular or temporal modes.

Its integral is $\tilde a_j\int_0^1|v(\theta)|_w^2\,d\theta=\tilde a_j\|v\|_w^2$. In particular the estimate does not require a bound for $\sup_\theta|v(\theta)|_w$.

For example, even $\mathsf R$ of finite $L^2$ norm would not suffice by Cauchy–Schwarz if $v\notin L^2$. The factor $|y|$ in the norm of the ordinary remainder supplies the missing weight through Hardy; a known angular expansion permits a smaller bound for the other part.

ns-b4-028.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.RemainderBounded: Write $v\cdot\mathsf R'=(v/|y|)\cdot(|y|\mathsf R')$. The first factor has norm at most $2\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H}$ by Hardy; thus the data need to bound twice the weighted norm of the second. This is the part of the dual bound that requires no information about angular frequencies.

ns-b4-029.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalBounded: Here $k$ is the wave number of a scalar Cartesian component, not the label $\iota_1$ in (B.2). Indeed a cylindrical mode of angular number $m$ has $u_1\pm iu_2=e^{\pm i\phi}(u_r\pm iu_\phi)$, hence scalar wave numbers $m\pm1$, and its third component has number $m$. It is these scalar numbers that enter $(|k|+1/2)^{-2}$. For $|k|=1$ the resulting dual norm coefficient is $2/3$ instead of $2$.

pdf-item-theorem-B-11.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.weightedPairingI: Although the modal estimate uses a smaller weighted sum, every term in that finite sum has a strictly positive coefficient. Consequently each $|y|g$ is in $L^2$, and ordinary Hardy makes the pairing integrable. The angular gain applies to the spatially integrated pairing, not to $\iint|v\cdot\mathsf R|$ with the same constant.
pdf-item-theorem-B-11.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.dualBoundedBound: For a given decomposition the cost is $\mathsf n'+\mathsf n''$. Orthogonality is available within the represented modal field but need not hold between that field and the ordinary remainder. The linked bound in fact tests arbitrary weak-gradient slices in $L^6$ with finite period gradient energy, without a solenoidality hypothesis.

ns-b4-031.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.dualBoundedBound: An adjoint residual with dual bound $\mathsf n$ contributes at most $\mathsf n\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H}\le (\mathsf n/\sqrt{w_*})\|v\|_w$. This is the estimate used not only for $\mathsf R_{j,\alpha}$ in (B.56) but also for the transposed stretching and time-derivative terms. No $L^2$ bound for $v$ is needed.

ns-b4-033.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.weightedPairingI: Before averaging or interchanging integrals, the proof obtains $|y|\mathsf R',|y|\mathsf R''\in\mathcal H$. Thus $\iint |v\cdot\mathsf R|\le\|v/|y|\|_{\mathcal H}\||y|\mathsf R\|_{\mathcal H}<\infty$. The constant obtained here need not be the small constant $\mathsf n$; that is the object of the remaining angular calculation.

To see the extra $m$, expand the last square: its cross term is $m\eta\partial_\eta|U|^2$, whose integral is $-m\int_{-1}^1|U|^2\,d\eta$ since $U$ vanishes at the poles. The linked theorem applies this estimate to the $k$th projection of the complex horizontal component of a smooth test, without requiring the original test itself to be a single mode.
pdf-item-equation-B-50.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.m: The paper passes (B.50) to a weak function of a prescribed angular number. This follows by passing each projected estimate to the limit and bounding the sum of the projected gradient energies. It will allow a test against several angular modes at once.

ns-b4-035.Breakdown.CertCell.Internal.slice_invers: At $k=0$ the coefficient in (B.50) is $1/4$, giving $\|U/|y|\|_2\le2\|\nabla U\|_2$. The argument for $k\ne0$ uses the vanishing of a smooth mode on the axis; that vanishing is not available for $k=0$ and is not needed.

ns-b4-037.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.m: Averaging a smooth approximant against $e^{-ik\phi'}$ preserves compact support in a ball and contracts the gradient norm. It bounds the sum of all angular gradient contributions by the gradient energy; time integration is carried out separately.
ns-b4-038.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.t: The paper projects the test in time as well as angle. Integrating $\||y|B_k(\theta)\|_2^2$ over one period gives the sum of $\||y|g_{k',k}\|_2^2$ by distinctness of the time integers. This is the estimate in `timeModeSum`; it requires no time derivative of the test.

ns-b4-050.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectBou: The weights $\varpi_i$ are auxiliary positive numbers, not the energy weight $w_*$. They allow large and small tangent fields to be charged differently: the coefficient vector is divided by $\sqrt{\varpi_i}$ and the field or dual norm multiplied by it. Common rescaling of all $\varpi_i$ leaves the product of the resulting bounds unchanged (with the norm enclosures rescaled accordingly). Only the relative weights can improve it.

pdf-item-theorem-B-12.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.adjointDefectBri: Lemma B.12 gives a bound for the difference between two linear functionals of $v$, before the constraints are imposed. In (B.56) the first line is the adjoint equation defect with its auxiliary terms, the second changes the operator to the one at the actual parameter, and the third changes the represented constraint back to (7.11). Each is bounded by a multiple of the same energy norm.
pdf-item-theorem-B-12.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt: The two operator-related costs in (B.53) make up `defectSum`: the first covers the residual of the adjoint about $W_\alpha^0$ with period $S(0)$, and the second covers the remaining changes in the operator. The two replacements have different costs. For $\Xi_l-\nabla\Phi_l$ one needs a matrix norm, since $\Xi_l$ is a rounded cell polynomial and not necessarily a gradient. For $\Phi_l-\tilde\Phi_l$ integration by parts moves the derivative to $v$, allowing a norm of the vector field itself. The solenoidal $\tilde\Phi_l$ is the one used in the adjoint source and its skew flux.
pdf-item-theorem-B-12.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectBou: Smallness of the remainder alone would be meaningless if the added auxiliary terms were large. The first term of (B.53) accounts for both; the next two terms then restore the parameter-dependent operator and the original constraints. The resulting estimate controls the adjoint of the full linearized operator, not only the residual of (B.52).
pdf-item-theorem-B-12.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Ad: To use the general adjoint bound, its data must describe the same operator and constraint as (7.33). The links set the adjoint field to the represented $\psi_j$, the coupling coefficients to the row $Y_{jl}$, and the base and tangent fields to $W_\alpha^0,W_\alpha^i$. They also identify the rates in $1/S(\alpha)$ and set the fitted set empty.

pdf-item-equation-B-53.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt: All three errors $w_*\mathsf n_{\mathsf U}$, $\mathsf n_{\mathsf F}$ and $\mathsf n_{\mathsf R}$ act on the same gradient of the perturbation; they have to be added before using Cauchy–Schwarz with the Laplacian term. Treating their squares as independent would not give a justified bound. The extra terms in `defectSum` account for changes in the operator, not these same gradient errors a second time.

The last two summands have different powers of the weight because their test fields are different. The error in the potential is multiplied by $\|\Delta v\|_{\mathcal H}$, whereas the error of the rounded constraint matrices is multiplied by $\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H}$. Hence only the latter coefficient, $\mathsf n_Yc_\Xi$, is divided by $\sqrt{w_*}$.
pdf-item-equation-B-53.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectBou: The number $a_j$ is an upper bound for an operator norm on the perturbation space, uniform over $\alpha\in\mathcal K$. For example, the first square root alone is not sufficient if the inverse period or the tangent fields change appreciably. The other terms in (B.53) restore the full operator and the actual constraint, respectively.
pdf-item-equation-B-53.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Ad: The expression in (B.53) is recovered from the general formal budget by substituting the links of this represented instance. In particular, no tangent direction is fitted by a separate potential, so the sum over fitted directions is zero and the free-direction sum runs over all coordinates. The row of coupling coefficients is the one used in the constraints.

ns-b4-053.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.IsAdjointField: Although $F$ is only specified modulo gradients, its pairing with the divergence-free $\psi$ is independent of the representative: $\langle F,\psi\rangle_{\mathcal H}=\langle PF,\psi\rangle_{\mathcal H}$. This is why the pressure of the unknown correction is absent from (B.54)–(B.56). The statement still assumes $F\in\mathcal H$.

ns-b4-054.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.representationHo: The domain requires the combined expression $S^{-1}\partial_\theta v+v/2+(y\cdot\nabla)v/2-\Delta v$ to be in $\mathcal H$, not separate bounds on the time and dilation derivatives. Transposition in the weak equation avoids those additional requirements. Lean first uses a smooth compactly supported time window with translates summing to one: integrating its derivative against a periodic integrand gives zero, leaving the period pairing (B.54).

ns-b4-057.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.testFieldDensity: Cutting off $\psi$ itself can destroy solenoidality, so for the weak solenoidal equation the formal proof uses a curl potential $A$ and takes $\operatorname{curl}(\chi A)=\chi\psi+\nabla\chi\times A$. The latter term is supported on the cutoff annulus. The decay assumptions allow convergence of the test and its gradient as well as of its time derivative and radial derivative in the norms needed for (B.54); smoothing gives admissible compact tests.

pdf-item-equation-B-55.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Internal.Potenti: Both sides of (B.55) extend from compact tests in the gradient norm. The matrix pairing uses $A\in L^2$ and the velocity pairing uses $\operatorname{div}A^{\mathsf T}\in L^{6/5}$ with Sobolev. The linked weak pairing instead uses $|y|\operatorname{div}A^{\mathsf T}\in L^2$ with Hardy, together with local integrability and the weak divergence identity. Neither argument requires $v\in L^2$.

The formal `pair_flux` verifies the hypotheses of the weak pairing from decay: if $A$ and $|y|\operatorname{div}A^{\mathsf T}$ are bounded by $B(1+|y|)^{-a}$ with $2a>3$, both are in $L^2$. The condition concerns the divergence with one factor of $|y|$, not its unweighted $L^2$ norm. This allows the indicated singularity at the origin.

ns-b4-059.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Internal.Potenti: For $A=q_j I$, the right side of (B.55) is $-\int q_j\operatorname{div}v=0$. This removes the auxiliary pressure from the defect bound, not from the definition of the strong residual. In B.13 the pairing will instead be restricted to a ball, where the same cancellation cannot be made without a boundary condition.

ns-b4-060.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Internal.transpo: The decomposition does not expand the radial phase in powers of $\alpha$. It is exact at the current phase: $W_\alpha^{\rm a}-W_\alpha^0=\sum_i\alpha_iW_\alpha^i$. No term involving $W_\alpha^0-W_0^0$ has to be added to (B.56).
ns-b4-060.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Ad: The base and tangent fields in the adjoint equation and in the offset calculation must come from the same represented family. `centre_eq` and `free_eq` use the phase at $\alpha$; `centrePeriod_eq` and `periodRate_eq` identify the reciprocal period and its affine coefficients with those in B.13. The matching-ball restriction in B.13, not these links, is what permits evaluating the fields at $\alpha=0$.

ns-b4-061.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Internal.Potenti: Solve (B.52) for the first line. The three auxiliary terms to be paired with $v$ are then $-\Delta\mathsf G_j$, $-w_*\Delta\mathsf U_j$ and $+\operatorname{div}\mathsf F_j^{\mathsf T}$. Moving two, one and one spatial derivatives respectively gives the signs $-,+,-$ in the first line of (B.56); the pressure pairing vanishes. The linked slice identity formalizes this part of the calculation.
ns-b4-061.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Internal.transpo: The inverse-period change contributes $-(\varsigma\cdot\alpha)\iint v\cdot\partial_\theta\psi$ because it is the adjoint of the time derivative. ns-b4-066.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.pinChargeHolds_p: It is the norm of the map $x\mapsto\sum_lx_l(\Xi_l-\nabla\Phi_l)$ that is bounded by $c_\Xi$. Inserting the row $(Y_{jl})_l$ in this bound gives $\mathsf n_Yc_\Xi$ in one step. There is no need to sum the norms of the individual errors, which would discard possible cancellations in that row.

ns-b4-067.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.adjointDefectBri: The final inequality has the form $|\langle F,\psi\rangle_{\mathcal H}-(Y(\alpha)\ell(v))_j|\le a_j\|v\|_w$. ns-b4-068.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.of: One could try to expand $F_\alpha^{\rm a}$ on the whole space, but a change of period changes the logarithmic radial phase at infinity (C.4). pdf-item-equation-B-57.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.qu: The second-order part of the interior residual comes only from multiplying the affine inverse period by $\partial_\theta W_\alpha^{\rm a}$, from convection, and from the gradient of the kinetic energy. In particular the centre and linear coefficients subtract the residual pairing from the corresponding force coefficient. For the quadratic part the force is affine, so its coefficient is just $-\langle F^{(ii')},\psi_j\rangle_\chi$.
pdf-item-theorem-B-13.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.of: The target polynomial has no constant or quadratic terms, and its linear coefficients vanish except for $d_j$ at $i=j$. Hence if the centre of the diagonal interval is exactly $d_j$, its contribution to the error is still $\tilde{\mathsf C}^1_{jj}\hat\varrho_j$. It is the displacement from the target interval, not the size of the original coefficient, that enters the bound.
pdf-item-theorem-B-13.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.co: The monomial estimates use an enclosing box of the parameter set. For distinct $i,i'\notin\mathcal J$ one could use $|d_i d_{i'}\alpha_i\alpha_{i'}|\le\varrho_*^2/2$ from the sum of their two squares; (B.59) instead uses the simpler product of the individual radii. Thus the budget is sufficient, not necessarily the supremum of the response error on $\mathcal K$.
pdf-item-theorem-B-13.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.of: Write the ball response as $P_j(\alpha)=V_j\cdot\beta^{\rm a}(\alpha)-\langle F_\alpha^{\rm a},\psi_j\rangle_\chi$. Then the quantity to bound in (7.34) is $P_j(\alpha)-d_j\alpha_j-\langle F_\alpha^{\rm a}\mathbf1_{|y|>r_\chi},\psi_j\mathbf1_{|y|>r_\chi}\rangle_{\mathcal H}$, since $\bar\ell=0$. The polynomial enclosures are used only for the first difference.

ns-b4-074.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is: The exterior residual is the actual $F_\alpha^{\rm a}$, including the pressure-gradient representative and the parameter-dependent phase. Its restricted $\mathcal H$ norm must be bounded for all parameters. The other factor is the exterior norm of the fixed test $\psi_j$, so a large residual where the adjoint is small may still give a small exterior pairing.

pdf-item-equation-B-59.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.of: A bound on the absolute response itself would also charge the term $d_j\alpha_j$ needed for the Newton update. Instead the diagonal linear coefficient is centered at $d_j$ and the other coefficients at zero. The sum in (B.59) encloses the remainder after these subtractions, which is the approximate-family part of $-d_j\alpha'_j$ in (7.35).

ns-b4-076.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.co: On the selected coordinates, (7.29) gives the individual radii $\varrho_i$. On the other coordinates it bounds the Euclidean norm of $(d_i\alpha_i)_{i\notin\mathcal J}$, hence also each $|d_i\alpha_i|$ by $\varrho_*$. Dividing by $|d_i|$ gives the second radius; it is essential that $d_i\ne0$. The formal definition writes $|\varrho_*|$, equal to $\varrho_*$ under the sign assumption.

ns-b4-077.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.of: Equation (7.34) is an enclosure of the approximate-family contribution to the new scaled coordinate, not the whole coordinate. In (7.35) one still needs the quadratic pairing, the linear adjoint defect, and the difference of the force pairings from $V_j$. The coordinates outside $\mathcal J$ are estimated by (7.36)–(7.37), without the ball polynomial for an adjoint row.

ns-b4-078.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.ba: On the open ball the correction to the radial phase is identically zero, so its derivatives vanish there as well. One may freeze the phase before taking derivatives in the residual. The boundary sphere has measure zero in the ball pairing, so no expansion across the transition of the radial phase is needed.

ns-b4-079.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.ba: The representation uses the phase in both the factors $E_{\iota,l}$ and the differential operators $\mathcal V_l$. Equality of the phases with their derivatives consequently gives equality of the represented velocity, gradient, second derivatives, pressure and pressure gradient. These are all needed to substitute into the residual; agreement only of the velocity values would not suffice.

ns-b4-080.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.In: Because $S(\alpha)^{-1}$, not $S(\alpha)$, is affine, all terms of the residual after substitution have degree at most two: the time coefficient multiplies an affine time derivative, and the convection and kinetic energy multiply affine velocities. Spatial differentiation does not change the degree. This is an exact polynomial on the matching ball, with no neglected third-order term.

ns-b4-081.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.of: The linked identity computes the response on the ball exactly. The full expression here is obtained by subtracting $d_j\alpha_j$ from its linear part and subtracting the actual exterior pairing. The latter is the only part of the response not expressed by the enclosed polynomial coefficients.

adapted.N6-31.1.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.CertificateCla: These conditions concern the parts of the analytic argument not supplied by the local coercivity inequality alone. For example the two residual budgets enter the first step of (7.59); the frozen-form and smallness conditions enter its second step; (7.28) prevents cancellation of the whole profile. Condition (7.26), unused in the paper's Schauder argument, is used for the fixed-parameter contraction in Lean. All must hold for the same family.

b4-prop-b14.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.isExtendedCert: Proposition B.14 replaces the analytic estimates of Section 7 by conditions on represented fields and cell data. It does not construct a new approximation: the same fields, force coefficients and parameter set are used in the analytic certificate. The linked theorem returns an `IsExtendedCertificate` for those data with a decay constant obtained from their representation; existence of admissible numerical data is not its conclusion.
b4-prop-b14.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.CellSystemCond: The conditions must hold for one common choice of fields and numbers. For instance, `offset_expansion` encloses the residual of the profile whose base and tangent fields occur in `adjoint_links`, and the same constraints occur in the coercivity and adjoint inequalities. This prevents combining individually valid estimates for different approximate families.

ns-b4-087.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.isExtendedCert: The conclusion supplies the hypotheses of Theorem 7.1, not its solution. The theorem will solve the constrained correction problem with the certified inverse estimate, choose the parameter using the adjoint and stiff-coordinate enclosures, and use (7.28) to exclude the zero profile. The formal assembly likewise establishes the certificate predicate; the profile construction is a subsequent theorem.

adapted.N6-32.1.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.isExtendedCert: The assembly theorem changes the hypotheses from cell data and their enclosures to the analytic certificate. It does not change the fitted fields in order to satisfy them: the residual, force fields, pins and adjoints are those of the same instance. The existential decay bound supplies a constant for the represented fields. From this point the existence proof uses the analytic inequalities of Section 7.

adapted.N5-15.2.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.breakdownOnSpa: The companion's linked theorem concludes the two global nonexistence statements from a common instance of `CellSystemCondition`, using the weak-profile theorem and the corresponding whole-space and torus implications. It does not claim the same-profile two-sided rate or the local error estimate in Theorem 1.1; the quantitative smooth torus trajectory is a separate open target. The numerical cell-system hypothesis is not discharged by the theorem.

ns-b4-094.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.CellSystemCond: The upper bounds on $M$ and $\varepsilon$ restrict the permitted correction radius before a numerical certificate is verified. Indeed (7.25) bounds $M$, and (7.27) gives $2\varepsilon\le\sqrt{w_*}M$ even without the other positive costs. The formal unresolved-mode and exterior conditions allow any stretching constant at least $\sqrt{7/2}$, subject to their remaining inequalities.

adapted.N6-39.1.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.shapeInfoF: The harmonic representation is complex-valued for convenience, while the velocity is real. `shapeInfoField` evaluates the complex field at the given time and point and takes its real part. The parameters and coefficients describing the numerical fit are supplied data, not determined by this definition.

ac-048.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.fieldClass: Writing $W(\theta,y)=\bar W(\bar S\theta,y)$, the generator identity reads $W(\theta+1/2,R_{\pi/19}y)=R_{\pi/19}W(\theta,y)$. Replacing $y$ by $R_{-\pi/19}y$ and returning to $s=\bar S\theta$ gives the half-period relation in the paper. Thus the sign of the rotation in the argument is fixed by the vector symmetry, not by the sense of either individual travelling pattern.

adapted.N6-42.1.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.fi: The exponent $h=1$ prescribes the leading inverse-radius decay; differentiating in space yields the corresponding extra powers under the radial phase and degree conditions. The linked field-decay theorem verifies these bounds for the represented field under its structural hypotheses. A decay constant for the fitted coefficients must be controlled using the actual supplied data.

ac-051.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.fi: The decay bound permits a leading term of size $R^{-1}$ with a logarithmically oscillating factor. Such a term can be compatible with a finite Eulerian limit away from the origin, as explained below, but the linked upper bound does not imply either a leading coefficient or an Eulerian limit by itself.

ac-049.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.logPhaseIs: For $f(\rho)=A\log(1+\rho/r_c^2)$ one has $\rho^j|f^{(j)}(\rho)|=|A|(j-1)!(\rho/(r_c^2+\rho))^j$ for $j=1,2,3$. These are bounded by $|A|(j-1)!$ since $r_c>0$. Thus the phase grows logarithmically but meets exactly the derivative conditions of B.1.

ac-037.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.keyPhase: At fixed $x\ne0$, the substitution (1.4) gives exactly $\log((T-t)+|x|^2/r_c^2)-\log T$ in the square brackets. The cancellation of the two $\log(T-t)$ terms explains the phase choice. A pointwise Eulerian limit still requires the leading meridian amplitudes to have the asymptotics stated below; the bound (7.38) for the corrected field is not such an expansion.

ac-038.Breakdown.SimilarityResidual: For a solenoidal smooth field, $-\Delta W=\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}W$. Also $(W\cdot\nabla)W=(\operatorname{curl}W)\times W+\nabla(|W|^2/2)$. Substituting both identities into (1.2) gives the curl formulation, with the kinetic-energy gradient absorbed into $H$. `SimilarityResidual` uses the original advection and diffusion form.
ac-038.Breakdown.Coercive.Internal.TestDensityP: For any smooth vector field, $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}W=\nabla\operatorname{div}W-\Delta W$. In (C.1) the second displayed equation sets the first term on the right to zero. The linked lemma is the solenoidal specialization of this identity; it explains why the diffusion term in the residual of (C.1) is the positive double curl.

ac-039.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.Internal.Rem: At a fixed point set $M=DW(y)$ and $x=W(y)$. The linked identity, tested against every vector $\psi$, is $Mx-(\operatorname{curl}W)\times x=M^Tx$. The chain rule gives $M^Tx=\nabla(|W|^2/2)$. Hence the pressure in the curl formulation is $q+|W|^2/2$, with the plus sign.

adapted.N6-46.1.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.defect_l: The norm is that of a selected residual representative on the whole period and all of space. If one adds a gradient to that representative the projected equation is unchanged, but the norm entering the inverse budget need not be unchanged. `defect_l2` bounds this selected field by $\delta(\alpha)$ at each parameter. The further bound by $\delta_{\max}$ is used when one common estimate is needed for the whole family.
adapted.N6-46.1.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.defect_r: The row bound controls the vector of weighted residual pairings, not the individual coefficients of the auxiliary force. It is possible to have $[F]=0$ and $\|F\|_{\mathcal H}>0$ when the residual is orthogonal to every row. The separate inequality $[F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}]\le\delta_0(\alpha)$ preserves that information in (7.24); the quadratic trial, for which no comparable directional information is given, uses the general bound (7.17).

ac-043.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsStrong: The differential expression in (C.2) is the linearization at the current profile. The formal strong right-hand side also allows the actuator forcing and the gradient of pressure: its diffusion term is minus the Hessian trace, using solenoidality to replace $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}v$ by $-\Delta v$. In Appendix C the expression is tested in a finite space to find an approximate field; in Appendix B its cellwise pairings are estimated for arbitrary perturbations of the reference field.
ac-043.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.coupling: Writing $\omega=\operatorname{curl}W$ and $\delta\omega=\operatorname{curl}v$, the first variation of $\omega\times W$ is $\delta\omega\times W+\omega\times v$. These are the two terms of `couplingField` once the supplied gradient is identified with $\nabla v$. Both are needed in the momentum rows of the linearized equation.
ac-043.Breakdown.Coercive.Internal.TestDensityP: The vector identity is $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}v=\nabla\operatorname{div}v-\Delta v$. On solenoidal smooth fields the divergence term vanishes, so the diffusion is $-\Delta v$. The formal identity is proved for smooth fields without imposing solenoidality; that additional restriction is what gives the expression here.

adapted.N6-52.1.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.af: At a fixed phase the represented field is the center plus $\sum_i\alpha_i$ times the corresponding tangent fields, evaluated at the same phase. In the region where $f_*=0$, the phase correction in (B.9) disappears and gives this affine representation. `affineField` defines the latter expression; its agreement with the phase-dependent field on the ball needs a separate identity.

adapted.N6-53.1.Breakdown.PieceWeights.frameFreq: For $j=2\iota_2-\iota_1$, the two frequencies at the trial period are $2\pi j/S(\alpha)\pm2\pi\iota_1/\bar S$. The larger absolute value is $2\pi(|j|/S(\alpha)+|\iota_1|/\bar S)$, attained by choosing a sign for which the summands agree in sign. The same choice works for every positive trial period. Thus if $S(\alpha)\le S_{\max}$, this modulus is at least $\min(1,\bar S/S_{\max})$ times the central maximum. This explains how a lower bound can persist under period changes; admissibility still has to be checked on the actual selected sets.
